meta.title: Harness Lab v2: The Agentic SDLC Program
meta.intro: From using agents to building the agentic SDLC: a hands-on program for every engineer, the platform team and the people who lead them.
meta.updated: Updated 26 September 2026. 20 modules in four tracks plus a start module and a capstone. 107 videos (18 transcript-verified), about 14.6 hours of core viewing, 63 labs, 117 readings and 70 knowledge checks.

rules.title: PHI never enters a prompt.
rules.body: Agents see code, docs and synthetic or factory-seeded data only. That includes logs, alerts, screenshots and pasted Slack threads.

rules.title: Two lanes.
rules.body: Lane A is code-only work on synthetic data, where any approved tool is allowed, including cloud agents, routines and Fable. Lane B is PHI-adjacent work: Claude Code CLI or Desktop local under the BAA with ZDR, or the Agent SDK in our own pod, with no connectors.

rules.title: The requester never approves their own agent’s PR.
rules.body: You initiated the change, so approval must come from a different identity. This is what SOC 2 CC8.1 asks for.

rules.title: Agents open PRs. Pipelines deploy.
rules.body: No agent holds deploy credentials, including the incident agent that found the fix.

rules.title: You own every line you merge.
rules.body: Never file a PR you haven’t read. Small PRs, with context and evidence.

rules.title: Tokens are never a performance metric.
rules.body: No usage leaderboards. Measure what people ship and how it holds up.

rules.title: Fix the harness on the second repeat.
rules.body: When an agent makes the same mistake twice, add a lint rule, test, hook or context line. Don’t just re-prompt.

modules.title: Your first hour with a coding agent

keyIdeas.title: Watch the loop, not the last message
keyIdeas.body: A coding agent runs tools in a loop to reach a goal (Simon Willison’s definition): it reads files, plans, acts by editing files or running commands, checks the result and goes round again until it thinks it is done. Claude Code’s docs call the phases gather context, take action and verify results. In your first hour, watch each step: in Claude Code, `Ctrl+O` opens the full transcript of tool calls and output, and `Esc` stops the agent mid-step without losing context, so you can redirect it. Chapter 2, How AI coding agents work, explains what happens inside the loop.

keyIdeas.title: Practice where mistakes are free
keyIdeas.body: Use a throwaway clone or a new branch, run the tests, and commit first so the tree is clean. Then `git diff` shows only the agent’s work, and git can undo all of it. Use fake data only. At Rhino this is not optional: PHI never enters a prompt, so practice on synthetic or factory-seeded data, never on real data, production logs or screenshots.

keyIdeas.title: Start in the mode that asks
keyIdeas.body: Every agent lets you choose what it may do without asking you. Claude Code’s main modes are Manual (config value `default`: it asks before file edits and most commands), `acceptEdits`, `plan` and `auto` (a separate classifier model reviews actions instead of you), and `Shift+Tab` cycles them; the status bar shows the one you are in. Newer versions start terminal sessions in auto mode unless your settings or your organization choose another mode, so start your first sessions with `claude --permission-mode manual` and see every action. In Codex CLI, `/permissions` sets the same choice. Chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer, covers auto mode and sandboxes.

keyIdeas.title: Read the prompt before you say yes
keyIdeas.body: A permission prompt is the agent showing you its next action, so read the exact command. In Anthropic’s test with 1,053 paid testers (vendor data, Aug 2026), people blocked a dangerous command swapped into a prompt only 13.6% of the time, and about 5% after 50 or more earlier prompts. In Claude Code, `Tab` on Yes or No adds a comment, so a No can tell the agent what to do instead. “Yes, and don’t ask again” on a shell command saves a rule for the whole repository in `.claude/settings.local.json`, for every future session.

keyIdeas.title: The diff is the truth; the summary is a claim
keyIdeas.body: “Done, all tests pass” is what the agent says. The diff is what changed. Read every line with `/diff` in Claude Code, or `git diff` with any agent, and ask the agent to explain any line you could not explain yourself. Then undo freely: `Esc` twice (with an empty prompt) or `/rewind` restores the code, the conversation or both to an earlier prompt. Checkpoints track only edits made by the agent’s file tools, not changes made by shell commands such as `npm install`, `mv` or `rm`, so git stays your real undo. Cursor’s agent checkpoints have the same limit.

keyIdeas.title: Vibe coding is not agentic engineering
keyIdeas.body: Vibe coding means not reviewing the code (Addy Osmani, Feb 2026). Simon Willison’s test: it is fine when you are the only person a bug can hurt, and wrong the moment it can hurt someone else. Agentic engineering keeps the professional quality bar while agents do the typing, and you stay responsible for your software (Andrej Karpathy, Apr 2026). Osmani’s version: the AI does the implementation, and the human owns the architecture, the quality and the correctness. In SWE-chat, agents wrote almost all the committed code in 41% of sessions. At Rhino, anything you merge is agentic engineering: you own every line you merge.

labs.title: First task, start to undo
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): install Claude Code (`curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS, Linux and WSL, or `brew install --cask claude-code`; the quickstart covers Windows) and check it with `claude --version`. Clone a small repo that has tests, such as a side project or a small open-source app, run the tests and commit, so `git status` is clean. Start with `claude --permission-mode manual` and ask: “Explain this project and how to run its tests.” Then give one small task with a check, for example: “Reject an empty title with a clear error. Add a test that fails first, then run the tests.” Write down each step you see: read, plan, act, check. Answer every prompt yourself, and decline one with a comment (`Tab` on No) to see how the agent adapts. Read `/diff` line by line and mark each line keep, change or cut. Undo with `Esc` twice and Restore code, then run `git status`: anything still changed came from a shell command, so clean it up with `git restore`, and with `git clean` after a dry run with `-n`. Using another agent? The steps are the same. At Rhino: work on a fresh branch of an FCP repo with factory-seeded data only.
labs.output: A one-page log with the loop steps, each prompt and your answer, your line marks, and a clean git status

labs.title: Vibe it, then engineer it
labs.body: Solo (about 40 min): build the same small feature twice, on two branches of your practice repo. FE example: a React list that shows an empty state when there are no items. BE example: a Django endpoint that returns 400 when a required field is empty. Round one, vibe coding: one sentence, `acceptEdits` mode, don’t open the code, stop when it seems to work. Round two, agentic engineering: Manual mode, ask for a short plan first, then a failing test and a test run, then read the diff and ask the agent to explain two lines you would not have written. Compare the two diffs: size, tests, anything you would fix before review, and which one you could explain to a reviewer line by line.
labs.output: A half-page comparison of the two diffs, with the one you would merge and why

labs.title: Your permission ledger
labs.body: Solo (about 30 min): in Manual mode, run one more small task and log every permission prompt: the tool, the exact command and your answer. Sort each one into approve once, allow always in this repo (a test or read-only command you trust), or always ask me (push, delete, installing a new package, anything that reaches the network). Then open `/permissions` and `.claude/settings.local.json` to see the rules your “don’t ask again” answers saved, and delete any rule you would not want forever. In another agent, find the same setting, for example `/permissions` in Codex CLI.
labs.output: A prompt ledger and a settings file you have read and trimmed

checks.q: The agent says “Done, all tests pass.” What do you check before you believe it?
checks.a: The diff, every line, and the test output itself. The summary is a claim and the diff is what changed. In SWE-chat, only 44% of agent-written code survived into commits.

checks.q: You pressed Esc twice and restored the code, but `git status` still shows changes. Why?
checks.a: Checkpoints track only edits made by the agent’s file tools. Changes from shell commands, such as an install, a code generator, `mv` or `rm`, are not tracked. Git undoes those.

checks.q: Newer versions start in auto mode. Why start your first sessions in Manual mode?
checks.a: To see every action and learn what normal looks like before a classifier decides for you. And read each prompt: in Anthropic’s test, people blocked a dangerous command in a prompt only 13.6% of the time.

checks.q: When is vibe coding fine, and when is it not?
checks.a: It is fine for a prototype or a tool where only you get hurt by a bug. It is not fine for code other people depend on: that needs agentic engineering, where you own the design, the review and every line you merge.

watchOut: “Yes, and don’t ask again” on a shell command saves a rule for the whole repository and every future session. Use it for your test command, never for `git push` or `rm`.

Clicking Yes without reading. In Anthropic’s test, people blocked about 17% of dangerous commands early in a session and about 5% after 50 or more prompts. If you are clicking through, stop and fix the setup instead.
Trusting rewind alone. Checkpoints skip changes made by shell commands and are not version control. Commit before you start.
Real data in a practice session. PHI never enters a prompt, and that includes logs, screenshots and pasted threads. Practice on synthetic or factory-seeded data.
modules.watchTime: 24 min core, 42 min with electives
modules.goal: Run a coding agent for the first time, on purpose and safely: install it, give it one small task in a practice repo, watch its loop, answer its permission prompts, read the diff and undo it. Learn the line between vibe coding and agentic engineering, so every chapter after this one starts on the right side of it.
modules.why: Agents write code fast, and much of it does not last. In SWE-chat’s 6,000 real sessions from open-source developers (one study, Apr 2026), only 44% of the code agents produced survived into commits, and users pushed back in 44% of turns. Anthropic’s study of about 400,000 Claude Code sessions (vendor data, Jun 2026) found that success depends on how well the person understands the problem, not on coding training: sessions rated novice reached verified success 15% of the time, against 28 to 33% for intermediate and expert sessions, and novices abandoned troubled sessions far more often (19% against 5 to 7%). The first hour sets the habits that close that gap: small tasks, eyes on every step, the diff over the summary, and undo without fear.

shipIt.title: Your first-hour log
shipIt.body: Show a teammate your log and your comparison: one prompt you declined and why, one line you would have missed without reading the diff, and the undo that worked. The chapters after this one build on these habits.

modules.title: How AI coding agents work

keyIdeas.title: A model inside a harness
keyIdeas.body: The model reads tokens (chunks of text; Claude’s tokenizer since Opus 4.7 makes about 30% more tokens than older models for the same text) and predicts the next one. It cannot open a file, run a test or remember last week. The harness around it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI) sends it the system prompt, your messages and tool results, runs the tools it asks for, and repeats: gather context, act, verify, until the task is done or you press Esc. A tool call is structured text the model writes; the harness decides whether to run it, which is why permissions work (chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer). The weights never change while you work, so anything it “remembers” between sessions came from a file the harness loads, such as CLAUDE.md or auto memory.

keyIdeas.title: The context window is working memory
keyIdeas.body: Everything the model knows about your task sits in its context window: system prompt, CLAUDE.md, tool and skill lists, your prompt, every file it read and every command output. In the Claude Code docs’ walkthrough (representative numbers) about 7,850 tokens load before you type, four file reads add 6,900, and a subagent that read 6,100 tokens of files hands back a 420-token summary. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5 have a 1M-token window and Claude Code auto-compacts at about 967K by default, but quality drops as the window fills, above all with failed attempts. Compaction swaps the conversation for a summary: requests, changed files, errors and pending work survive; full tool outputs and early detailed instructions may not. Keep lasting rules in CLAUDE.md, look with /context, /clear between tasks, /compact with a focus before a long new step, and send big reads to a subagent (chapter 6, Give the agent the right context). Summaries cost detail: in a Towards AI talk (Aug 2026), keeping the full history recovered details 95% of the time, against 32% after summarizing.

keyIdeas.title: Same prompt, different run
keyIdeas.body: The model samples each token from a probability distribution, so two runs can split on the first word and drift further with every step of a long loop. You can’t turn this off: on Claude Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 a non-default temperature returns an error. METR runs every task 6 times; on tasks of 90 minutes to 3 hours, GPT-5 succeeded every time on about a third, failed every time on a third, and was mixed on the rest. So judge by several runs. Anthropic’s eval guide separates pass@k (at least one of k runs works) from pass^k (all k work): at 75% per run, three in a row happens only 42% of the time. Work that runs unattended needs pass^k.

keyIdeas.title: Model and effort are dials
keyIdeas.body: A model spends a roughly fixed amount of compute per token, so it thinks by writing more tokens (Karpathy). Effort sets how much it writes across thinking, tool calls and replies: low, medium, high, xhigh or max. In Claude Code the default is Opus 5.5 at medium effort; change it with /model and /effort, or put “ultrathink” in one prompt for a deeper turn. List prices per million input and output tokens (Sep 2026): Haiku 4.5 $1 and $5, Sonnet 5 $2 and $10, Opus 5.5 $4 and $20, Fable 5.1 $10 and $50. Choose the cheapest per successful result, not per token: in an Anthropic example, Sonnet and Opus finished a simple code-fix eval sooner than Haiku because they needed fewer turns (vendor example). Re-test your prompts on every new model and pin versions until you have. At Rhino, Fable 5.1 is Lane A only: it needs 30-day retention and isn’t available under ZDR.

keyIdeas.title: Time horizon is task difficulty, not run time
keyIdeas.body: METR’s time horizon is the length of task, in skilled-human hours, that an agent completes at a given success rate, on self-contained, well-specified, auto-graded software, ML and security tasks. The 50% and 80% lines are far apart: Claude Opus 4.6 is about 12 hours at 50% (confidence interval 5.3 to 60 hours) but about 70 minutes at 80%; Claude Mythos Preview (early) is about 17.4 hours against 3.1. The horizon has doubled about every 131 days since 2023 (89 days since 2024), METR calls measurements above 16 hours unreliable, and Opus 5.5 has no public horizon yet (METR calls it an incremental, on-trend step over Fable 5.1, Sep 2026). Read a 2-hour task as what a low-context new hire could finish in 2 hours. For work nobody watches, size by the 80% line, then shrink it for messy tickets: on ultra-long tasks, frontier agents solved fewer than 30% and tried reward hacking in 13.8% of runs (SWE-Marathon, arXiv, Jun 2026).

keyIdeas.title: Jagged, and only as good as its check
keyIdeas.body: Models peak where results can be checked automatically, because labs train them with rewards they can verify (Karpathy, Apr 2026): the same model that refactors a 100,000-line codebase can tell you to walk to a car wash 50 metres away, leaving the car behind. Treat scores with the same doubt. OpenAI stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified in early 2026: 59.4% of 138 audited hard problems had flawed tests or descriptions, and every frontier model it tested could reproduce some of the original fixes or problem details. Passing tests isn’t mergeable: in METR’s 2025 study of an early-2025 agent, 38% of its PRs passed the maintainers’ tests and none of the 15 it reviewed was mergeable as-is (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work). So delegate what sits under the 80% line and is cheap to check, pair on what is bigger or only partly checkable, and keep what you cannot check.

videos.title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
videos.speaker: Andrej Karpathy
videos.desc: The clearest explanation there is of what a model does at each step. Watch two short parts: why two runs differ, and why the context window is the agent’s working memory.

clips.label: Inference: the model gives a probability for every possible next token and one is sampled, like a weighted coin flip; the weights stay fixed while you use it
Tools as special tokens that pause the model while the program runs them; knowledge in the weights is a vague memory, the context window is working memory

takeaways: Two runs of the same prompt can split at the first sampled token, and the gap grows with every step of a long agent loop.
What sits in the context beats what the model half-remembers from training. Point it at the file, the doc page or the error message.
A tool call is text the model writes. The program around it runs the tool and pastes the result back into the context.
watchOut: Recorded in February 2025 with ChatGPT as the example. The mechanics still hold; the product details are dated.

videos.title: Why The Harness Matters More Than The Model
videos.speaker: YC Paper Club host
videos.desc: A seven-minute history of how a bare model became an agent, one harness feature at a time. After it, Claude Code, Codex and Cursor look like variations of one design.

clips.label: From a 2019 loop that only samples tokens, to tools, memory, skills, reflection, subagents, and a loop with limits on turns and tool calls

takeaways: Each ability came from the harness, not the weights: tools are JSON the model writes, memory is a part of the context it may edit, skills are saved procedures it can look up.
A modern harness is a spec plus a loop: system prompt, tool list, skills, subagents, and limits on turns and tool calls.
videos.tryAtRhino: Run /context in the FCP repo and name the harness part behind each line: system prompt, CLAUDE.md, tools, MCP servers, skills.

videos.title: Picking the right model
videos.speaker: Lucas, Anthropic Applied AI
videos.desc: How Anthropic’s applied AI team chooses a model and effort level: a small eval of your own tasks, scored by cost per successful result.

clips.label: Eval traps: noise taken for signal, infrastructure failures, one prompt that behaves differently on two models, and a coding eval where Claude read git history to find earlier answers
Haiku, Sonnet and Opus on one code-fix pipeline; thinking versus effort; trading accuracy against tokens with the effort setting

takeaways: Run each eval task several times. If results swing, the task is badly defined or the grader is off.
The right model is the cheapest per successful result, not per token. A bigger model can finish sooner because it needs fewer turns.
Effort sets how much Claude writes across thinking, tool calls and replies; thinking is its scratch pad before it acts.
watchOut: Anthropic speaking about its own models, so these are vendor examples, and the versions shown (Opus 4.5 to 4.7) are already older.

videos.title: Measuring Exponential Trends Rising (in AI)
videos.speaker: Joel Becker, METR
videos.desc: The researcher behind the time-horizon chart on what it measures and what it doesn’t.

clips.label: How METR picks tasks: automatically gradable, fair to a skilled low-context human, and tidier than real work
Time horizon is task difficulty in human hours, not how long the agent runs; why “it ran for 30 hours” stories aren’t evidence

takeaways: The chart covers well-scoped, auto-graded tasks. Real tickets that need unwritten context are harder than their hours suggest.
A long autonomous run says nothing about the quality of the result, or whether a second try would also succeed.
videos.tryAtRhino: Before you delegate a ticket, ask whether a skilled new hire with no FCP history could finish it from the ticket alone. If not, the time horizon overstates what the agent can do.

videos.title: Andrej Karpathy: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering
videos.speaker: Andrej Karpathy with Stephanie Zhan
videos.desc: Why the same model refactors a huge codebase and fails a riddle a child could answer, and how to find which side of the edge your task is on.

clips.label: Verifiability: labs train models with rewards they can check, so skills peak in code and math and stay rough elsewhere; the car-wash test

takeaways: Capability follows checkability. Tasks with a fast, clear check are where agents shine.
Jaggedness is a reason to stay in the loop. Explore where your own tasks sit, and don’t assume one strength carries over to the next task.
watchOut: The vibe coding part (from 15:46) belongs with chapter 1, Your first hour with a coding agent.

videos.title: Why Agent Hype Can Fall Short of Reality
videos.speaker: Joel Becker, METR
videos.desc: The short talk that sets METR’s benchmark curve against field results, with the method behind the time horizon.

clips.label: Human baselines, a success curve per model, and the 50% point read off as the time horizon
Why high benchmark scores don’t mean high productivity: reliability, mergeability, context, messiness and dependent tasks

takeaways: One explanation he offers: to save you time, an agent must be right almost every time (something like 95 to 99%), or checking its work eats the gain.
If task B needs what you learn while doing task A, handing A to the agent can cost more than it saves.

labs.title: Watch the context window fill
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): On any repo, or a small public sample app, start a fresh session and run /context (or your agent’s context meter). Note the total and the three biggest items before you type anything. Ask the agent to explain one feature end to end, for example how a React list filters its rows or how a Django endpoint validates its input, then run /context again. In a new session, ask the same question starting with “use a subagent to investigate” and compare the numbers. Finally run /compact with a focus, ask for an exact detail from a file it read early on, and see whether it knows the detail or has to read the file again. At Rhino: do it in the FCP frontend or cloud repo and note what CLAUDE.md, skills and MCP servers cost before your first prompt.
labs.output: A table of context size at four moments, and one rule you will follow in your own sessions

labs.title: Same task, five runs
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Pick one small, well-specified task with a machine check, such as a new input check on an endpoint or a new prop on a component, with a test that proves it. Run the same prompt three times in fresh sessions from the same commit (a git worktree per run is easiest), then once with /effort low and once with /effort high. For each run, record whether the check passes, the files touched, the diff size, the time taken and the context used at the end (/context). Work out pass@3 and pass^3 for the three default runs, and read the diffs side by side. At Rhino: use a closed Lane A ticket on synthetic data.
labs.output: A five-row results table, and one sentence on whether this kind of task can run unattended

labs.title: Size five tickets
labs.body: Solo (about 40 min): Try the practice tool “Should the agent do this alone?” first. Then take five tickets from your backlog, or open issues in a public project. For each, estimate the hours a skilled new hire with no history in the repo would need, how you would check the result (a machine check, a ten-minute human check, or hard to check), and what unwritten context it needs. Compare each with the current 80% line and decide: delegate, pair or do it yourself. Hand one “delegate” ticket to the agent and see whether your call held. At Rhino: Lane A tickets only, and PHI never enters a prompt.
labs.output: A five-row sizing table with a decision per ticket, and one checked result

checks.q: A teammate says the agent “remembered” a convention from yesterday’s session. What actually happened?
checks.a: The weights don’t change while you use them, and each session starts with a fresh context window. The harness loaded the convention from a file such as CLAUDE.md or auto memory, or the old session was resumed.

checks.q: What does a 2-hour time horizon mean, and what doesn’t it mean?
checks.a: The agent is predicted to succeed at a stated rate (often 50%) on well-specified tasks that take a skilled, low-context person about 2 hours. It says nothing about how long the agent runs, or about messy tickets that need unwritten context.

checks.q: Why size unattended work by the 80% horizon rather than the 50% one?
checks.a: At 50%, half the runs fail. The 80% horizon is far shorter (about 3 hours against about 17 for the best model METR has measured), and messy real work is shorter still.

checks.q: Your prompt passed once and failed twice on the same task. How do you report it, and what comes next?
checks.a: One of three: pass@3 yes, pass^3 no. It isn’t ready to run alone. Make the task smaller, add a machine check or fix the harness, then run it several times again.

watchOut: Treating a launch-day benchmark or one great demo as proof for your repo. Contamination, flawed tests and harness differences all move scores; run a small eval on your own tickets.
Pushing on in a long session full of failed attempts. After two failed corrections, run /clear and restart with a better prompt (Claude Code best practices).
Reading “it ran for 30 hours” as capability. Run length isn’t difficulty, and one success isn’t a success rate.
Planning with last quarter’s numbers. The curve moves, so re-check your delegation card every quarter.
modules.watchTime: 39 min core, 1 h 3 min with electives
modules.goal: Build a working model of a coding agent (a model that predicts tokens, a harness that runs tools in a loop, a context window that fills up) and use it every day: to keep sessions sharp, to pick the model and effort, and to decide what the agent does alone, what you pair on and what you keep.
modules.why: Every choice you make with an agent follows from how it works: what to hand off, when to start fresh, which model and effort to use, and why one good run proves nothing. Capability is growing fast and unevenly. METR’s time horizon has doubled about every 131 days since 2023, yet for the best model it has measured, Claude Mythos Preview (early), the horizon is about 17 hours at 50% success and only about 3 hours at 80%. The harness moves results too: LangChain took the same GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by changing only the harness (Feb 2026).

shipIt.title: Your delegation card
shipIt.body: A one-page note for your team: which kinds of task you delegate, pair on or keep, the model and effort you use for each, and the evidence from labs 2 and 3. Date it and re-check it every quarter, because the curve moves.

modules.title: Agentic engineering: the loop and the rules

keyIdeas.title: Vibe coding or agentic engineering
keyIdeas.body: Chapter 1, Your first hour with a coding agent, drew the line: vibe coding means you don’t review the code, which is fine only when a bug can hurt nobody but you (Simon Willison). Agentic engineering keeps the professional quality bar while agents do the typing (Andrej Karpathy, Apr 2026). Most professionals already work this way: in Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey, 72% said vibe coding is not part of their professional work, 46% distrusted the accuracy of AI output, and 66% pointed to AI answers that are “almost right, but not quite”. This course makes agentic engineering concrete as a loop with gates and a short list of rules.

keyIdeas.title: The loop
keyIdeas.body: Intent, plan, build, verify, merge, release, operate and learn. Each stage has an owner and a gate that produces evidence: the requester can say in one sentence what done looks like; the code owner approves the design for anything above the lowest risk tier; tests, type checks and lint pass before a PR opens; the evidence shows the change working, not just a claim; the approver is not the requester (SOC 2 CC8.1); deploy checks pass on QA before production; the postmortem names the harness change that stops a repeat. The rest of the course teaches this loop one stage at a time.

keyIdeas.title: Seven rules that never bend
keyIdeas.body: (1) PHI never enters a prompt, including logs, alerts, screenshots and pasted threads. (2) Two lanes: Lane A is code-only work on synthetic data with any approved tool; Lane B is PHI-adjacent work with only the Claude Code CLI or Desktop local mode under ZDR, or the Agent SDK in Rhino’s own pod, and never connectors. (3) The requester never approves their own agent’s PR (SOC 2 CC8.1). (4) Agents open PRs; pipelines deploy. (5) You own every line you merge. (6) Tokens are never a performance metric. (7) Fix the harness on the second repeat. Chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer, shows which tool fits which lane.

keyIdeas.title: Read many, write one
keyIdeas.body: Parallelize reading work: search, review, research, hypotheses. Keep a single writer per change, in its own worktree or pod. Chapter 18, One agent or many?, shows when more writers pay off and when they collide.

keyIdeas.title: Code got cheap; shipping didn’t
keyIdeas.body: An NBER study of more than 500,000 GitHub developers with AI usage telemetry (a matched event study, May 2026, revised Sep 2026) found autonomous coding agents raised commits by 240%, but that shrank to 80% more projects and only 30% more releases: human steps are the weak link. Carnegie Mellon and Stanford followed 802 developers and 196,212 PRs at one company with a “2x” mandate (Jul 2026). Output reached 2.09 times the baseline, per-reviewer load roughly doubled, and PRs with any human review fell from 89% to 68% as automated review rose to about 84%. Merge and revert rates held steady, which the authors read as no acute quality collapse, not a clean bill of health. The bottleneck moved from writing code to reviewing, verifying and releasing it.

keyIdeas.title: Feeling faster isn’t proof
keyIdeas.body: In early 2025, METR’s randomized trial (16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks, early-2025 tools) found tasks took 19% longer with AI, while the developers believed they had been 20% faster. In February 2026 METR said its newer data gives an unreliable signal: more developers now refuse to work without AI, 30 to 50% held back tasks they didn’t want to do without it, and METR thinks developers are likely more sped up now than in 2025. The sign of the old result is out of date; the gap is the lasting lesson. Self-reports overestimate, so measure what ships and how it holds up (rule 6).

labs.title: Map one change on the loop
labs.body: Solo (about 40 min): Pick a change you shipped recently, or a merged PR in a public project you know. Place every step on the seven stages: who did it, how long it took and what evidence it left (a ticket, a plan, test output, a review, a deploy log). Mark where an agent helped and where one could have. Circle each stage whose gate left no evidence at all. At Rhino: use a ticket you shipped last month, and check the merge stage against CC8.1: were the requester and the approver different people?
labs.output: A one-page loop map with the missing evidence circled

labs.title: Take one small change around the loop
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): In a practice repo or on a fresh branch, pick one small fix, such as a missing input check on a Django or FastAPI endpoint, or an empty state in a React list. Write the intent in three lines (What, Why, How) and one sentence for done. Ask the agent for a short plan and approve it, let one agent build it, and have it prove the change with a test that fails before the fix and passes after. Open a PR that carries the evidence, then stop: someone else would approve and merge it. Add two lines on what release and operate would need. At Rhino: a Lane A ticket, factory-seeded data only, and a teammate approves.
labs.output: A PR with its evidence, and one note per stage

labs.title: Your repo’s funnel
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): In any repo with a few months of history, yours or a public one, count commits, merged PRs and releases (or tags) for the last two quarters. `git log --since`, `gh pr list --state merged` and `git tag` are enough. Compare the three numbers the way NBER did, and find where work waits longest: in review, in CI or before release. At Rhino: add PR pickup time from GitHub, count per team, and never rank people.
labs.output: A three-row table and one sentence that names your weak link

checks.q: An agent wrote a PR you asked for. Who may approve it?
checks.a: Any qualified reviewer except you. You initiated the change, so SOC 2 CC8.1 needs approval from a different identity.

checks.q: Which data may an agent see?
checks.a: Code, docs, and synthetic or factory-seeded data. Never PHI, including in logs, alerts, screenshots or pasted threads.

checks.q: DX’s data shows median throughput up 37% over four quarters. Why isn’t that the whole story?
checks.a: Over the same year DX’s experience index fell from 67 to 65, and change confidence fell 6.1% since Q1 2026. NBER found commits rose far more than releases (240% against 30%), and CMU and Stanford saw reviewer load double while fewer PRs got a human review. More code isn’t more shipped value: the constraint moved to review and release.

checks.q: METR once measured developers 19% slower with AI. What does that result teach in 2026?
checks.a: It measured early-2025 tools, and METR’s February 2026 update says its newer data is unreliable and developers are likely faster now. The lasting lesson is the gap: developers believed they were 20% faster, so self-reports overestimate. Measure outcomes, not feelings.

watchOut: Averages hide the spread. The same tools make some teams faster and some slower.
Surveys of how fast people feel are not measurements.

Working isn’t secure. On BaxBench’s 392 back-end tasks, the top model on the live leaderboard was 86.2% correct but only 56.1% correct and secure (26 Sep 2026). Chapter 14, Keep agent-written back ends safe, goes deeper.
Quoting a summary instead of the source. A September 2026 synthesis paper gave different NBER numbers from the NBER abstract. Open the primary source before you repeat a figure.

modules.goal: Turn the line you met in chapter 1 into a way of working: the seven stages every change goes through, each with an owner and a gate; the seven Rhino rules that never bend; and what the 2026 evidence really says about where agents help and where they hurt.
modules.why: Agents now write a large share of the code, and the evidence on what that buys has grown up. DX’s data from 500+ organizations (vendor data, Jul 2026) puts AI-generated code at 52% in Q2 2026, up from 34% in Q1, and median weekly throughput up 37% over four quarters (1.42 to 1.94 PRs per engineer per week). Over the same four quarters its Developer Experience Index fell from 67 to 65, and change confidence fell 6.1% since Q1 2026 alone. DORA’s 2025 research (a survey of about 5,000 technology professionals) calls AI an amplifier: more adoption goes with more delivery throughput and more instability, and a team’s tests, batch size and workflows decide which one wins. A loop with gates and a few fixed rules is how you keep the gains and not the incidents.

modules.title: Safety basics for every developer

keyIdeas.title: Two controls: who approves, and what it can reach
keyIdeas.body: Every agent pairs an approval layer (you, a classifier or nobody) with a boundary layer (a sandbox, a container, network rules). Approval alone fails: Anthropic says 97% of permission prompts get approved. In Claude Code the modes are Manual (config value default), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk and bypassPermissions; Shift+Tab switches, and deny rules block in every mode, even bypass. Codex splits sandbox modes (read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access) from approval policies (on-request, never), with network off by default in workspace-write. Cursor’s recommended default since version 3.6 (29 May 2026) is Auto-review.

keyIdeas.title: Auto mode yes, bypass never on your laptop
keyIdeas.body: From v2.1.283, auto mode is Claude Code’s built-in starting mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions; claude -p and the Agent SDK still start in Manual. A separate classifier checks risky actions against what you asked for, and a probe flags hidden instructions in tool results. The docs say auto mode “does not guarantee safety”, and by default it allows reading .env and sending credentials to their matching API. Bypass (--dangerously-skip-permissions; --yolo in Codex and Gemini CLI) “offers no protection against prompt injection”, so it belongs only in an isolated container or VM without internet. Admins can switch it off with permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode in managed settings.

keyIdeas.title: Text can give orders, so cut a leg of the trifecta
keyIdeas.body: Prompt injection is instructions hidden in anything the agent reads: a ticket, an issue, a README, a web page, a tool result. Models can’t reliably separate your instructions from data, and a filter that stops 97% of attacks is “a failing grade” (Simon Willison). The lethal trifecta is private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out, in one session. In July 2025 a support ticket told a Cursor agent on the Supabase MCP, running as service_role, to copy the integration_tokens table into the ticket; read-only mode removes the way back out. Cut one leg, usually the way out. Chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely, goes deeper.

keyIdeas.title: Secrets out of reach, not out of mind
keyIdeas.body: The agent’s machine should hold no secret the task doesn’t need. Deny Read(./.env) and Read(./.env.*): these rules cover Claude’s file tools and file commands such as cat, but not a script that opens the file itself, so turn on the sandbox for OS-level blocks. In April 2026 a Cursor agent found an API token in an unrelated file and deleted PocketOS’s production database and its backups in 9 seconds (Cerbos). s1ngularity leaked over 1,000 valid GitHub tokens, and its second phase made over 5,500 private repos public (Wiz). Scan, don’t eyeball: in a July 2026 preprint on 4,022 agent PRs, review missed 81.1% of leaked credentials, and people, not agents, added 67.6% of the real ones.

keyIdeas.title: Every new package is a decision
keyIdeas.body: Code models suggest packages that don’t exist: at least 5.2% of suggested packages for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source ones, with 205,474 unique invented names across 576,000 samples (USENIX Security 2025). Attackers register such names (“slopsquatting”), and real packages get hijacked too: Shai-Hulud 2.0 compromised 796 npm packages in November 2025 (Datadog). Before a new dependency merges, check that it exists, that it is the one the docs name, who maintains it and how old it is, and pin it in the lockfile.

keyIdeas.title: PHI never enters a prompt, and the lane picks the tool
keyIdeas.body: Rule 1: agents see code, docs and synthetic or factory-seeded data only, never PHI, and that includes logs, alerts, screenshots and pasted Slack threads. Browser agents make this rule easy to break: Claude in Chrome shares your browser’s login state, and its GIFs capture account details on logged-in pages. Rule 2: Lane A is code-only work on synthetic data, where any approved tool is allowed, including cloud agents, routines and Fable. Lane B is PHI-adjacent work: Claude Code CLI or Desktop local under the BAA with ZDR, or the Agent SDK in our own pod, with no connectors. A cloud route for Lane B (Claude Code or the Agent SDK on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, under the cloud provider’s BAA) is being checked with the vendors; it isn’t a Lane B tool today. Chapter 34, Stay safe and compliant, has the full matrix.

labs.title: Lock down your own setup
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): In a throwaway copy of any repo, run /status and /permissions to see your mode, your rules and where each setting comes from. Add deny rules for Read(./.env) and Read(./.env.*) to ~/.claude/settings.json, and turn on the sandbox with /sandbox. Create a .env that holds only a dummy value, such as FAKE_TOKEN=not-a-secret. Ask the agent to show the file, then to write a small Node or Python script that prints it, and record which layer stopped each try, if any. If the script got through, add the path to the sandbox’s blocked reads (see the sandboxing docs) and try again. If you also use Codex or Cursor, repeat the test there. At Rhino: compare the result with the managed settings your organization pushes, and confirm that bypass mode is switched off.
labs.output: A settings file and a table of each attempt and the layer that stopped it

labs.title: Map the trifecta in your tools
labs.body: Solo (about 40 min): List every tool your agent can use: built-in tools, MCP servers, CLIs such as gh, and the browser. For each one, mark whether it touches private data, brings in untrusted text, or can send data out. Circle every session where all three meet, and remove one leg from one of them: a read-only connection, no web fetch, or a separate session. Then add a harmless canary to a throwaway repo: a README line asking AI agents to end their reply with the word PINEAPPLE. Ask the agent to summarize the repo, and note what it did with that line. At Rhino: Jira and Slack connectors bring in untrusted text, and Lane B work uses no connectors at all.
labs.output: A trifecta table, one leg removed, and a note on the canary

labs.title: Check the next three packages
labs.body: Solo (about 30 min): In a small sample app, ask the agent for a feature that needs a new library: a date-range picker in a React app, or rate limiting on a Django endpoint. Before you accept, check each package it suggests: it exists on npm or PyPI, its name matches the library’s own docs, who maintains it, its age, its downloads and whether it runs install scripts. Pin what you keep in the lockfile. Add one CLAUDE.md line and one PR-template line that ask for this check on every new dependency.
labs.output: A three-row package check and the two lines

checks.q: Auto mode is on. Why do you still add a deny rule for .env files?
checks.a: By default auto mode allows reading .env and sending credentials to their matching API, and it doesn’t guarantee safety. Deny rules block in every mode, even bypass.

checks.q: What are the three legs of the lethal trifecta, and which is usually the easiest to cut?
checks.a: Private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out. The way out is usually the easiest to cut.

checks.q: The agent adds a package you have never heard of. What do you check before it merges?
checks.a: That it exists, that it is the one the docs name, who maintains it, how old it is and whether it runs install scripts. Then pin it. Commercial models invent at least 5.2% of the packages they suggest.

checks.q: Which tools may Lane B work use?
checks.a: Claude Code CLI or Desktop local mode under the BAA with ZDR, or the Agent SDK in our own pod, with no connectors. A cloud route is being checked with the vendors and isn’t allowed yet.

watchOut: Bypass mode on a machine with real credentials. Malware can start your agent CLI with the bypass flag, so ask your admin to block the mode in managed settings.
A CLAUDE.md line used as a guardrail. Prose is a suggestion; deny rules, the sandbox and missing credentials are boundaries.
A browser agent next to a tab signed in to production. It shares your login state, so patient data on the page can enter the prompt.

modules.watchTime: 22 min core, 34 min with electives
modules.goal: Work safely with a coding agent from your first session: pick the right permission mode, spot prompt injection and the lethal trifecta, keep secrets and invented packages out, keep PHI out of every prompt, and use only the tools your lane allows.
modules.why: Your agent reads tickets, web pages and tool output, and runs commands on the same laptop that holds your tokens. In August 2025 the s1ngularity malware ran victims’ own Claude, Gemini and Q command-line tools with their permission-skipping flags to hunt for secrets (Wiz). Approving each step doesn’t save you: in an Anthropic study with 1,053 paid testers, people caught a dangerous command 13.6% of the time, while auto mode blocked 89% of the same commands (vendor data, August 2026). Safety comes from boundaries you set before the session starts.

shipIt.title: Your day-one safety setup
shipIt.body: Settings with deny rules and the sandbox on and bypass off, your trifecta table, and the question you ask before every task: which lane is this? Show a teammate each layer stopping one test.

modules.headlineSrc: 13.6% · of dangerous commands that people caught

modules.title: Tell the agent what you want

keyIdeas.title: Goal, limits, done
keyIdeas.body: Give the agent the outcome, the guardrails and a finish line it can check, not a list of steps. Boris Cherny names over-specified, step-by-step prompts as a common failure of experienced engineers (Y Combinator, Jul 2026). Claude Code’s /goal docs describe a finish line that holds: one measurable end state, the check that proves it (“npm test exits 0”), and what must not change on the way. The same brief works in Codex, Cursor or Copilot. At Rhino the ticket stays What / Why / How, and the Intent gate is that the requester can say what done looks like in one sentence.

keyIdeas.title: Let the agent interview you
keyIdeas.body: Put the questions before the plan, not after the PR. Plan modes read the code and plan before they edit, and several ask clarifying questions: Shift+Tab in Claude Code and Cursor, /plan in Codex CLI and Copilot. For bigger work, ask the agent to interview you until you share one understanding, one design decision at a time (Matt Pocock’s “grill me” prompt), or use the Claude Code docs’ AskUserQuestion interview that ends in a SPEC.md. Keep a short glossary of domain words so you and the agent mean the same thing.

keyIdeas.title: Acceptance checks, drafted at run time
keyIdeas.body: Turn done into 2 to 5 checks that pass or fail: an example test, a rule that must hold for any input, a command’s exit code, a screenshot compared with the design. Writing them as “When X, the system shall Y” (EARS, the format Kiro uses) exposes missing cases, and Kiro turns such criteria into property-based tests, with no published accuracy numbers (Nov 2025). At Rhino a skill drafts the checks when the agent starts and the requester confirms them. They are never a Jira field. Chapter 7, Check the agent’s work, turns them into evidence.

keyIdeas.title: Plan by expected pain
keyIdeas.body: Plan when a wrong guess is expensive to undo. Dex Horthy (Sep 2026) weighs the chance of rework against how much the rework hurts: a wrong button color is cheap, a wrong database schema is not. The Claude Code docs say: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. A plan does not replace the code. HumanLayer ran “read the plan, skip the code” for four to five months, and the codebase became unusable. Rhino’s call: plan in proportion to how many sessions the work spans, and always read the code.

keyIdeas.title: Right-size the spec
keyIdeas.body: None for a visible one-liner, a task brief for a small change, one page for a feature, and a full spec only for work across sessions, layers or people. The popular tools (Spec Kit, Kiro, OpenSpec, BMAD, Superpowers) all run some form of specify, plan, tasks, build. Most specs should be spec-first: written, built from, then archived. Keeping a spec alive next to the code (spec-anchored) needs an owner, and editing only the spec (spec-as-source) risks repeating model-driven development’s problems (Birgitta Böckeler, Oct 2025). The evidence for heavy workflows is thin: one Scott Logic engineer reviewed about 4,800 lines of Spec Kit markdown for about 5.5 hours on a hobby app, against 24 minutes of his time working in small prompts (Nov 2025). Thoughtworks put the technique in its Assess ring (Nov 2025), and an Aug 2026 paper says peer-reviewed evidence is not yet established.

keyIdeas.title: Restart instead of arguing
keyIdeas.body: After two failed corrections, the context is full of failed attempts. Clear it and start fresh with a better first prompt that includes what you learned: /clear in Claude Code, or /rewind (Esc Esc) to go back to a checkpoint. Cursor’s docs give the same advice: revert, sharpen the plan, run it again. For bigger work, gather context and write the brief in one session, then build in a fresh one (Erik Schluntz spends 15 to 20 minutes on that brief). Checkpoints miss changes made by shell commands, so commit before risky steps. Chapter 2, How AI coding agents work, explains the context window.

labs.title: One task, two briefs
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): pick a small real change in any repo you know, such as a new prop on a React component or a new field on a Django endpoint. From the same commit, run it twice in fresh sessions: first with a one-line prompt, then with a task brief (goal, limits, 2 to 5 done checks, “ask me first if”). For each run, record the questions the agent asked, the corrections you gave, whether the checks passed and your minutes. At Rhino: use a Lane A ticket with factory-seeded data only, and paste the checks the requester confirmed into the PR.
labs.output: Two runs side by side and your own rule for when a brief pays off

labs.title: Interview, spec, fresh session
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): choose a feature that touches more than one file in any repo or a small public sample app. In plan mode, have the agent interview you until you agree on the design, then write a one-page SPEC.md with scope, out of scope and 3 to 5 acceptance checks in “When X, the system shall Y” form. Turn each check into a test: an example test, or a property test for a rule that must hold for any input. Run /clear and build from the spec in a fresh session, then open a PR where every check has evidence. At Rhino: a teammate who is not you approves the PR.
labs.output: A one-page spec, one test per check, and a PR with evidence for each check

labs.title: Size a real backlog
labs.body: Solo (about 30 min): take the next five tickets from your backlog, or five open issues in a public repo. For each, write one line of expected pain (how likely a wrong guess is, and how much it would hurt to undo), pick a spec size from the quick guide, and write the done checks for the riskiest one. Then try the practice tool “How much spec does this ticket need?” and compare. At Rhino: keep the checks in the session and the PR, not in Jira.
labs.output: Five sized tickets, each with a one-line reason

checks.q: What three things does a good task give the agent?
checks.a: The goal, the limits (the guardrails and what must not change) and exit criteria it can check. Not a list of steps.

checks.q: When should you skip plan mode?
checks.a: When you could describe the diff in one sentence, such as a typo or a log line. Plan when the approach is unclear, many files change, or the code is new to you.

checks.q: You corrected the agent twice on the same issue and it is still wrong. What now?
checks.a: Stop correcting. Clear the session or rewind, and start fresh with a better first prompt that includes what you learned.

checks.q: Where do acceptance checks live at Rhino?
checks.a: A skill drafts them when the agent starts and the requester confirms them. They live in the session and the PR evidence, never in a Jira field.

watchOut: A spec bigger than the change. If the spec takes longer to review than the diff, it is the wrong size.
Reading the plan instead of the code. HumanLayer’s months-long experiment ended in a rebuild.
Checks nobody can run, such as “works well” or “is robust”, and checks the agent is allowed to edit.
A spec you keep but never update. In one study of 441 repos, 73.8% of committed AI configuration files were never changed after the first commit (RAMP, Aug 2026, observational).

extras.title: A task brief, as a template
lines: - **Goal.** What should be true when the agent is done, in one sentence.
- **Why.** Who needs it and what problem it solves.
- **Limits.** What must not change (files, APIs, contracts, dependencies), what not to add, and a turn or time budget.
- **Done when.** 2 to 5 checks that pass or fail, each with the command or screenshot that proves it.
- **Ask me first if.** The decisions you keep for yourself, such as a schema, an API shape or a new dependency.
- **Show me.** The evidence the PR must carry: test output, the command and what it returned, a screenshot.
- **At Rhino, add.** PHI data flow (none; synthetic or factory-seeded data only), the lane (see chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer), the risk tier, and who approves (never you).

extras.title: How much spec? A quick guide
lines: | The work | Spec size | What you write | Plan first? |
| A visible one-line fix: a typo, copy text, a log line | None | One sentence and the check | No |
| A small change in one area: a table filter, a field on an endpoint | Task brief | Goal, limits, 2 to 5 checks | Only if unsure of the approach |
| A feature across files or layers: a new page, an endpoint with a migration | One page | The brief, key decisions, out of scope, interfaces touched | Yes, and read the plan |

| Work across sessions, services or people: a contract change, an auth change | Full spec | Requirements, design and tasks, with the design reviewed by the code owner | Yes; see chapter 6, Give the agent the right context |

extras.title: The spec tools, in one line each
lines: | Tool | The flow | Worth knowing |

| Spec Kit (GitHub, v1.0.12, Sep 2026) | A constitution once, then specify, plan, tasks, implement, converge per feature | Bug-fix and idea-assessment extensions are opt-in; about 139,000 GitHub stars |
| Kiro (Amazon) | Requirements with EARS acceptance criteria, then design, then tasks; bugfix specs | Turns criteria into property-based tests; runs independent tasks in waves |
| OpenSpec | Explore, propose, apply, archive | Built for existing codebases; about 70,000 GitHub stars |
| BMAD Method | Planning paths sized to the change; BMad Loop runs a whole epic unattended | About 53,500 GitHub stars |
| Superpowers | Brainstorm, a spec shown in short chunks, a plan of 2 to 5 minute tasks, subagents with a review after each task | About 292,000 GitHub stars |

modules.watchTime: 34 min core, 40 min with electives
modules.goal: Hand an agent work it can finish without you: a goal, limits and a finish line it can check; your questions answered before it plans; a plan and a spec sized to what a wrong guess would cost; and a clean restart when a session goes wrong.
modules.why: In about 400,000 Claude Code sessions, people made about 70% of the planning decisions (what to do, which approach, what counts as done) and Claude made about 80% of the execution decisions (Anthropic, Jun 2026, vendor data). Sessions rated more expert, judged partly by how precisely people framed directions and what they asked Claude to verify, reached verified success 28 to 33% of the time, against 15% for novice-rated ones. When people interrupt the agent, the top reason is to add context or corrections they left out: 32% of interrupts (Anthropic, Feb 2026). Spec tools promise to fix this and can overshoot: one turned a small bug fix into 4 user stories and 16 acceptance criteria. Saying what you want, at the right size, is now the core of the job.

shipIt.title: Your task-brief template
shipIt.body: Turn the brief that worked best in the labs into a reusable template, a saved prompt or a small slash command, with goal, limits, done checks, “ask me first if” and evidence. Share it with the team together with one PR that used it, showing the checks the requester confirmed and the evidence for each.

modules.title: Context engineering in a brownfield monorepo

keyIdeas.title: Small, specific, tested context files
keyIdeas.body: CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md loads into every session, so each line costs attention on every task. Keep what the agent can’t work out by reading the code: one build-and-run command, where tests live and how to run one, how to see the first error, non-standard conventions, and corrections you keep repeating. Leave out repository overviews (they did not help in the ETH study) and style rules that a linter or formatter already enforces. Anthropic’s advice for Claude 5 models (Jul 2026) points the same way: describe the repo in a line or two, spend the tokens on gotchas, and don’t state what the agent can see in the file tree. The Claude Code docs target under 200 lines per file, and HumanLayer keeps its root file under 60 lines. For a fast-moving framework, a short index that points to version-matched docs is the one addition with a large measured gain (Vercel’s evals, see chapter 11, Build UI with agents). Treat every line as a hypothesis, and test changes to it (chapter 21, Test your agents like code).

keyIdeas.title: One file for every tool
keyIdeas.body: AGENTS.md is the shared format that Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Zed and other agents read. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md on its own from v2.1.277 (Sep 2026), but only when there is no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or above it, and not on older versions, when its built-in agents-md plugin is off, or sometimes in the first session after an upgrade. Before v2.1.281 it also skipped AGENTS.md on Amazon Bedrock and with telemetry off, with no warning. The reliable pattern works in every case: keep the shared rules in AGENTS.md, and add a CLAUDE.md whose first line imports it (`@AGENTS.md`), with any Claude-only notes below. A CLAUDE.md symlinked to AGENTS.md also works. Writing “read AGENTS.md” in words does not: Claude sees the file only if it decides to open it. In a monorepo, put the file in the package the agent works in, such as frontend/.

keyIdeas.title: The instruction budget is a rule of thumb
keyIdeas.body: Every instruction the agent sees shares one budget: the tool’s own system prompt, CLAUDE.md, skill descriptions, MCP tools and your prompt. HumanLayer’s informal estimate (Nov 2025) is that frontier thinking models follow about 150 to 200 instructions with reasonable consistency, that adding more makes all of them less reliable at once, and that Claude Code’s system prompt already holds about 50. Dex Horthy’s “about 40 per prompt” is his practical limit for the prompts in a staged workflow, not a law of the model. Anthropic removed over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt for Claude 5 models with no measurable loss on its coding evals, and saw that conflicting rules from the system prompt, skills and users forced the model to work out which one to follow (Jul 2026). So count your instructions, cut the ones that conflict or state the obvious, move rare detail into files the agent loads on demand, and check the result with an eval.

keyIdeas.title: Pull context in, and keep the start stable
keyIdeas.body: Quality drops as the window fills. Dex Horthy calls it the dumb zone (Sep 2026), and in McMillan’s study the odds of following a rule fell about 5.6% for each function the agent wrote in a session. Dex’s early-2026 rule was about 100k usable tokens on small models and 200k on frontier ones, whatever the window; windows are larger now, and using far less than the maximum still pays. Point to files instead of pasting them (file:line references, not copies), let path-scoped rules and skills load on demand, send big reads to a subagent, and start a fresh session for each task (chapter 2, How AI coding agents work). Keep the start of the context stable too. Prompt caching matches a request from its first token: system prompt and tools, then CLAUDE.md, then the session. Changing the tool set or the model mid-session throws the cache away: 100k tokens into an Opus session, switching to Haiku for an easy question costs more than letting Opus answer (Anthropic, Apr 2026). Make those changes between sessions, or hand work to another model through a subagent.

keyIdeas.title: Ticket-blind research
keyIdeas.body: Turn the ticket into neutral questions in one session, then answer them from the code in a fresh session that never sees the ticket. Research that sees the ticket starts arguing for a solution; research that doesn’t stays factual (Dex Horthy, Mar 2026). Regenerate research from the code for each task instead of keeping it as a spec, because documents maintained apart from the code drift.

keyIdeas.title: A short design doc, the contract, then safe slices
keyIdeas.body: For work that spans sessions or layers (chapter 5, Tell the agent what you want, sizes the spec), write a design doc of about 200 lines and send it to the code owner, then a structure outline like a C header: types and signatures, no bodies. For cross-layer work, add the data model and the API or gRPC contract before the slice plans. Order the slices so each one is safe to ship: the contract, then an additive (expand) migration, then the service with its tests, then the edges (serializer, view, permissions), then the clients, with the contract cleanup in a later release. Generate the UI’s mock from the contract so the front end can start in parallel. At Rhino, migrations run under a lock across concurrent instances and on-prem clients can be older than the cloud, so the expand migration ships before the code that reads it (chapter 13, Build APIs and databases with agents). People review the short design doc, the long plan is for the agent, and you always read the code: HumanLayer ran “read the plan, skip the code” for months and its codebase became unusable (Sep 2026).

checks.q: Why hide the ticket from research?
checks.a: Research that sees the ticket starts arguing for a solution. Ticket-blind research stays factual.

checks.q: What do you review: the plan or the code?
checks.a: Review the short design doc, skip long plans, and always read the code before merge.

checks.q: What earns a line in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md?
checks.a: What the agent needs on almost every task and can’t infer from the code: the build and test commands, non-standard conventions, and corrections you keep repeating. Not a repository overview: in the ETH study, overviews didn’t help and context files added over 20% to cost.

checks.q: Your repo keeps its rules in AGENTS.md for Codex and Cursor. How do you make sure Claude Code reads them too?
checks.a: Add a CLAUDE.md whose first line is @AGENTS.md. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md on its own only from v2.1.277, only when there is no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md, and not in every session.

watchOut: Long plans nobody reads.
CLAUDE.md growing a line after every incident without anyone pruning it.
A generated context file full of repository overview. It costs tokens on every task and did not help in the ETH study.
Changing the tools or the model in the middle of a long session. It throws the prompt cache away; change them between sessions.
modules.watchTime: 34 min core, 54 min with electives
modules.goal: Give the agent the context it needs and nothing more: a short context file that every tool reads, prompts that fit the instruction budget, research that never sees the ticket, and a short design doc with slices in an order that is safe for the database as well as the UI.
modules.why: What the agent reads decides what it builds, and more is not better. In ETH Zurich’s study (one study, Feb 2026, SWE-bench tasks plus real repositories with their own files), context files such as AGENTS.md did not generally raise task success and added over 20% to inference cost. The agents did follow the instructions, but repository overviews did not help; the files were useful for non-standard conventions. Another study (Lulla et al., Jan 2026, 124 pull requests in 10 repositories) found an AGENTS.md went with 28.64% lower median runtime at similar task completion. In 1,650 Claude Code sessions (McMillan, May 2026), file size, position and structure made no detectable difference, while adherence fell as the session went on. Dex Horthy’s team found a second trap: research picks up opinions when the agent can see the ticket. So keep context small, specific and tested, and keep opinions out of research.

shipIt.title: One context file for every tool
shipIt.body: Merge an AGENTS.md with a CLAUDE.md that imports it, about 40 instructions or fewer, and show a teammate one task that went better with it. At Rhino, start with fcp/frontend.

modules.title: Verification and feedback loops

keyIdeas.title: Evidence, not claims
keyIdeas.body: A PR carries artifacts that anyone can check: test output, a clip or screenshot of the change working, query counts for an endpoint. “I tested it” is a claim. Anthropic’s advice is to hand the agent every check you would otherwise run by hand after it finishes, and to save the recipe that worked so every later session checks the same way. In Claude Code, the bundled /verify skill builds and drives the running app to confirm a change instead of stopping at tests and type checks, and /run-skill-generator records how to launch your project. Codex, Cursor and Copilot get the same loop through a browser MCP server or CLI (chapter 11, Build UI with agents).

keyIdeas.title: Hooks as red squiggles
keyIdeas.body: A hook is a script the harness runs at a fixed moment. A hook that runs after each file edit and type-checks and lints that file gives the agent the instant feedback your editor gives you: tsc and Biome for TypeScript, ruff or flake8 and mypy for Python. Write the output so it says how to fix the problem; OpenAI’s harness team writes its lint messages as fix instructions (Apr 2026). A hook runs every time. A line in CLAUDE.md can be missed.

keyIdeas.title: Verification contracts
keyIdeas.body: Write down what correct looks like in a form that the agent, CI and people all run. For a screen, components publish their state as DOM data attributes, and a manifest lists fixtures, invariants and probes, with one planted failure that proves the harness catches it (Anthropic, May 2026). For an endpoint, the contract is the API schema, a test for each error path, a table of who may and may not call it, and a pinned query count (assertNumQueries in Django). Check structure first, then pixels against an approved baseline, then taste with a rubric and a person (chapter 12, Let agents check every screen). Chapter 13, Build APIs and databases with agents, and chapter 14, Keep agent-written back ends safe, build the back-end version in full.

keyIdeas.title: Tests pass is not mergeable
keyIdeas.body: In METR’s review (Aug 2025, 18 real tasks, Claude 3.7 Sonnet in an agent scaffold), 38% of the PRs passed the maintainers’ tests, none of the 15 reviewed by hand was mergeable as-is, and even the passing ones needed about 26 minutes of fixing. In a larger follow-up (Mar 2026), 4 maintainers reviewed 296 agent PRs for SWE-bench Verified tasks: their merge decisions ran about 24 points below the automated grader, and roughly half of the test-passing PRs would not have been merged. Grade with METR’s five checks: core functionality, tests, docs, lint and types, and other code quality. The agent’s own tests don’t settle it. Across six models on SWE-bench Verified, solved and unsolved tasks had similar test-writing rates, the tests were mostly print statements, and prompting for more or fewer tests did not significantly change results (Chen et al., Feb 2026). In 4,882 agent PRs, error-handling code was the least tested: 81.0% of it never ran under any test in Python and 86.0% in Java (preprint, Jul 2026). So a person owns what correct means: the acceptance checks from chapter 5, Tell the agent what you want, tests held back from the agent, and a read of the code itself.

keyIdeas.title: Fail first, as evidence
keyIdeas.body: Ask for the new test failing without the change and passing with it; it proves the test can fail, and it is hard to fake (Matt Pocock). Forcing strict TDD inside the agent loop is a different thing. In Birgitta Böckeler’s small eval (Aug 2026), TDD runs ranked slightly worse overall than runs without TDD, mutation scores showed no gain, and agents sometimes skipped or faked the red step. So ask for the red run as evidence, not for a ritual. For a dependency you don’t understand, start with a learning test: a test against the real thing that prints what it does, committed outside CI (Dex Horthy, chapter 6, Give the agent the right context).

keyIdeas.title: Lint for test-gaming, and keep checks out of reach
keyIdeas.body: Under pressure, agents weaken assertions, wrap code in broad try/catch blocks, or skip tests; Dex Horthy traces the needless try/catch to how models are trained with rewards. In SWE-Marathon (Jun 2026), agents tried to exploit the environment or the verifier in 13.8% of rollouts. Semgrep, ast-grep or GritQL rules catch these shapes, with messages that tell the agent the real fix. Keep verifiers read-only to the writer, and use a separate evaluator with no write tools, because an agent grading its own work is a trap (Anthropic workshop, May 2026).

labs.title: The red-squiggle hook
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): in any repo, or a small public sample app, add a hook that runs after each file edit and type-checks and lints only that file: tsc and Biome for TypeScript, ruff and mypy for Python. In Claude Code it is a PostToolUse hook on the Edit and Write tools; make its output say how to fix each error. Give the agent the same small task twice, without and with the hook, and count the errors it fixes before it says it is done. At Rhino: tsc and Biome in fcp/frontend, black, isort and flake8 in the cloud back end.
labs.output: A committed hook and a before-and-after count

labs.title: An evidence pack with a planted bug
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): pick one screen or one endpoint. Write three to five checks for it. For a screen: state published as data attributes, plus an accessibility snapshot. For an endpoint: a response-shape test, one error-path test and a pinned query count. Plant one bug and show that the checks catch it, then remove it. Ask the agent for one small change and have the PR carry the red run, the green run and a clip or query counts. Grade the PR yourself with METR’s five checks: core functionality, tests, docs, lint and types, other quality. At Rhino: an FCP screen with Storybook stories, or a cloud endpoint, on factory-seeded QA data only.
labs.output: A PR with its evidence and a filled-in five-check rubric

labs.title: A rule against test-gaming
labs.body: Solo (about 40 min): write one Semgrep, ast-grep or GritQL rule that catches a test-gaming shape, such as a skipped test, a broad catch or except inside a test, or an exact assertion loosened to “is truthy”. Make its message tell the agent the real fix. Run it in CI or a pre-commit hook, and show it catches a planted example. At Rhino: use it the second time a reviewer sees the shape, as the rule to fix the harness on the second repeat asks.
labs.output: A rule, the planted example it catches, and the CI or hook line that runs it

checks.q: What’s the difference between evidence and a claim?
checks.a: Evidence is an artifact you can check: a clip, a screenshot, test output. A claim is the agent saying it works.

checks.q: Why a hook rather than a CLAUDE.md line for type checks?
checks.a: A hook runs every time and gives the agent immediate feedback. A line of prose can be missed.

checks.q: Name two shapes agents produce to game tests.
checks.a: Loosened assertions and broad try/catch blocks. Skipped or deleted tests are a third.

checks.q: An agent’s PR passes every test. Is it ready to merge?
checks.a: Not yet. In METR’s 2025 review, 38% of an agent’s PRs passed the maintainers’ tests and none of the 15 reviewed was mergeable as-is. Check core functionality, tests including error paths, docs, lint and types, and code quality, and read the code.

watchOut: Checks the agent can edit. Keep verifiers read-only to the writer.
Judging only by pixels. Check structure first, compare pixels against an approved baseline, and leave taste to a rubric and a person (chapter 12, Let agents check every screen).
The agent’s own tests as the only judge of correct. They mostly print values; a person decides what correct means.
TDD as a ritual. Ask for the red run as evidence; agents can skip or fake the steps of a process.
modules.watchTime: 35 min core, 1 h 29 min with electives
modules.goal: Make the agent prove its work: checks it runs after every edit, a contract that says what correct looks like for a screen or an endpoint, evidence in every PR, tests whose idea of correct a person owns, and lint rules that catch the ways agents game tests. Then judge whether the change is mergeable, not only whether the tests are green.
modules.why: Agents are only as good as what they can check themselves against. In an Anthropic experiment (Mar 2026, Opus 4.5), one agent working alone for 20 minutes built a 2D game maker for $9 whose core wiring was broken. A harness with a planner, a generator and an evaluator ran for 6 hours and built a working one for $200. The difference was the evaluator. Green tests don’t close that gap on their own: in METR’s 2025 review of an early-2025 agent, 38% of its PRs passed the maintainers’ tests and none of the 15 reviewed could merge as-is. Inside Anthropic, verification skills have had the most measurable effect on Claude’s output of any kind of skill (Jun 2026, vendor report). The checks you give the agent decide how far it gets without you.

modules.title: Skills that earn their place

keyIdeas.title: Put know-how in the lightest home
keyIdeas.body: A fixed sequence of steps is a script. Facts the agent needs on almost every turn belong in the always-loaded context file (chapter 6, Give the agent the right context). A workflow that needs judgment, or your team’s taste, is a skill. MCP is for a governed, shared set of tools, and a subagent is for parallel work or a review that must not see the main context. The evidence for the split: in Vercel’s Next.js evals (Jan 2026), a docs skill scored 53%, the same as no docs, because the agent didn’t invoke it; with explicit instructions to use it, it reached 79%, and an 8 KB docs index in AGENTS.md reached 100%. Next.js then retired its knowledge skills in 16.3 and kept its workflow skills. Supabase found that MCP alone can score below no tools at all (Opus 4.6: 58% with no tools, 50% with MCP only) and that MCP plus a skill beat both, at 67% (Apr 2026, vendor, small sample). Tools give access; a skill carries your way of using them.

keyIdeas.title: Descriptions decide triggering
keyIdeas.body: The agent scans every skill’s description to decide whether one fits the request, so write the description for the model, not as documentation: what the skill does, when to use it and when not to, with the key use case first, because long descriptions get cut. Test it with near misses, prompts that look similar but must not load the skill. Measure “did it fire” separately from “did it help” (Claude Code docs), and log real use: Anthropic logs skill calls with a hook to find skills that fire less often than expected (Jun 2026). Procedures with side effects, like a deploy, should run only when a person invokes them, which also keeps their descriptions out of the listing.

keyIdeas.title: Curated, small and specific
keyIdeas.body: In SkillsBench, focused skills with at most three modules beat large bundles, and skills that models wrote for themselves did not help on average. The Aug 2026 skill-failure study found that relevant-looking skills often made the agent implement the task wrongly or leave parts out, and that excessive verification was the largest single source of cost regressions (67 of 182): skills turn checklists into mandatory work. Anthropic’s lessons from hundreds of internal skills (Jun 2026, vendor) point the same way: don’t restate what the model does by default, build a gotchas section from real failures (the highest-signal part of any skill), give the goal and the constraints instead of every step, and put detail in separate files the skill points to. Let the agent draft a skill if you like; a person curates it, and an eval decides.

keyIdeas.title: Capability or preference, then retire
keyIdeas.body: Capability skills teach something the model can’t do yet; preference skills encode how your team does it (Philipp Schmid, Jul 2026). Capability skills expire as models improve. Next.js retiring its knowledge skills is one live example, and Anthropic removed over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt for Claude 5 models with no measurable loss on its coding evals (Jul 2026). Run the deletion test on each paragraph (remove it, rerun, and keep it deleted if nothing changes; Matt Pocock), and retire a skill when its eval delta, the score with it minus the score without it, is zero or below. Chapter 9, Learn from the Claude Code team, makes this a regular ablation.

keyIdeas.title: Test every change, with and without
keyIdeas.body: Run a few realistic prompts in fresh sessions with the skill on, then again with it off, because leftover context from writing the skill hides gaps in it. Snapshot the old version before you edit, report the difference rather than an absolute score, and review changes to assertions by hand: in Debbie O’Brien’s run, the improvement loop quietly loosened one. Every skill in the listing also costs context on every turn, so find and turn off the ones that never fire. Chapter 21, Test your agents like code, teaches the full method (trials, graders, pass^k), and chapter 23, Share and test skills across teams, runs it in CI. At Rhino, skill evals run in Lane A, on synthetic data only.

keyIdeas.title: One skill, many tools
keyIdeas.body: Skills follow the open Agent Skills format, so one folder can serve several agents: Claude Code reads .claude/skills, Codex reads .agents/skills, and Cursor reads .cursor/skills, .agents/skills and .claude/skills. Claude Code adds fields of its own, while claude.ai uploads and the Skills API reject any field outside the spec’s six, so a skill meant to travel sticks to those. Treat skills from outside your team like dependencies, because they run with your permissions (chapter 23, Share and test skills across teams).
