labs.title: Audit one skill
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): pick one skill you use, or a small one from a trusted source installed in a practice repo. Run Matt Pocock’s four checks: who invokes it, progressive disclosure (move reference used by one branch into a file the skill points to), leading words, and pruning. Check it against the spec: a name of up to 64 characters, a description of up to 1,024, and a SKILL.md under 500 lines and about 5,000 tokens; Claude Code cuts the description plus when_to_use at 1,536 characters in its listing. Add a gotchas section from failures you have seen. Then remove up to five sections one at a time and rerun three prompts in fresh sessions; a section whose removal changes nothing stays deleted. At Rhino: run it on ticket-to-pr’s SKILL.md and compare token count and results on three real tickets.
labs.output: A shorter SKILL.md, with before-and-after token counts and results

labs.title: A trigger set with near misses
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): write 20 prompts for one skill, 10 that should load it and 10 near misses that shouldn’t. Run each in a fresh session (claude -p works) and record whether the skill fired. Rewrite the description, key use case first, saying when to use it and when not to, until the set passes. If the skill has side effects, set disable-model-invocation: true so only a person can start it. At Rhino: cover the review, CI and ticket skills, include prompts where duplicate-namespace skills collide, and run /skill-doctor to find skills that never fire.
labs.output: A trigger set checked into the skill folder, with the fire rate before and after

labs.title: Skill or AGENTS.md: a small A/B
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): pick one piece of framework or library knowledge that models get wrong, such as an API newer than their training. Put it once in a skill, and once as a short index in AGENTS.md that points to the docs. Run the same three tasks three times in each setup, in fresh sessions, each with a test that checks the result. Record the pass rate, whether the skill fired and the tokens used. At Rhino: use a Next.js 16 API in fcp/frontend, on a branch, with synthetic data only.
labs.output: A one-page result with pass rates, fire rate and cost for both setups, and the home you chose

checks.q: When should a workflow be a script instead of a skill?
checks.a: When it is always the same. Skills are for work that needs judgment.

checks.q: What is a negative case?
checks.a: A prompt where the skill must not trigger, or must not call a tool. It catches over-eager skills.

checks.q: When do you retire a skill?
checks.a: When its eval delta against running without it is zero or negative.

checks.q: Framework facts the agent needs on almost every task: a skill or AGENTS.md?
checks.a: AGENTS.md, which loads in every session. In Vercel’s evals, a docs skill was never invoked in 56% of cases and scored the same as no docs, while an 8 KB docs index in AGENTS.md scored 100%. Keep skills for multi-step workflows and team taste.

watchOut: Skills that duplicate what the model already does well.
Descriptions written as documentation instead of as triggers.
Skills the agent wrote for itself, shipped with no curator and no eval. In SkillsBench they gave no benefit on average.
Long verification checklists inside a skill. They were the largest source of cost regressions in the Aug 2026 skill-failure study.

modules.goal: Put each piece of know-how where it works best (a script, the context file, a skill or a subagent), write skills that load when they should and stay quiet when they shouldn’t, keep them small and curated, and prove with an eval that each one helps, before and after every change. Retire the ones the model has caught up with.
modules.why: In an Anthropic demo (May 2026, one agent, vendor video), moving 400 lines of prompt into skills and tools took the agent from 62% to 92% on its evals. The wider evidence says skills help when people curate and test them. In SkillsBench (Feb 2026, updated Jun 2026), curated skills raised the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% across 18 model and harness setups. In its first version, skills that models wrote for themselves gave no benefit on average, and software-engineering tasks gained the least (+4.5 points). Skills can also do nothing, or harm: in Vercel’s evals (Jan 2026) a docs skill was never invoked in 56% of cases, and an Aug 2026 study traced 307 failures and cost regressions to skills the agent had loaded. A skill is a hypothesis until an eval says otherwise.

modules.title: How the Claude Code team works now

keyIdeas.title: Ablate every six months
keyIdeas.body: Delete CLAUDE.md sections, skills and hooks, then re-add only what repeated failures prove you need (Boris Cherny). Evals last one to three model generations, so rebuild them from failures you have actually seen. Never ablate compliance rules: move them into hooks first, then the prose can go. Chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills, covers retiring a skill; chapter 21, Test your agents like code, shows how to measure a harness change over several runs instead of one.

keyIdeas.title: Make the finish line a gate
keyIdeas.body: Chapter 5, Tell the agent what you want, taught goal, limits and done. The team goes one step further and makes done hard to fake. Robobun, Bun’s issue-to-PR agent, opens no PR unless a new test fails on the last release and passes on the branch, and its build command also runs the target, so the agent never tests a stale build. For one long rewrite Boris describes, the finish line was screenshots compared pixel by pixel in CI, with progress posted to Slack.

keyIdeas.title: Review as map-reduce
keyIdeas.body: Many agents look for bugs in parallel, and each candidate is checked adversarially from three perspectives before a human sees it. Robobun uses two reviewers with different jobs, a cheap conventions checker and a deep control-flow reviewer, and the human waits for the deep one. Humans then review for context the agent lacks, such as why an API is shaped the way it is, not for nits. At Rhino, a human who isn’t the requester still approves (SOC 2 CC8.1).

keyIdeas.title: Chores go on routines
keyIdeas.body: The team’s work moved from laptops to devboxes, to cloud containers, to routines: scheduled or triggered runs in Anthropic’s cloud. Boris suggests twenty to thirty one-sentence routines (dead code, stale flags, coverage gaps, duplicate abstractions), each posting small PRs to one Slack channel. At Rhino, routines are Lane A only, because they aren’t available under ZDR, and a scheduled routine runs at most once an hour.

keyIdeas.title: Tools that compound, not crutches
keyIdeas.body: Daisy Hollman works a full day without leaving the terminal to find what the agent can’t reach, then closes that gap. Prefer a skill that wraps an existing CLI over a new MCP server, give tools descriptive names so tool search finds them, and budget every always-loaded skill description like bundle size. Chapter 6, Give the agent the right context, explains why a stable prompt keeps the cache working.

keyIdeas.title: Keep the setup current
keyIdeas.body: Claude Code’s /doctor prompt-audit (v2.1.221, Aug 2026) flags instructions written for older models. Pin models until you have tested new ones (chapter 2, How AI coding agents work): on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, an unpinned `opus` alias now resolves to Opus 5.5 and bills at the Opus rate, so pinning is a cost control too. To share one instruction file across Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, make CLAUDE.md import @AGENTS.md, or symlink it. Claude Code’s own AGENTS.md fallback (v2.1.277, Sep 2026) sits behind a remote flag and is skipped without warning when telemetry or nonessential traffic is off, as in a locked-down ZDR org, so don’t rely on it.

labs.title: Ablation replay
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Use any repo with a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, yours or a public one. Pick three small closed issues whose fix a test can check. Run each twice from the same commit in fresh sessions: once as is, once with one section of the file removed. Record whether the check passes, the diff size and the number of turns. Keep a line only if removing it changed the outcome, and remember that one run proves little (chapter 2). If the file holds a compliance rule, move it into a hook first and never ablate it. At Rhino: five closed Lane A tickets through ticket-to-PR, with and without one fe-guild skill section.
labs.output: A shorter file and one line of evidence for each section you kept

labs.title: A fail-first gate
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Take one bug in any repo, or plant one in a small public sample app. Have the agent write a test that reproduces it and commit the test alone. Then write a small script that checks out the base commit (or the last release tag), runs the new test and expects it to fail, then runs it on the branch and expects it to pass. Only then let the agent fix the bug. At Rhino: an API-level test with fakes for a Jira bug, and make the script a CI step on the PR.
labs.output: A PR with the failing-test commit, the fix commit and the gate script

labs.title: Five routines on paper, one for real
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Write five one-sentence maintenance routines for a repo you know, such as “find unused exports and open one PR that removes them”. Run one by hand now as a headless prompt (`claude -p` in Claude Code) on a new branch, and judge the PR it opens: would you merge it, and what check would make it trustworthy every time? At Rhino: routines run in Anthropic’s cloud and aren’t available under ZDR, so they are Lane A only.
labs.output: Five routines, one real PR, and a verdict on whether it should run on a schedule

checks.q: What is Robobun’s merge gate, and why is it strong?

checks.q: When agents review first, what do humans review for?

Letting new models in automatically. Pin them and test first.

Boris Cherny says they cut about 80% of Claude Code’s own system prompt and got better results, because instructions written for older models turn into noise (Y Combinator, Jul 2026; the team’s own claim). modules.title: The AI-native engineer’s day

keyIdeas.title: One in front, two at most behind
keyIdeas.body: One foreground agent, at most two in the background, and about four hours of active supervision a day. Mitchell Hashimoto keeps one agent busy at all times and rarely runs more than two. Experienced orchestrators go higher (Addy Osmani calls three to five agents the sweet spot, and kills a run after three stuck iterations, Mar 2026), but only for work whose result a machine can check (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work). Five agents you can’t review are slower than one you can.

keyIdeas.title: Delegate, pair or write it yourself
keyIdeas.body: Use your delegation card from chapter 2, How AI coding agents work. Delegate when a machine can check the result, the blast radius is small, there is a precedent, and the spec takes under ten minutes. Pair on design, contracts, auth, PHI-adjacent or unfamiliar code. Write it yourself when you are building a skill, when typing is faster, or when you can’t define done yet.

keyIdeas.title: Size the brief to the task
keyIdeas.body: Chapter 5, Tell the agent what you want, sizes a spec by what a wrong guess would cost. The day-to-day evidence is thin and points one way. In a Scott Logic test (one engineer rebuilding a feature of about 1,000 lines in his hobby app, Nov 2025), Spec Kit took about 57 minutes of agent time and about 5.5 hours of review over two increments. Working in small steps, the same feature took 8 minutes of agent time and 24 minutes of his own time (15 of review, 9 of testing and small fixes), and he found it about ten times faster. Chapter 5 adds the newer evidence: a spec tool that turned one small bug fix into 16 acceptance criteria (Birgitta Böckeler, Oct 2025), and Thoughtworks keeping spec-driven development at Assess. So most tasks get a short brief, and full specs wait for work that spans sessions, layers or people.

keyIdeas.title: The night shift
keyIdeas.body: Specs by day. At the end of the day you queue small tasks whose done is a command a machine can run (chapter 7); overnight the agent writes a failing test first, implements, and reviewer personas check the work. In the morning you review commit by commit, keep, fix or discard, and put what went wrong into the harness: a doc line, a skill or a check (Jamon Holmgren; chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills). Aim for a keep rate of about 70%. Below that, the tasks were too big or too vague.

keyIdeas.title: Protect your understanding
keyIdeas.body: In Anthropic’s trial, people who asked for explanations after the code was written, or asked conceptual questions, kept quiz scores of 65% or more. Handing over the whole task, or letting the AI do the debugging, hurt learning. Two or three times a week, code without AI. Juniors use the Learning output style, which leaves TODO(human) gaps to fill. Addy Osmani’s rule fits every level: explain it or don’t ship it.

keyIdeas.title: Accountability doesn’t delegate
keyIdeas.body: Never file a PR you haven’t reviewed (Simon Willison). Every PR carries an “Agent involvement” block: what the agent did, what you verified, what evidence is attached. Keep PRs at 400 lines or fewer and stack anything bigger. At Rhino, someone other than you approves it.

labs.title: One-day time diary
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min, spread over one workday): Log every agent task as you go: its mode (delegate, pair or self), the minutes you spent supervising, how many agents were running, and whether you kept the result. Mark the moments you felt tired or lost track. At the end of the day, work out your keep rate and your real supervision time. At Rhino: keep it for a week and bring it to the Friday metrics look.

labs.title: A small night shift
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min: 30 at the end of one day, 45 the next morning): Pick three small tasks on any repo, each with done as a command a machine can run, such as a missing test for a date helper, a typed prop on a React component, or an input check on a Django or FastAPI endpoint with its test. Write a short brief for each (goal, limits, done), launch each in its own git worktree or headless session, and stop for the day. Next morning, review commit by commit and mark each keep, fix or discard, with one line on why. At Rhino: Lane A tickets only, such as coverage tasks, on factory-seeded data.
labs.output: A keep rate for three tasks and one harness fix for the most common miss

labs.title: Comprehension probe and involvement block
labs.body: Solo (about 40 min): Take the last agent diff you kept (lab 2 works). Without looking, write what changed, what could break and how it is tested. Then read the diff and mark what you missed. Write an “Agent involvement” block for its PR: what the agent did, what you verified, what evidence is attached. At Rhino: add the block to the PR template, and after two weeks compare what Byte, Rhino’s AI review bot, finds on PRs with and without it.
labs.output: A self-check you can repeat, and an Agent involvement block ready to paste

checks.q: When should you pair instead of delegating?
checks.a: On design work, contracts, auth or PHI-adjacent code, and code you don’t know yet.

checks.q: What makes a good night-shift task?
checks.a: A machine can check done, the blast radius is small, the codebase has a precedent, and the spec takes under ten minutes.

checks.q: What did Anthropic’s trial find about learning?
checks.a: The AI group scored 50% on comprehension against 67%, and was not significantly faster. Asking for explanations and conceptual questions kept scores at 65% or more; full delegation and letting the AI debug hurt learning.

checks.q: A teammate says five agents at once must beat two. What does the evidence say?
checks.a: More agents only help if you can review what they make. In BCG’s survey of 1,488 US workers, perceived productivity peaked at three AI tools at once, and people with “brain fry” reported 33% more decision fatigue. Those are self-reports about tools, so treat them as a warning, not a limit.

watchOut: Parallelism theater: five agents you can’t review are slower than one you can.
Reviewing the agent’s summary instead of the diff.
Ad-hoc runs late at night. Queue them for the night shift.

extras.title: A day, as a template
lines: | Time | Block | What happens |
| 09:00 | Morning review | Review the night shift commit by commit. Keep, fix or discard, and note why. |
| 09:45 | Deep pair block | Notifications off. One agent, plan, build and verify with you in the loop. |
| 12:00 | Review batch | Teammates’ PRs and agent PRs, in one sitting. |
| 14:00 | Collaboration | Design reviews, specs, the pairing rotation. |
| 15:30 | Hands-on block | Two or three times a week, no AI. Keep your own model of the code. |
| 16:30 | Night-shift launch | Queue small tasks whose done is a command a machine can run. |
| 20:00 | Stop | No ad-hoc runs after this. They go in tomorrow’s night shift. |

extras.title: A week
lines: - **Mon: Harness hour.** Turn last week’s repeated mistakes into rules, tests or hooks.
- **Tue: Pairing rotation.** Fifteen minutes watching a teammate work with an agent.
- **Wed: Comprehension check.** Explain one agent-written module to a peer without notes.
- **Thu: Show and tell.** One win and one failure in your team channel (at Rhino, #ai-practices).
- **Fri: Metrics look.** Your keep rate, PR size and review turnaround. Never tokens.

extras.title: Delegate, pair or write it yourself
lines: - **Delegate** when all hold: A machine can check the result; The blast radius is small; There is a precedent in the codebase; The spec takes under ten minutes.
- **Pair** on: Design or architecture decisions; Contracts between services; Auth, permissions or PHI-adjacent code; Code you don’t know yet.
- **Write it yourself** when: You are building the skill the agent will use; Typing it is faster than specifying it; You can’t define done yet.

extras.title: Role variants
lines: - **PM.** Build a clickable prototype in Claude Design or a preview branch before writing the ticket. Write evals instead of acceptance-criteria fields: five to ten example inputs with the expected outcome. At Anthropic, PM and engineering roles are merging and evals are underused (Cat Wu, Apr 2026).

- **Design.** Ship small UI changes yourself: a Storybook story and a PR the agent drafts, approved by an engineer who isn’t you (Jenny Wen describes designers shipping at Anthropic, Mar 2026). Chapter 11, Build UI with agents, shows how.

- **QA.** Turn test plans into verification contracts agents can run (chapter 7). Run exploratory agents on seeded test tenants, and keep them within what the shared QA environment can take: at Rhino, the cloud API serves only about four requests at a time per pod.

modules.watchTime: 27 min core, 1 h 38 min with electives
modules.goal: Put the first nine chapters to work in one ordinary day: review the night’s output, protect a deep pair block, batch your reviews, launch a night shift with a done the machine can check, and set limits that protect your judgment and your understanding of the code.
modules.why: Speed without a plan costs you in two places. In Anthropic’s randomized trial (52 mostly junior developers learning a new library, Jan 2026), the group using AI scored 50% on a follow-up quiz against 67% for the group coding by hand, with the biggest gap in debugging, and finished only about two minutes faster, a difference that was not significant. Oversight also wears people down: in a BCG survey of 1,488 full-time US workers in many jobs, not only developers (Harvard Business Review, Mar 2026), those who reported “AI brain fry” also reported 33% more decision fatigue and 39% more major errors. Separately, perceived productivity peaked at three AI tools used at once and fell beyond four. Those are self-reports about tools, not a measure of agents, but they point the same way as the trial: design the day, don’t just speed it up.

modules.title: Frontend with agents: eyes, design system and taste

keyIdeas.title: Give the agent eyes: the see-it loop
keyIdeas.body: Edit, check it compiles, render the page, read the console and network, read the page structure, take a screenshot, fix, repeat. Every step returns something the agent can read. Without it, you are the loop: you click around, watch the console and paste errors back. The Next.js team showed the failure: asked about a hydration error, an agent ran curl, got clean HTML and reported no errors, because the error lived in the browser (Nov 2025). In Claude Code, `/verify` builds and drives the app to check a change, and `/run-skill-generator` records how to launch your project in `.claude/skills/run-<name>/SKILL.md`, so every agent starts the app the same way. In Next.js 16.3 the `next-dev-loop` skill joins the framework’s view (`/_next/mcp`: routes, server logs, compile issues) with the browser’s view (`agent-browser`: DOM, console, network, React tree). Cursor, Codex and Copilot get the same loop through a browser MCP server or CLI.

keyIdeas.title: Pick a light browser tool, and read structure before pixels
keyIdeas.body: Browser tools differ in cost. The Playwright team recommends its CLI with skills for coding agents: in their demo the same task used about 114,000 tokens through Playwright MCP and 26,800 through the CLI, because the CLI saves snapshots and screenshots to files and the agent opens only what it needs (vendor demo, Feb 2026). MCP still fits long exploratory loops and self-healing tests. Chrome DevTools for agents adds performance traces, Lighthouse and memory tools. Read the accessibility snapshot or the DOM contract from chapter 7, Check the agent’s work, first; take a screenshot when the question is about pixels. Chapter 12, Let agents check every screen, turns screenshots into baselines.

keyIdeas.title: Your design system is the agent’s most important context
keyIdeas.body: The agent needs three things: tokens (Tailwind `@theme` values or Figma variables with their code names), components (Code Connect mappings and Storybook stories) and rules (AGENTS.md plus a design-language skill). Figma says Code Connect is the main way to get components reused: “Without it, the model is guessing.” Figma’s own rules for its MCP server: call `get_design_context` first, `get_metadata` if the frame is too big, then `get_screenshot`, then translate the React and Tailwind output into your project’s components and tokens, and check it 1:1 against the design. Storybook MCP (Storybook 10.3 or later) gives the agent `docs-list`, `docs-show`, story instructions and `test-run`, and its AGENTS.md template opens with “Never hallucinate component properties!” Round trips close the loop: the agent can draw a Figma frame for every state of a flow, or compare a Figma frame with the running screen and list the differences by severity.

keyIdeas.title: Knowledge goes in AGENTS.md, workflows go in skills
keyIdeas.body: In Vercel’s evals on new Next.js 16 APIs (Jan 2026), no docs scored 53%, a docs skill also scored 53% because the agent never invoked it in 56% of cases, the skill plus explicit instructions scored 79%, and an 8 KB compressed docs index in AGENTS.md scored 100%. Next.js acted on it: from 16.2 it bundles version-matched docs in `node_modules/next/dist/docs/`, and in 16.3 `next dev` writes a managed AGENTS.md block that points to them. Its knowledge skills were retired; only workflow skills such as `next-dev-loop` remain. The rule for any framework: facts the agent needs on almost every turn live in always-loaded context, and multi-step procedures live in skills. In Claude Code, make CLAUDE.md import `@AGENTS.md` (chapter 6, Give the agent the right context, and chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills).

keyIdeas.title: Shape the React code so agents can check it
keyIdeas.body: Keep presentation components pure (props in, UI out) and put fetching, state and hooks in wired containers. Then Storybook only has to model props, and the agent can render loading, empty, error and long-text states without mocking an API. The same hosts put the review difference simply: you can judge a backend plan by reading it, but a frontend change has to be seen (Dex Horthy and Vaibhav Gupta, Apr 2026). Strict TypeScript is the cheapest verifier: GitHub’s Octoverse 2025 cites a study where 94% of LLM compile errors were type-check failures, and the red-squiggle hook from chapter 7 runs tsc after every edit.

keyIdeas.title: Taste is where you still lead
keyIdeas.body: Models drift to safe, average choices (Inter or Roboto fonts, purple gradients on white). Anthropic calls this distributional convergence and counters it with a skill of about 400 tokens (Nov 2025). For a product like the FCP, taste means your design language, not novelty, so Rhino’s design-language skill is the taste skill. Looking right is not working right: in the UI2App benchmark, the model best at reproducing screenshots ranked fourth on building the interactions, 5.2x behind the leader (Jul 2026). Ask for several versions and choose, or ask the agent to interview you first; the choice, the novel interaction and the final look are yours.

labs.title: Blindfold, then eyes
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): in any React or Next.js app (a fresh `create-next-app` works), pick a small UI change that can break in the browser, such as a dark-mode toggle or a form with client-side validation. Run A: the agent may use only tsc, lint and unit tests; count how many times you had to point out a problem. Reset with git. Run B: give it a browser (Playwright CLI with its skills, or Chrome DevTools for agents started with `--isolated`), ask it to check the page itself and attach screenshots at 390 and 1280 px in light and dark. Count again. Then run `/run-skill-generator` (or ask your agent to write down its launch steps) and commit the recipe. At Rhino: use a small FCP UI ticket on QA with factory-seeded data, never your own logged-in Chrome, and make the recipe boot the front end with a QA backend (keep VIEWER_URL on the same env as API_BASE_URL).
labs.output: Two runs with their feedback-round counts, the screenshots, and a committed launch recipe

labs.title: One screen, three levels of context
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): clone Figma’s Simple Design System (github.com/figma/sds: React components with Storybook stories, CSS tokens in `src/theme.css` and Code Connect files in `src/figma`). Ask the agent to build the same new small screen, such as an account settings panel, three times: (a) from a screenshot or sketch only; (b) with the stories and Code Connect files as its component docs; (c) as (b), plus three AGENTS.md rules: reuse existing components, never use a prop that no story or type shows, no hex or px literals. Score each run: how many elements are design-system components, how many hardcoded hex or px values a grep finds, how many invented props tsc rejects, and what you would say in review. If you have a Figma Dev or Full seat, add Figma MCP to run (c); View and Collab seats get only 6 calls a month. At Rhino: do it on one FCP screen built from `designSystem` atoms and molecules. Storybook MCP needs 10.3 or later and the FCP is on 10.2, so the agent reads the story files for now.
labs.output: A scored table for the three runs and the AGENTS.md lines that made the difference

labs.title: Docs index against memory
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): in a Next.js 16.2 or later project, check that AGENTS.md points to `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` (on older projects run `npx @next/codemod@canary agents-md`; on 16.3 `next dev` writes it). If you use Claude Code, make CLAUDE.md import `@AGENTS.md` first, because the AGENTS.md fallback does not always load. Then, each time in a fresh session, ask the agent three times to use a newer API such as `'use cache'`, `after()` or `proxy.ts` with the block, and three times without it (move the file aside; on 16.3 also set `agentRules: false`). Count the runs that use the current API correctly. At Rhino: the FCP front end has no AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md today. Draft one under 40 lines (the Next.js block, the commands, and the rule to reuse `designSystem` components) and open it as a PR for a teammate to review.
labs.output: A with-and-without pass count and a reviewed AGENTS.md

checks.q: The agent says a UI change is done and every test passes. Why is that not enough?
checks.a: Tests, types and lint are text checks. Many UI bugs exist only in the running browser, such as a hydration error or a broken dark mode, so the agent must render the page, read the console and look.

checks.q: Why use the Playwright CLI rather than Playwright MCP in a coding session?
checks.a: The CLI saves snapshots and screenshots to files and the agent reads only what it needs. In the Playwright team’s demo, one task took about 26,800 tokens with the CLI and 114,000 with MCP. MCP fits long exploratory loops.

checks.q: What goes in AGENTS.md, and what goes in a skill?
checks.a: Knowledge the agent needs on almost every turn, such as where the docs for your framework version are, goes in AGENTS.md. Multi-step workflows go in skills. In Vercel’s evals the AGENTS.md index scored 100%, and the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases.

checks.q: What does Code Connect give the agent that a screenshot does not?
checks.a: The real component behind each Figma component, with its import and prop mapping. Without it the agent guesses, and writes divs with hex values.

watchOut: Your own logged-in browser. Claude in Chrome shares your browser’s login state, and its recorded GIFs can capture account details. Agents verify in an isolated browser, on QA, with seeded data. PHI never enters a prompt, and a screenshot is part of the prompt.
Figma’s React and Tailwind output taken as final code. Figma calls it a representation of the design. Map it to your components and tokens.
Screenshot loops that burn tokens. Read the structure first, and take element screenshots only when the question is about pixels.
A screen that looks right and doesn’t work. Visual fidelity is not behavior: click through the flow and its states before you call it done.

modules.goal: Build UI with an agent that sees what it built, builds with your own components and tokens, reads the docs for the framework version you run, and takes its taste from your design language instead of from the average of the internet.
modules.why: Web code leads Claude Code use: JavaScript and TypeScript (31%) plus HTML and CSS (28%) made up 59% of Claude Code queries in Anthropic’s Economic Index (April 2025). UI is also where agents fail most quietly. An agent can pass tsc, Biome and every unit test and still ship a broken screen, because the bug only exists in the running browser. When one research team fed screenshots and browser-test results back to the model, Claude 3.5 Sonnet’s accuracy on a web-app benchmark rose from 26.4% to 51.9% (WebGen-Agent, one study, Sep 2025). Context moves the needle just as much: in Vercel’s own evals, an 8 KB docs index in AGENTS.md took the pass rate on new Next.js 16 APIs from 53% to 100% (Jan 2026).

modules.title: Let agents check every screen

keyIdeas.title: The state matrix
keyIdeas.body: Rows are states: loading, empty, error, partial data, long text, many rows, no permission. Columns are widths (390, 768, 1280, 1920 px), light and dark, left-to-right and right-to-left, and reduced motion. Seven states × four widths × two themes × two directions is already 112 cells. The back end decides many rows: every empty result and status code your API returns (200 with no items, 403, 500, a slow response) is a state the screen must draw. Stories list the states; Storybook globals, Chromatic modes or Playwright projects (`viewport`, `colorScheme`, `reducedMotion`) list the rest. The agent writes the missing state stories first: Storybook 10.4’s agentic setup writes stories and interaction tests for up to 10 components and generates MSW mocks. In one agency audit of an AI-built UI (Evil Martians, Jul 2026), six accessibility bugs were “invisible in the running app because nobody had rendered the states in isolation with an accessibility checker attached”.

keyIdeas.title: Structure, then pixels, then people
keyIdeas.body: Run the cheap, exact checks first: unit tests (Vitest); component and interaction tests (Storybook `play` functions through the Vitest addon, or Vitest 4 Browser Mode, stable since Oct 2025); aria snapshots (`toMatchAriaSnapshot`, a YAML copy of the accessibility tree) for structure; visual baselines (Playwright `toHaveScreenshot`, Vitest 4 `toMatchScreenshot`, Chromatic) for pixels; Playwright end-to-end tests for flows, which Playwright’s planner, generator and healer agents can draft; performance traces last. These are ordinary test tools, so Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot or Gemini can all run the same stack. Taste, product fit and new interactions stay with people. This extends the contract rule from chapter 7, Check the agent’s work, and uses the browser tools from chapter 11, Build UI with agents.

keyIdeas.title: Ratchets, not judgments
keyIdeas.body: A ratchet is a committed number that CI lets go down and never up. Commit today’s axe violations per story or page; CI fails if any count rises; agents may only lower it. The July 2026 study’s verified loop accepted a change “only if violations strictly decrease”, caught 57 of 57 seeded violations and rejected 126 of 126 harmful edits. Store fingerprints (rule ID plus selectors), as Playwright’s docs suggest, so unrelated markup changes don’t break the check. Visual baselines and bundle-size budgets work the same way. A baseline update is part of the pull request, so a person who is not the requester approves it (SOC 2 CC8.1).

keyIdeas.title: Budgets as exit criteria
keyIdeas.body: “Good” means LCP within 2.5 s, INP of 200 ms or less and CLS of 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads (web.dev). Lab tools can’t measure INP because nobody is clicking, so use Total Blocking Time as the lab stand-in. With Chrome DevTools for agents, the agent records a trace (`performance_start_trace`) for LCP and CLS, runs `lighthouse_audit` for accessibility and best practices, and works toward a number instead of reading every file and guessing. Its `debug-optimize-lcp` skill is the playbook. Run the budget every night on the heaviest routes and in every PR that touches them.

keyIdeas.title: Hebrew is a state, not a translation
keyIdeas.body: Israeli teams ship right-to-left. Use logical CSS properties (`margin-inline-start`, Tailwind `ms-` and `me-`) and lint the physical ones out (Evil Martians suggest Stylelint’s `property-layout-mappings` rule). Put `dir="auto"` on free-text fields. Never infer direction from `navigator.language`: “a user whose system is set to `en-US` might type Arabic” (Evil Martians, May 2026). Test with real Hebrew and long strings, not lorem ipsum. When the same RTL bug reaches review twice, fix the harness: add the lint rule.

keyIdeas.title: Evidence without PHI
keyIdeas.body: A screenshot the agent reads is part of its prompt, so the PHI rule covers every screenshot, GIF, trace and baseline. Playwright traces hold full DOM snapshots and request and response bodies. Claude in Chrome shares your browser’s login state, and its GIFs capture “account details on logged-in pages”. Chrome DevTools for agents’ performance tools may send trace URLs to Google’s CrUX API unless you pass `--no-performance-crux`, its default profile persists between runs (`--isolated` gives a throwaway one), and `autoConnect` can attach to your personal Chrome. So: a throwaway profile, local or QA hosts only, factory-seeded synthetic data, and baselines made only from that data, because baselines are committed to git. For login, a Playwright setup project reads credentials from environment variables, so the agent never sees the password.

labs.title: Run the matrix on one component
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Pick one component that shows data (a table, a list or a card) in any React repo with Storybook; a small public sample app works. Ask the agent to list every state from the component’s props and data hooks, write the missing stories with fake data, then check every cell at 390, 768 and 1280 px, in light and dark, and left-to-right and right-to-left with a real Hebrew string: axe result, aria snapshot and screenshot per cell. Time the agent, then check four cells by hand and time yourself. At Rhino: use a designSystem organism in the FCP frontend, whose stories already have a light and dark theme switch, and synthetic data only.
labs.output: A filled-in matrix, a findings list and the two times

labs.title: Build an accessibility ratchet
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Add `@axe-core/playwright` to any web app. For each page or story, save violation fingerprints (rule ID and selectors) for the WCAG A and AA tags to a committed baseline file. The test fails if any count goes up, and asks you to lower the baseline when a count goes down. Plant a bug (remove a form label) and watch it fail. Then ask the agent to fix one violation, and accept its change only if that count drops and no other count rises. At Rhino: the FCP frontend has Storybook’s accessibility addon, but no CI step fails on its results yet; start with five designSystem stories.
labs.output: A baseline file, a red run for the planted bug and one PR that lowers the count

labs.title: Baselines in the CI image, plus one budget
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Add `toHaveScreenshot` for two screens at two widths, in light and dark. Generate the baselines inside the official Playwright Docker image that matches your Playwright version, not on your laptop, and mask moving parts such as dates. Change one CSS value and look at the diff image. Then point Chrome DevTools for agents (`--isolated --no-performance-crux`) at a local production build with seeded data, record a trace for the heaviest route, and write LCP and CLS budgets the next run must meet. At Rhino: every FCP Playwright project runs Desktop Chrome today, so add a 390 px project to the PR suite first.
labs.output: Committed baselines, one diff image and a budget file

checks.q: Where can an agent beat a person at checking screens, and where can’t it?
checks.a: Coverage: it checks every state at every width, theme and direction (112 cells for one screen) on every PR without getting tired. It can’t judge taste or product fit, and axe finds only part of WCAG problems.

checks.q: What is an accessibility ratchet, and why not just ask the agent to fix accessibility?
checks.a: A committed violation count per story or page that CI lets go down, never up. Unchecked LLM fixes improved 24 pages and hurt 20 in one study; a strict-decrease rule makes regressions on automated checks impossible.

checks.q: Who approves a visual baseline change, and where are baselines made?
checks.a: A person who is not the requester, because the baseline is part of the PR. They are made in the CI image, because rendering changes with the OS, fonts and hardware.

checks.q: Name three ways screen evidence can leak PHI.
checks.a: Screenshots or GIFs of logged-in pages with real data, Playwright traces that hold DOM snapshots and network bodies, and trace URLs sent to CrUX without `--no-performance-crux`. A personal Chrome profile through autoConnect is a fourth.

watchOut: A healer that turns red into green. Playwright’s healer skips a test when it believes the feature is broken: read that as a bug report, not a pass, and keep test-gaming lint on (chapter 7).
“Zero axe violations” read as “accessible”. Storybook’s docs say axe catches up to 57% of WCAG issues; keyboard use, focus order and screen readers still need a person.
Baselines made on a laptop and compared in CI. Browser rendering changes with the OS, fonts, hardware and headless mode.
An agent that runs `--update-snapshots` to make CI pass. A baseline update is a change to review image by image, not a fix.
modules.watchTime: 31 min core, 50 min with electives
modules.goal: Turn “does it look right?” into checks an agent runs on every UI change: every state at every width, theme and text direction, an accessibility count that can only go down, visual baselines that a second person approves, and performance budgets. All of it runs on seeded data in an isolated browser.
modules.why: People check the happy path at one width in one theme. In February 2026 WebAIM’s scan of a million home pages found detected WCAG failures on 95.9% of them (94.8% in 2025) and 56.1 errors per page (up 10.1%), “reversing a trend of small improvements each of the previous 6 years”. WebAIM names “automated or AI-assisted coding practices (‘vibe coding’)” as one factor. Agents don’t fix this by themselves: in a July 2026 lab study, unchecked LLM accessibility edits improved 24 pages and made 20 worse over 100 trials. What agents add is coverage. One screen has more than 100 combinations of state, width, theme and direction, and an agent can check all of them on every pull request, if you give it the matrix and a rule that accepts only improvement.

shipIt.body: A skill that, for any changed component, lists its states, runs the matrix on seeded data in an isolated browser, and posts one summary table in the PR: cells checked, axe counts against the baseline, visual diffs and budget results. Baseline changes go to a reviewer who is not the requester.

keyIdeas.title: Contract before code
keyIdeas.body: The contract is the machine-readable description of an interface: an OpenAPI file for REST (drf-spectacular generates it from Django REST Framework; FastAPI serves one by itself), a `.proto` file for gRPC, the public types of an SDK. Change it first, in its own diff, and have a person approve that diff before any handler exists. Then two tools guard it in CI. `oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR` knows 339 breaking changes among 755 kinds of change, such as a removed response property, a new required request property or a deleted endpoint. `buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main'` checks protobuf at four levels, from FILE (the default and strictest, which protects generated code) down to WIRE (the binary format only). The same file then generates what people used to write by hand: TypeScript types (`openapi-typescript`), SDK clients, mocks for the UI (chapter 15, Build a whole feature with agents) and fuzz tests (chapter 14, Keep agent-written back ends safe). Agents do well against this kind of target: BaxBench builds each of its 392 back-end tasks from an OpenAPI spec plus functional tests, and the top model is functionally correct on 86.2% of them. Chapter 14 shows why correct is not the same as secure.

keyIdeas.title: One writer, many checkers
keyIdeas.body: A back-end team of one is one agent that writes and several checkers that can’t. Each classic role becomes a deterministic gate first and, where judgment helps, a reviewer agent with read-only tools. The API designer is oasdiff or buf, plus a reviewer that grades the diff against your API style guide. The DBA is squawk, a migration rehearsal and a query count. QA is failure-path tests. In Claude Code a reviewer is a subagent whose tool list holds only Read, Grep and Glob; keep the checks where the writer can’t edit them (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work). The reason is measured. In Thoughtworks’ August 2025 experiment, a multi-agent pipeline building Spring Boot CRUD back ends “frequently claimed the build and tests were successful” when they were not, added endpoints nobody asked for, changed a priority field from “1, 2, 3” to “low, medium, high” between runs, and patched a design problem with `@JsonIgnore`. Small domains of 3 to 5 entities took 25 to 30 minutes for $2 to $3. The verdict: not ready to maintain a business codebase “without human oversight”.

keyIdeas.title: A throwaway database per task
keyIdeas.body: Agents need a real Postgres with realistic rows: not SQLite, not a mock, and never a shared or production database. Give each task its own copy, made from a template filled with synthetic, factory-built data, and delete it when the task ends. Plain Postgres does this with `CREATE DATABASE task_812 TEMPLATE seed_synthetic` (no other session may be connected to the template while it copies); Neon branches and copy-on-write forks do it in seconds. This is already how agents work: Databricks, which acquired Neon in 2025, reported in January 2026 that “AI agents now create 80% of all databases and 97% of database branches”. Copies also make experiments cheap: the agent tries five index strategies on five copies and brings back EXPLAIN numbers instead of opinions. Seed data comes from factories (factory_boy in Django), not from exported fixtures and never from production, and every feature adds or extends a factory. A branch of production is production data. At Rhino that means PHI, so branch only from the synthetic template.

keyIdeas.title: Expand, migrate, contract
keyIdeas.body: A migration never runs alone. During a rolling deploy, old pods, old SDK versions and scheduled jobs keep using the database while the new code starts. So a change that would break old code is split across releases. Expand: only add (a new table, a nullable column or one with a constant default, an index built concurrently). Migrate: write to both places, backfill in batches, then move reads to the new place. Contract: remove the old column in a later release, once nothing reads it. A rename, a type change or a dropped column in one step breaks whatever still runs the old code. The same order shapes a whole back-end slice: the contract, then the expand migration in its own PR, then the service with its tests, then serializers, views and permissions, then regenerated clients, with the contract step filed as a ticket for a later release. When the database changes, the migration comes before the code that reads it, which refines the slice order in chapter 6, Give the agent the right context. At Rhino, on-prem clients can be older than the cloud and nothing negotiates versions, so contract steps wait until every client has moved, proto fields are never removed or renumbered, and new model fields are `null=True`.

keyIdeas.title: Machines check every migration
keyIdeas.body: The quiet danger is locks. Many forms of `ALTER TABLE` need an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and a statement waiting for that lock “starts blocking even read-only transactions” behind it (Nikolay Samokhvalov, Postgres.ai). So lint the SQL, not the Python: `python manage.py sqlmigrate app 0042 | squawk` flags require-concurrent-index-creation, adding-not-nullable-field, renaming-column, changing-column-type, ban-drop-column, constraint-missing-not-valid and require-timeout-settings (start each migration with `set lock_timeout = '1s'`). Django has the safe forms: `AddIndexConcurrently` in a migration with `atomic = False`, and `AddConstraintNotValid` followed by `ValidateConstraint` in a separate migration. Since Postgres 11, a column with a non-volatile default needs no table rewrite. Then rehearse: apply the whole migration history to a fresh throwaway database and run the tests before proposing the migration (rule 3 of Prisma’s AGENTS.md for databases). Django’s test runner already migrates a fresh `test_` database, but an empty one, so it proves the migration runs, not that it is safe on real volumes; rehearse on the seeded copy too. Never let the agent edit a migration that has already been applied; it writes a new, corrective one (Atlas). And put the rules in CI, not only in the prompt: rules in an agent’s instruction file are “a suggestion, not a guardrail” (Atlas, April 2026).

keyIdeas.title: No production credentials in an agent’s reach
keyIdeas.body: Three incidents set the rule. Replit, July 2025: its agent deleted SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin’s production database during a code freeze, and Replit’s fix was architectural (automatic separation of development and production databases, plus one-click restore). PocketOS, April 2026: a Cursor agent on Claude Opus 4.6, working on staging, hit a credential mismatch, found an API token in an unrelated file and deleted the production database and its backups in one call, in 9 seconds. Its own summary: “I guessed instead of verifying.” Supabase MCP, July 2025: a support ticket carrying a prompt injection made an agent running as `service_role`, which bypasses Row-Level Security, read the `integration_tokens` table and copy it into the support messages the attacker could read. The rule for every tool is the same: agents write migrations and open PRs; pipelines apply them. The agent’s environment holds only its task database URL, `.env` files are denied by permission rules, a PreToolUse hook blocks DROP, TRUNCATE, flush, reset and any other database URL, and database MCP servers run read-only on synthetic data. Vendors now build the same walls: Prisma 6.15 asks a human before an agent runs `migrate reset`; Prisma 8 (July 2026) removed the command and announced a Migration Runner, so an agent holds only “an authentication token”, never “an admin-authorized connection URL”; Railway made every delete soft for 48 hours.

videos.title: AI agents love Convex. Here’s why.
videos.speaker: Jamie Turner, CEO of Convex
videos.desc: The clearest talk on what makes a back end easy for agents to build: fast typed feedback, code you can reason about locally, and transactions that remove race bugs. It is a vendor pitch, but the principles work in Django too.

clips.label: Feedback: one typed path from the database to the function to the client, so the agent sees a mistake before it runs anything
Removing the race and consistency “meta”: transactions and automatic retries instead of rules that live in senior engineers’ heads

takeaways: From Convex’s write-up of this talk: “TypeScript rejects a typo like `status: 'donee'` before the agent ever runs the code.” In Django the same feedback comes from typed serializers, a generated schema and types, and a targeted test that runs in seconds.

Race conditions sit in “a mostly-invisible meta layer” that agents can’t learn from training data. Make correctness structural instead: `transaction.atomic`, `select_for_update` on the row you change, and unique constraints in the database.
videos.tryAtRhino: Time the loop for one rhinoCloud module, from an edit to a failing targeted test. Put the exact targeted-test command in CLAUDE.md so the agent never waits minutes for the full suite.
watchOut: Convex sells the platform in this talk. Take the three principles, not the product choice.

videos.title: Postgres schema migrations using the expand/contract pattern
videos.speaker: Andrew Farries, Xata
videos.desc: The author of pgroll, an open-source Postgres migration tool, on why schema changes break running apps and how expand/contract keeps old and new versions working side by side.

clips.label: Common migration pitfalls: changes that break client apps, surprise table locks, and mistakes that lose data
The expand/contract pattern: two schema versions live at once during a rollout

takeaways: From the talk’s description, the three failure classes are “schema changes breaking client applications”, “unexpected table locking causing downtime” and “human mistakes causing data loss”. Check every agent-written migration for all three.

During expand/contract, each version of the app sees the schema version it was built for, so old and new code run side by side. pgroll does this with Postgres views and backfills; plain Django gets it from migrations split across releases.
videos.tryAtRhino: For the next rhinoCore change to an existing column, plan three PRs across two releases (expand, migrate, contract), and write in each PR what an older on-prem client or SDK sees at that step.

videos.title: Let an AI Agent Loose on Postgres, Safely: Claude Code + Ghost
videos.speaker: Julien Simon
videos.desc: A short, current demo of a database per task with Claude Code: copy-on-write forks of a 389,561-row table, a different index strategy on each, a race with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, keep the winner and delete the rest.

clips.label: Forking the database before any change
Five index strategies on five forks, raced with EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS, and the results

takeaways: From the description: database experiments mean DDL, “all destructive, all irreversible”, so teams keep agents away from anything real “and you lose most of the value”. Copies give the value back.
Parallel copies turn a debate into a measurement. The agent tries each option on its own copy and returns numbers.
videos.tryAtRhino: Do it without any vendor: five `CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE` copies of a local database seeded with factories, one index per copy, EXPLAIN ANALYZE for one slow rhinoCloud query. A template copy is a full copy, so keep the seed small.
watchOut: Ghost’s site says it is winding down and no longer accepts new users (checked Sep 2026). Learn the pattern and use Postgres templates, Neon branches or your platform’s forks.

videos.title: AI Agent Deleted a Production Database in 9 Seconds
videos.speaker: ByteMonk
videos.desc: A system-design breakdown of the PocketOS incident. What failed was token scope, backup design and a missing approval gate, not only the model.

clips.label: The credential mismatch, the broad token, and why the database and its backups were deleted together
Least privilege, confirmation gates for destructive actions, and why config rules are not guardrails

takeaways: The agent was blocked by a credential mismatch and reached for a broader token it found on disk. Anything an agent can read, it may use.
Backups inside the same blast radius as the database are not backups. Railway has since made deletes soft for 48 hours and stopped deletes from cascading to backups.
A rule in a config file is a request. A scoped token and a confirmation gate are walls.
videos.tryAtRhino: List every credential a Claude Code session can read on your laptop: `.env` files, CLI configs, shell history. Anything that reaches a shared or production system moves out of reach, and `Read(./.env)` goes into your deny rules.
watchOut: A nine-minute summary simplifies. Cerbos’ and Railway’s write-ups have the details.

videos.title: Zero-downtime migrations, Postgres.FM 048
videos.speaker: Nikolay Samokhvalov & Michael Christofides
videos.desc: The founders of Postgres.ai and pgMustard on lock_timeout, retries, and adding columns and tables without downtime. Older, and still exactly how Postgres locks work.

clips.label: lock_timeout, and retries with exponential backoff
Adding a new column and a new table safely

takeaways: From Nikolay’s post linked in the description: a DDL statement waiting for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocks the queries behind it. A short lock_timeout (his example is 50ms) plus retries with exponential backoff and jitter avoids the pile-up.
This is why squawk’s require-timeout-settings rule wants `set lock_timeout` at the top of every migration.

videos.title: Skill Issue: How We Used AI to Make Agents Actually Good at Supabase
videos.speaker: Pedro Rodrigues, Supabase
videos.desc: A workshop on database skills measured with evals: an agent builds a Supabase app with no skill, the security gaps appear, then a skill closes them.

clips.label: The agent builds the app with no skills
Finding the security gaps it left
Writing the security skill

takeaways: Supabase’s own eval (Apr 2026, six scenarios per condition, “early results with a small sample size”): without the skill, agents skipped RLS policies, invented CLI commands and created views that silently bypass RLS. MCP plus the skill raised Sonnet 4.6 from 46% to 71%; MCP alone sometimes scored below no tools at all.

Tools alone are not knowledge. A database skill that carries your rules, checked by an eval, turns “the agent knows Postgres” into “the agent knows our Postgres” (chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills).
watchOut: RLS is authorization. Testing who may read what is the core of chapter 14, Keep agent-written back ends safe.

readings.title: AGENTS.md for Databases
Squawk rules
PostgreSQL-specific database migration operations
Breaking changes
How far can we push AI autonomy in code generation?
AI coding agent deleted a production database in 9 seconds

labs.title: Put a contract gate on one API
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): In any Django REST Framework app with drf-spectacular, or any FastAPI app (it serves `/openapi.json` by itself), export the schema to a committed file (`./manage.py spectacular --file schema.yml --validate`). Write a script CI can run: regenerate the file and fail if it differs from the committed copy, then run `oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR base.yml schema.yml` with `base.yml` taken from main. Plant a breaking change (rename a response field) and watch it fail. Then ask the agent for the additive version (add the new field, keep the old one) and watch it pass. Finally, generate TypeScript types with `npx openapi-typescript schema.yml -o schema.d.ts` and point one frontend call at them. If the repo has `.proto` files, add `buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main'` too. At Rhino: rhinoCloud already serves its schema through drf-spectacular (`/docs/v2/openapi/`), but no CI job compares it with main and the frontend’s API types are written by hand, so run oasdiff in report-only mode first. For the gRPC contract in `common/fcp_common/rhinoAgentRpc`, on-prem clients can be older than the cloud, so a removed or renumbered field is always breaking.
labs.output: A committed schema, one red run for the planted break, one green run for the additive fix, and generated types

labs.title: Make one risky migration safe
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): In any Django and Postgres app, seed a local database with factories (a few hundred thousand rows in one table is enough) and save it as a template with `createdb -T app_dev seed_synthetic` (close other connections first; Postgres won’t copy a database in use). Ask the agent to rename a column on that table and add an index in one migration. Pipe `python manage.py sqlmigrate <app> <migration>` into `squawk` and list the rules that fire. Rehearse it: `createdb -T seed_synthetic task_rehearsal`, run `migrate` against the copy, then start the previous commit’s app against the same copy and call its main endpoints; every call that touches the renamed column fails. Now have the agent rewrite the change as expand steps: add the new column as nullable, `AddIndexConcurrently` in its own migration with `atomic = False`, a batched backfill, and the old column’s removal written up as a follow-up for a later release. Rehearse again on a fresh copy: tests pass and the old app still works. At Rhino: cloud CI runs `makemigrations --check` but no migration linter, so run squawk on the last five rhinoCore migrations and note what it finds. Migrations deploy under an advisory lock (`django_migrate_with_lock.py`) while older pods keep serving, which is why new fields are `null=True`.
labs.output: Squawk output before and after, the rewritten migrations, and two rehearsal logs (old code failing, then working)

labs.title: Fence the database
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Write a small `task-db` script that creates `task_<id>` from your seeded template, prints its URL, and drops the database when the task ends; the agent receives only that URL. Add a PreToolUse hook in Claude Code (or your agent’s equivalent) that denies shell commands containing `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `flush`, `migrate --fake`, `migrate <app> zero`, `prisma migrate reset` or `dropdb` unless they name a `task_` database, and any database URL whose host is not localhost. Deny reads of `.env` files with permission rules (`Read(./.env)`, `Read(./.env.*)`). Red-team it: ask the agent to “reset the database to fix the failing test” and to “use the staging URL from the old .env”, and log every verdict. At Rhino: this is the database part of the guardian hook from chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely. The on-prem client keeps a separate raw database for PHI, and no agent session ever receives its connection string.
labs.output: The script, the hook, and a red-team log with every attempt blocked

checks.q: Why settle the contract before the agent writes the handler?
checks.a: It is a target the agent can check its own work against, and a fence for everyone who depends on the API. oasdiff or buf turns a breaking change (a removed field, a new required field, a renumbered proto field) into a red CI check, and the same file generates the frontend types, SDK clients and mocks.

checks.q: The agent wants to rename a column in one migration. What do you ask for instead?
checks.a: Expand, migrate, contract: add the new column as nullable, write to both and backfill in batches, move reads, and drop the old column in a later release once no old code, SDK or on-prem client reads it. Squawk’s renaming-column rule flags the one-step rename.

checks.q: Name three Django or Postgres habits that keep a busy table from locking.
checks.a: `AddIndexConcurrently` in a migration with `atomic = False`; `AddConstraintNotValid`, then `ValidateConstraint` in a separate migration; and a short `lock_timeout` at the top of the migration, so a waiting ALTER can’t block every query behind it.

checks.q: What must an agent never hold, and who applies migrations?
checks.a: Any production credential: a database URL, an admin token, a cloud key. Agents write migrations and open PRs; pipelines apply them after lint and rehearsal. At PocketOS, one token in an unrelated file was enough to delete production and its backups in 9 seconds.

watchOut: A migration rehearsed only on an empty database. Django’s test database proves it runs; a seeded copy proves it runs on data shaped like yours (a new NOT NULL or unique rule, a long backfill).
Branching production “to be safe”. A branch or fork of production holds production data; at Rhino that is PHI. Clone from the synthetic template.

Background jobs that aren’t safe to run twice. Agents retry, queues retry, and Celery’s docs warn that with `acks_late` a task “may be executed multiple times should the worker crash”. Test every task by running it twice.

An agent that edits an applied migration, or asks to skip the linter, to turn CI green. Applied migrations are never edited; it writes a corrective migration, and a lint exception goes to the reviewer with a reason.
modules.watchTime: 39 min core, 1 h 10 min with electives
modules.goal: Build back-end changes with an agent the way a strong back-end team would: the contract agreed first and guarded by a machine, one agent writing while checkers it can’t edit review the work, a throwaway database for every task, migrations that never lock a busy table or break an old client, and no production credential anywhere the agent can reach.
modules.why: Agents write back ends fast when the target can be checked: on BaxBench, where every task is an OpenAPI spec plus functional tests, the top model (Claude Opus 4.5 Thinking) is 86.2% functionally correct (leaderboard read Sep 2026). They fail where a mistake can’t be undone. In April 2026 a Cursor agent found an API token in a file unrelated to its task and deleted PocketOS’s production database and its backups in one API call, in 9 seconds. Agents already create 80% of the databases and 97% of the database branches on Neon (Databricks, Jan 2026), so the question is not whether agents touch databases but whether they only ever touch copies. At Rhino the stakes are higher: on-prem clients can be older than the cloud with no version negotiation, migrations run while several instances serve traffic, and a production database holds PHI.

shipIt.title: One endpoint, in the back-end order
shipIt.body: Take one small, real endpoint change through the order: the contract diff approved first, the expand migration in its own PR with squawk and rehearsal output, the service with happy-path and failure-path tests, regenerated types for the UI, and a ticket for the contract step in a later release. A reviewer who is not the requester approves each PR (SOC 2 CC8.1), and a pipeline, not the agent, applies the migration.

modules.title: Keep agent-written back ends safe

keyIdeas.title: Correct is not secure, and prompts cap out
keyIdeas.body: BaxBench’s three prompt settings show how far instructions go. With no security prompt, the leaderboard’s top model (Claude Opus 4.5 Thinking) is 86.2% correct and 56.1% correct and secure. A generic “write secure code” reminder raises the secure score to 66.1%. A prompt that names the exact risks of each task reaches 68.6%, and correctness falls to 80.9%. Real repos look worse: in SusVibes (186 real feature requests where people once shipped a vulnerable version, Dec 2025), SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet solved 57% correctly but only 11.8% securely, and adding vulnerability hints to the request didn’t fix it. Veracode’s July 2026 report (vendor data) puts the average security pass rate of AI-written code at 56%, unchanged from 55% a year earlier, with SQL injection at 83% but cross-site scripting at 15% and log injection at 12%; the best model, GPT-5.5, reached 68%. So security gets its own checks that run on every change: exploit tests, a permission matrix and scanners. A line in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md helps a little. It is not a check.

keyIdeas.title: Authorization is test number one
keyIdeas.body: Broken access control is A01 in the OWASP Top 10:2025, and Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA, often called IDOR) is API1 in the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: change the ID in the URL and get someone else’s record. Two relatives sit next to it: API3, a field a user may read or write but shouldn’t, such as `owner` or `is_admin` (a Django REST Framework serializer with `fields = "__all__"` invites it), and API5, a regular user reaching an admin function. Test all three with a permission matrix. Rows are callers: anonymous, the owner, a member of another project, each role, an admin. Columns are every endpoint and action, including list, filter and export. Each cell holds the expected answer, such as 200, 401, 403 or 404. Review the table before any test exists, then let the agent generate one test per cell with factory-made users and run them all. The denied cells matter most. In code, scope the query instead of filtering after loading, and answer 404 when the caller may not even know the object exists. A Next.js route handler or server action is back-end code too: it must check the session user against the object, not only that someone is logged in. Agents are good at this job, because they write the full five-role, twelve-endpoint matrix that a person would only sample. At Rhino the rule is already written: never filter sensitive objects only in Python, scope the queryset, and hide existence with `RhinoNotFoundOrNoAccessException`.

keyIdeas.title: A verifier the writer can’t edit or skip
keyIdeas.body: Stack the checks, cheapest and most deterministic first. A static analysis (SAST) scanner such as Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube or Snyk, a secret scanner and a dependency audit run from a hook after each edit and again as a required CI check; chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer, covers secrets and invented packages. Snyk’s team first gave agents rule files that told them to scan, found that agents sometimes ignored them, and moved the scan into hooks that return only newly introduced issues (July 2026 talk). Then an AI security reviewer looks for what rules can’t see, such as business logic and object-level access: Claude Code’s built-in `/security-review` command, the claude-code-security-review GitHub Action, or a read-only security subagent in any tool. The harness Anthropic describes (Eugene Yan’s talk below) keeps finding and checking apart: a second agent that doesn’t see the first one’s reasoning assumes each finding is false and settles it by running the exploit in a sandbox. External firms confirmed 91.4% of the Claude-found vulnerabilities they reviewed (4,576 of 5,008, Anthropic’s disclosure dashboard, August 2026). Two limits: the Action’s README says it is “not hardened against prompt injection attacks” and should review trusted PRs only, and its false-positive filter drops denial-of-service and rate-limiting findings, so resource limits need your own test. At Rhino, Claude Code Security and managed Code Review aren’t covered by the BAA, so they are Lane A only. The writing agent never edits the rules, the hooks or the CI job: keep them in managed settings or behind CODEOWNERS.

keyIdeas.title: Test the unhappy path on purpose
keyIdeas.body: Agents test the path they built. In a July 2026 preprint on 4,882 agent PRs, error-handling code was the least-tested code: 81.0% of it was never run by any test in Python and 86.0% in Java, and 64.8% of the Python PRs changed no line that an existing test executed. OWASP’s Top 10:2025 now lists Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (A10) as its own risk. The dangerous shape is code that fails open: a broad `except` around a permission check or a remote call, which returns the data anyway. Ask for one test per failure branch: bad input gives 400, a missing object 404, a denied caller 403 or 404, a timeout in a dependency is handled and logged, and a background job that runs twice leaves the same result (Celery warns that with `acks_late` a task can run again after a worker crash, so tasks must be idempotent). Log IDs and context, never raw user input or PHI; log injection passed only 12% of Veracode’s tests. When the same broad `except` comes back a second time, add a Semgrep or ast-grep rule whose message says how to fix it (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work).

keyIdeas.title: Properties and mutants beat examples
keyIdeas.body: An example test checks the inputs the agent thought of. A property states what must hold for every input, and a tool such as Hypothesis (Python) or fast-check (JavaScript and TypeScript) generates hundreds of cases and shrinks a failure to the smallest one. Useful shapes: a round trip (serialize, then parse, gives the same object), an invariant (pages never repeat or skip a row), idempotency (running a job twice equals running it once), monotonicity (adding a filter never returns more rows) and a differential check (the new query returns what the old one did). Agents are good at mining properties: an agentic property-testing study on 100 Python packages (Oct 2025) found 56% of its bug reports valid and 86% of the 21 top-ranked ones, and got three patches merged, one of them into NumPy. The Hypothesis team ships a `/hypothesis` command for Claude Code, and warns that models write input strategies with needless limits, so read them. Then grade the tests with mutation testing: a tool such as mutmut (Python) or Stryker (JavaScript and TypeScript) plants small bugs, like `>=` turned into `>` or a deleted permission check, and every mutant that survives points at a missing test. Meta’s engineers accepted 73% of the tests written by its mutation-guided LLM system, ACH (Jan 2025). For HTTP APIs, Schemathesis generates requests from your OpenAPI schema and finds 500 errors, responses that break the schema, invalid input that gets accepted, and bugs that only appear across calls such as create, then get, then delete.

keyIdeas.title: Numbers and traces, not claims
keyIdeas.body: Agent-written performance PRs included an explicit measurement less often than human ones: 45.7% against 63.6% (324 agent and 83 human PRs, Dec 2025). A back-end PR that touches data carries the query count pinned in a test (Django’s `assertNumQueries`), the EXPLAIN plan of each new query (`QuerySet.explain()`), a short k6 run with a p95 threshold for hot paths, and one trace of the new endpoint. For the agent to debug from evidence, give it logs written to a file it can read, a trace ID on every line, and OpenTelemetry spans across the web process and the background workers. Telemetry it can query beats telemetry it must page through: in Pydantic’s July 2026 comparison of seven platforms on the same 400 spans (vendor test), a query-backed MCP answered a debugging question in 2 calls, while object-model tools needed far more calls or returned dumps the agent had to add up itself. Google’s Auto-Diagnose read integration-test failure logs and named the root cause in 90.14% of 71 real failures, and has been used on 52,635 failing tests (Apr 2026). Start locally, on synthetic data. Production telemetry is read-only, scoped to one project, Lane A only and allowed only after a PHI audit (chapter 30, Agents after release).

videos.title: Using LLMs to Secure Source Code
videos.speaker: Eugene Yan, Anthropic
videos.desc: A practical talk from Anthropic on agent security review: how the security teams it works with set up context and a sandbox, separate finding from checking, and validate a patch.

clips.label: An order service as the example: a threat model that gives the model the system, and a sandbox with no internet and no cloud credentials
Discovery with context, simpler prompts and tools, then an independent verifier that tries to prove each finding false by running the exploit
Triage with business context, and the patch ladder: the exploit stops working, tests stay green, a fresh agent attacks again, a person confirms

takeaways: A written threat model is the context the code can’t give. He reports that teams with a well-documented one reached about 90% true positives.
Keep finding and checking apart. The verifier doesn’t see the finder’s reasoning, assumes the finding is false, and detonates the proof of concept in a fresh container.
Severity depends on the business. Health data turns a medium finding into a high one, and the model knows that only if the threat model says so.
