labs.title: Build the permission matrix for one resource
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): In any API you can run locally (Django REST Framework, FastAPI, Express or Next.js route handlers; a small public sample app works), pick one resource that belongs to someone, such as an order or a project. Ask the agent to list every endpoint and action on it, including list, filter and export, and every kind of caller: anonymous, the owner, a user from another team, each role and an admin. Have it write the matrix as a table with the expected answer in each cell (200, 401, 403 or 404), and check the table yourself before any test exists. Then have it generate one parametrized test per cell with factory-made users and data, and run them. Plant a bug: remove the ownership filter from the detail query, and confirm that exactly the right cells turn red. At Rhino: pick one rhinoCloud viewset and use the personas PLA, PLM, CA, CM and RA plus a user from another project, with factory_boy data only; where existence must stay hidden, expect the not-found-or-no-access answer.
labs.output: A reviewed matrix, a test file and the count of cells that no test covered before

labs.title: Three layers against three planted bugs
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): On a throwaway branch of a small API, plant three bugs in separate commits: a detail endpoint that loads any object by its ID, a SQL query built by string formatting from user input, and a broad except around a permission check that returns the data anyway. Run three layers and record what each catches: a scanner (Semgrep, or Bandit for Python), Claude Code’s /security-review on the diff (or a read-only security prompt in your agent), and the permission matrix from lab 1. For every AI finding, open a fresh session that sees only the finding and the code, and ask it to prove the finding false by running the exploit against your local server. Then run the scanner from a PostToolUse hook, so it runs after every edit, and plant a fourth bug to watch the hook flag it. At Rhino: use the local stack and synthetic data only; Claude Code Security and managed Code Review stay in Lane A.
labs.output: A table of bugs against layers, the verifier’s verdicts and a committed hook

labs.title: Properties, mutants and one number
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Pick one small, pure piece of your back end: pagination, a serializer, a date or price calculation, a permission helper. Ask the agent to propose properties before any test code: which round trip, invariant, idempotency or monotonicity must hold. Keep only the ones you agree are true, then have it write them with Hypothesis (the /hypothesis command) or fast-check, and read its input strategies for needless limits. Run a mutation tool (mutmut or Stryker) on that module before and after, and list the mutants that survive. Finish with one number: pin the query count of one list endpoint in a test and save its EXPLAIN plan in the PR. At Rhino: write the versioned-model property (a new version keeps base_version_uid and adds one to the version) and run it with the backend unit-test runner on one module.
labs.output: A property test file, mutation scores before and after, and one pinned query count with its plan

checks.q: The best BaxBench model builds back ends that pass the functional tests 86.2% of the time. Why isn’t that enough, and why won’t a better prompt fix it?
checks.a: Only 56.1% of its solutions were both correct and secure, so about a third of the working back ends could be exploited. Even a prompt that named the exact risks reached only 68.6%. Security needs its own checks: exploit tests, a permission matrix and scanners.

checks.q: What does a permission matrix test that the agent’s own tests usually don’t?
checks.a: The denied cells: anonymous callers, users from other projects, lower roles and admin-only actions, for every endpoint and action. The agent’s tests usually cover the owner on the happy path.

checks.q: Why is the AI security reviewer a second layer and not the only gate?
checks.a: It can miss or invent findings, it filters out some classes such as rate limiting, and the GitHub Action isn’t hardened against prompt injection, so it reviews trusted PRs only. Deterministic scanners and tests run first, and a separate agent tries to disprove each AI finding.

checks.q: An agent’s PR says it made the list endpoint “much faster”. What do you ask for?
checks.a: Numbers: the query count before and after, the EXPLAIN plan of the new query, and a short load run with its p95. Agent performance PRs included a measurement 45.7% of the time, against 63.6% for human ones.

watchOut: Tests from the same session that wrote the code. They check what the agent believed. Review the matrix and the properties yourself, and keep rules, hooks and CI jobs out of the writer’s reach.
Code that fails open. A permission check inside a broad except, or “allow” as the default when a service times out, turns every error into access.
“No findings” read as “secure”. AI reviewers miss things, drop some classes on purpose and don’t know your roles unless the threat model says so.
Telemetry as a PHI path. Logs, traces and error payloads the agent reads become part of its prompt. Log IDs, not values, and keep production telemetry read-only and in Lane A.
modules.watchTime: 39 min core, 1 h 1 min with electives
modules.goal: Make every agent-written back-end change prove two things before it merges: only the right people reach the data, and the code holds up under bad input, failure and load. The tools are a permission matrix per resource, a security check the writing agent can’t edit or skip, an AI security reviewer whose findings a second agent tries to disprove, failure-path and property tests, mutants that grade those tests, and numbers in the pull request: query counts, EXPLAIN plans, a p95 and one trace.
modules.why: Agents now write back ends that work far more often than back ends that are safe. On the BaxBench leaderboard (392 back-end tasks, each with functional tests and expert-written exploits; read in September 2026), the best model passes the functional tests 86.2% of the time, but only 56.1% of its solutions are both correct and secure, so about a third of its working back ends can be exploited. In a June 2026 preprint that audited 200 deployed apps built with Claude Code and Lovable, 91.0% had at least one vulnerability and 65.77% of the findings were Critical or High, concentrated in broken access control, injection and authentication. The agent’s own tests rarely look there: they prove the feature for the user who owns the data, and the attacker is always the other user. At Rhino a leak is patient data. The good news is that the checks which catch these failures are exhaustive and boring, which is exactly the work agents do better than people. Chapter 13, Build APIs and databases with agents, made the contract and the database safe to change; this chapter makes the code behind them safe to merge.

shipIt.title: A back-end evidence pack
shipIt.body: A PR template or skill that makes every agent-written back-end PR carry the permission-matrix result, the scanner output, failure-path tests, one property test, query counts and EXPLAIN plans for new queries, a p95 for hot paths and one trace. Show a teammate one PR that carries it, approved by someone other than the requester; chapter 15, Build a whole feature with agents, uses the same pack for every slice.

modules.title: The one-person feature team, idea to release

keyIdeas.title: Contract first, then split
keyIdeas.body: The data model and the API contract are the decisions that hurt most to change, so settle them before any slice code. Chapter 5, Tell the agent what you want, calls this planning by expected pain. Spec Kit’s plan step writes them down as files (data-model.md, a contracts/ folder and a quickstart.md of test scenarios), and its task step reads them. With the contract reviewed and fixed, the UI builder works against a mock of it while the service builder writes the real handler, and one contract test runs against both. Chapter 13, Build APIs and databases with agents, makes the contract checkable with OpenAPI or proto diffs. At Rhino, a reviewed program-design doc comes first for any change to the gRPC contract, the SDK’s public API or PHI-handling code. The FCP Workflows screens show the pattern in our own code: environment flags choose a mock data layer or the real backend, and the feature fails closed (stays off) when a flag is missing or its project allowlist is empty.

keyIdeas.title: Split by independence, not by headcount
keyIdeas.body: A task can run in parallel only if it touches different files and waits on no unfinished task. That is Spec Kit’s rule for its [P] marker, and Kiro runs such tasks together in execution waves. Files that every slice touches, such as the migrations folder, the URL router, the generated API client or a lockfile, belong to one lane that goes first. More agents on coupled work is slower, not faster: when Cursor’s agents coordinated through shared locks, 20 of them moved at the throughput of 2 or 3, and the team moved to planners, workers and a judge (Jan 2026). Give each builder its own worktree and a list of paths it owns: `claude --worktree api` in Claude Code creates `.claude/worktrees/api/` on its own branch, and `git worktree add` works with Codex, Cursor or any other agent. Your attention is the real ceiling. As Addy Osmani put it, “More AI agents running does not mean that there is more of you available” (Jul 2026). Keep chapter 10’s one in front, two behind, and see chapter 18, One agent or many?, for the orchestration tools.

keyIdeas.title: Oracles before builders
keyIdeas.body: An oracle is a check that already knows the right answer: a conformance suite, a reference implementation or a contract test. With one, a builder can finish without you. Simon Willison ported an HTML5 parser from Python to JavaScript with Codex CLI in about 4.5 hours and 8 prompts: 9,000 lines, 9,200 html5lib tests passing, about $29.41 at API prices (Dec 2025). Anthropic’s C compiler (16 agents, about 2,000 sessions, under $20,000, 100,000 lines) could split into parallel work only once GCC served as the oracle each agent compared against (Feb 2026). For a feature, write three oracles before the builders start: the contract test both sides must pass, one end-to-end test of the flag-on path on seeded data, and the acceptance checks from the spec. Make them read-only to the builders (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work). Green is still not mergeable: when maintainers reviewed 296 agent PRs that passed SWE-bench, their merge decisions ran about 24 points below the automated grader (METR, Mar 2026).

keyIdeas.title: One feature, one stack, merged dark
keyIdeas.body: Ship the feature as layers, each a small PR with its own evidence: contract, then migration, then service and API, then UI, then the flag or infra change. GitHub’s native stacked PRs (public preview since 30 Jul 2026) let a reviewer open one layer’s diff at a time under a stack map, and merging the top ready PR lands it with every layer below. Branch protections and required checks still apply, and `gh extension install github/gh-stack` adds the CLI plus a skill that agents can drive. A human who is not the requester approves each layer (SOC 2 CC8.1). The code merges with the flag off, the pipeline deploys it, and turning the flag on, for internal users first, is its own reviewed change. A preview environment per PR lets the reviewer try the feature before it merges; Simon Willison lists it among the practices agents reward (Oct 2025). Some teams skip PRs entirely (Amp, Sep 2026) or commit straight to main (Peter Steinberger). With SOC 2 review, worktrees plus stacked PRs are Rhino’s way. Chapter 16, From quick prototype to real product, covers the gate before real users.

keyIdeas.title: Dollars per merged feature
keyIdeas.body: Log hours and dollars per merged feature, not per seat and never per person. Reference points: $29.41 for the 4.5-hour parser port; $124.70 and 3 h 50 min for a digital audio workstation built by a planner, a generator and an evaluator on Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, Mar 2026); $3 to $33 to merge the same OAuth device-flow feature across 23 model and harness setups, where the harness alone moved cost about 2.5x and, with the cheapest coding models, up to 97% of the bill was the review gate (Veli-Matti Vanamo, 29 runs, Jul 2026, who warns that a single run is a hypothesis). Across enterprise deployments, Claude Code averages about $13 per developer per active day (vendor figure). In Claude Code, `/usage` shows a session’s cost, `--max-budget-usd` caps a headless run, and `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` can tag every cost metric with the feature’s name. The number is a cost line for the team’s harness, never a score for a person (Rhino rule 6).

keyIdeas.title: Compound: the next feature should be easier
keyIdeas.body: Every’s loop is plan, work, review and compound, with about 80% of the time in plan and review (Every, Dec 2025, one company’s account). Kieran Klaassen, rebuilding the Cora email client as its sole engineer with design and specialist support, spends half his time building the feature and half teaching the system what it got wrong. His bar: the next feature should be easier because this one shipped (Aug 2026). The human works at both ends, deciding what the problem is before the agents run and raising the bar when they finish, while the middle should be boring. Compounding means writing each lesson where the next agent will find it: a lint rule, a test, a skill line, a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md line, or a short solution note in the repo. At Rhino this is rule 7, fix the harness on the second repeat, done at the end of every feature.

labs.title: Contract first, two builders
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): pick a small feature that crosses layers in any repo with a front end and an API, or in a small public full-stack sample app, such as a new field shown in a React table and returned by a Django or FastAPI endpoint. Write a one-page spec with 3 to 5 checks. Have one agent write the contract (an OpenAPI file or shared TypeScript types), a mock and one contract test; review them and commit. Then start two sessions in separate worktrees (`claude --worktree api` and `claude --worktree ui`, or `git worktree add` for any agent). The API builder implements until the contract test passes; the UI builder builds against the mock. Neither may edit the contract or the test: add a permission deny rule for those paths, and check each diff. Merge both, run the test against the real API, and note every place the halves disagreed. At Rhino: Lane A only, factory-seeded data, and pick a feature that doesn’t touch the gRPC contract, the SDK’s public API or PHI-handling code.
labs.output: A contract, two branches built in parallel, and a list of where they disagreed and why

labs.title: Stack it and flag it
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): take the work from lab 1, or any feature branch over 400 lines, and split it into a stack of 3 to 5 PRs: contract, backend, UI, then the flag. Use GitHub’s stacked PRs (`gh extension install github/gh-stack`, or ask your agent to use the gh-stack skill), or plain branches that each target the one below. Put the feature behind a flag that defaults to off, and add one end-to-end test of the flag-on path. Give each PR a two-line description and its own evidence. Ask a teammate, or yourself the next morning, to review one layer at a time, and record the minutes per layer. At Rhino: a teammate who is not the requester approves each layer, and the upper layers get no frontend CI or preview links until they target main, so attach local test output as their evidence.
labs.output: A stack of small PRs, a flag that is off by default, and review minutes per layer

labs.title: A feature-log line and one compound step
labs.body: Solo (about 30 min): for the feature you just built, or your last merged one, write one line of a feature log: the number of PRs, your hours, the agent’s hours, the dollars (from `/usage` or your provider’s console), the review rounds and what went wrong. Pick the one mistake most likely to repeat and turn it into something the next feature will reuse: a lint rule, a test, a skill line or a line in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. Re-run the step that failed in a fresh session to prove the fix works. At Rhino: the log line is a team cost record, never a personal score.
labs.output: One feature-log line and one committed harness change, with proof that it works

checks.q: When can two slices of a feature run in parallel?
checks.a: When they touch different files and neither waits on unfinished work (Spec Kit’s [P] rule). Shared files, such as migrations, the router or the generated client, stay in one lane that goes first.

checks.q: Why write the contract before the UI and the API?
checks.a: It is the decision that hurts most to change, and it lets the UI builder work against a mock while the service builder writes the real handler, with one contract test for both.

checks.q: What does one feature’s set of PRs look like at Rhino?
checks.a: A stack of small layers, such as contract, migration, service, UI and flag, each with its own evidence and approved by someone who is not the requester. The code merges with the flag off, and the pipeline deploys it.

checks.q: What does “compound” mean once a feature ships?
checks.a: Turn what went wrong into something the next feature reuses, such as a lint rule, a test, a skill line or a context line, so the next feature is easier. At Rhino, do it by the second repeat at the latest.

watchOut: Parallel slices that share a file. If two slices touch the same file, they are one slice, or the shared part goes first.
Builders that can edit the contract or the oracles. Change them only through a reviewed PR.
An LLM reviewer as the only gate. In the $3 to $33 experiment, an LLM reviewer alone approved code that the team’s own CI would fail.
Upper stack layers with no CI. In the FCP repo, frontend CI and the preview links run only for PRs that target main.

| Slice plan | The slices, the paths each one owns, what waits on what, and the parallel markers | One agent drafts, you edit | No two parallel slices touch the same file |
| Oracles | The contract test, one flag-on end-to-end test, the acceptance checks | You, or one agent before the builders | Each check fails before the build starts |
| Build | One builder per slice, each in its own worktree, on synthetic or factory-seeded data | One writer per slice | Tests, types and lint pass in the worktree |
| Verify | Checkers with a clean context and no write access, including the permission tests from chapter 14 | Checkers that never write code | Evidence for every check, not claims |
| Merge | A stack of small PRs, with the flag off | A human who is not the requester approves each layer | Branch protection and required checks pass |
| Release | The pipeline deploys; the flag goes on for internal users first | The pipeline, never the agent | Deploy checks pass on QA |
| Compound | One feature-log line and one harness change | You | The next feature reuses the lesson |

modules.watchTime: 28 min core, 1 h 6 min with electives
modules.goal: Take one feature across every layer, from a one-page spec to a release behind a flag: settle the data model and the contract first, split the work into slices that can safely run in parallel, give each builder its own worktree and checks it can’t edit, ship the feature as a stack of small PRs that someone else approves, count what it cost, and leave behind one lesson that makes the next feature easier.
modules.why: Agents have made one-person, full-stack work normal. Anthropic surveyed 132 of its engineers and researchers: 27% of their Claude-assisted work would not have been done otherwise, and “everyone is becoming more full-stack”. In 200,000 of its internal Claude Code transcripts, building new features grew from 14% to 37% of use between February and August 2025 (Anthropic, Dec 2025, one company’s data). Every runs five products, each primarily built and run by one person (Every, Dec 2025). But more agents is not more output. When Cursor’s agents shared locks, 20 of them moved at the throughput of 2 or 3 (Jan 2026). Across more than 10,000 developers, teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs while review time rose 91% and PR size 154% (Faros AI, Jul 2025). The cost of the same feature swings more than tenfold: $3 to $33 to merge one OAuth feature across 23 model and harness setups (one practitioner’s experiment, Jul 2026). One developer can be a whole feature team only when the contract, the split, the stack and the checks are designed on purpose.

shipIt.title: A feature playbook
shipIt.body: Turn this chapter into a skill or template your team can reuse: the one-page spec, the contract-first step, the slice table with parallel markers and owned paths, the stack order, the flag rule and the feature-log line. Share it with one real feature that used it: its stack of PRs, its log line and the harness change it left behind.

modules.title: From quick prototype to real product

keyIdeas.title: Give the prototype one job, and pick the tool for it
keyIdeas.body: A prototype buys learning cheaply. Name its job before the first prompt: an answer to one question (then delete it), a spec for the real build (keep the screens, flows and decisions, not the code), or the first version of a product (then it must pass the gate below). Pick the tool to match. Claude Design, Figma Make and v0 explore screens and flows; Lovable, Bolt or Replit give you a clickable full-stack demo; your coding agent in a scratch folder answers a technical question. The vendors draw the same line. Claude Design’s own designer: “if you’re shipping production software, stick with Claude Code”; a finished design goes to Claude Code as a handoff bundle, or through `/design` inside a Claude Code session, so the build continues from the design instead of a screenshot (Claude blog, Jul 2026). Vercel calls vibe coding “the world’s largest shadow IT problem” and says prototypes fail “because they live outside real codebases” (vendor post, Feb 2026, launching v0’s Git panel with a branch per chat and PRs against main). Chapter 1, Your first hour with a coding agent, drew the line between vibe coding and agentic engineering; this chapter is where a project crosses it.

keyIdeas.title: Builders fail in the same three places: access, secrets and data
keyIdeas.body: Many builder apps let the browser query the database directly (Supabase’s generated REST API), so the public key in the page is safe only if row-level security (RLS) is correct on every table. CVE-2025-48757: 170 of 1,645 scanned Lovable projects, across 303 endpoints, had insecure RLS, scored CVSS 9.3. Lovable disputes it, saying each customer is responsible for protecting their own app’s data, and the finder works at Replit, a competitor. His sharpest point is about tools: Lovable’s later security scanner “merely checks for the existence of any RLS policy, not its correctness” (May 2025). In January 2026 Wiz found Moltbook’s Supabase key in client JavaScript with no RLS behind it: 1.5 million API tokens and 35,000 emails, readable and writable by anyone, in an app whose founder said he “didn’t write a single line of code”. Agents make the same mistake with a human watching: in Supabase’s own demo, Claude Code built a reporting view, said everything worked, and every employee could see every department’s salaries, because a Postgres view skips RLS unless it is created with `security_invoker = true`. Georgia Tech’s researcher put it plainly: “When an agent builds something without authentication, that’s not a typo. It’s a design flaw baked in from the start.”

keyIdeas.title: The promotion gate: evidence before real users
keyIdeas.body: Before anyone outside the builder uses it, each check below has proof in the PR, not a sentence. (1) Owner: a named engineer who can explain the design and the data model and will answer for it (“explain it or don’t ship it”, chapter 1). (2) Access: every route needs a login and every read and write checks ownership, proven with two users: B tries to read and change A’s rows through the API, views, exports and admin routes. Chapter 14, Keep agent-written back ends safe, tests this for every role. (3) Secrets: nothing secret in the built client bundle (Next.js inlines every `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable into browser JavaScript at build time, Vite every `VITE_` one), a secret scan over the whole git history, and every key the prototype used rotated. (4) Data: separate dev and prod databases (Replit’s apps used “a single database for both development and live customer data” until its agent deleted a production database during a code freeze, Jul 2025), no real data in dev, the schema as migrations in the repo, and a restore you have actually run. (5) Tests that can fail: every line of the feature ledger (next idea) is a test that goes red when you break its feature. (6) Scans in CI: dependency audit and lockfile, static analysis and secret scanning. (7) Operations: rate limits (Moltbook had none, so anyone could register agents in a loop), errors and logs without PHI, and a rollback path. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Copilot can run most of these checks; none of them can be the one who says the gate passed.

keyIdeas.title: Keep the knowledge, rebuild the trunk
keyIdeas.body: The prototype’s best output is a spec: screens and states, three to five acceptance examples, the decisions, what went wrong, and a feature ledger with every instruction you gave. Keep the ledger because generation forgets: in the FronTalk benchmark (100 multi-turn front-end dialogues, 20 models), models overwrote features they had built in earlier turns, and an agent that re-checked every past instruction in the browser cut forgetting to nearly zero and raised the score from 56.0% to 65.3% (one benchmark study, Dec 2025, updated Aug 2026). Then decide part by part with Erik Schluntz’s rule (Anthropic, May 2025): agent-heavy code and its tech debt are acceptable in leaf nodes, the parts nothing else depends on, while the trunk (login, access rules, the data model, shared APIs) is built in the repo by someone who understands it. Harden when the prototype already lives in your repo and stack and its access model fits. Rewrite when it lives in a builder, when the browser talks straight to the database but you need server-side rules, when the data model is wrong (Karpathy’s agent linked purchases to accounts by email instead of a user ID, chapter 1), or when nobody can explain it. At Rhino, anything that becomes part of the FCP is rebuilt in the FCP repo with the design system (chapter 11, Build UI with agents) and the normal loop.

keyIdeas.title: Review alone won’t catch it, and success finds every hole
keyIdeas.body: Cloudflare’s OAuth library was “largely written with the help of Claude”, and its README says it is “not ‘vibe coded’”: security experts reviewed every line against the RFCs. It still shipped two medium advisories in May 2025, a PKCE downgrade bypass and missing `redirect_uri` validation. Newer models don’t remove the need either: Veracode found 45% of AI code samples from over 100 models failed security tests, flat across model size (vendor, Jul 2025), and CodeRabbit counted up to 2.74x more security issues in AI-co-authored PRs (vendor, 470 PRs, authorship guessed from signals, Dec 2025). Popularity multiplies the bill: Peter Steinberger’s OpenClaw drew 1,142 security advisories in about five months, 99 of them critical, about 16.6 a day (Apr 2026). So the gate is a human owner plus tests that attack the app plus scanners, and it gets stricter as the audience grows.

keyIdeas.title: Anyone may prototype; only the loop promotes
keyIdeas.body: PMs, designers and engineers all prototype now, and the rules don’t change for any of them. Use approved tools and synthetic data only: PHI never enters a prompt, and that includes a CSV you upload, a screenshot, or Claude Design’s web capture of a logged-in page. Builders are cloud services, so whatever you paste leaves your laptop. Check the vendor matrix in chapter 34, Stay safe and compliant, before you use one at work. Promotion is a PR in the repo: the agent opens it, someone who is not the requester approves it (SOC 2 CC8.1), a pipeline deploys it, and the owner owns every line. A builder’s Publish button is not a road to real users. Designers can ship UI through the same door: a story and a PR (Meaghan Choi, Claude Code’s design lead, ships code herself).

labs.title: Gate a vibe-coded app
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Build a small app in vibe mode, without reading the code: a notes or tasks app with sign-in and one table, made in a builder (Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Replit) or by your agent in a scratch folder on Supabase (`npx supabase start` runs it locally in Docker). Use fake data only. Then run the gate yourself and save the evidence for each check: sign up two users and, with user B’s login token, try to read and change user A’s rows through the REST API (curl works); search the built bundle for keys (`grep -rE "service_role|sk_|secret" dist .next/static`); run a secret scanner such as gitleaks over the git history; run `npm audit`; look for any view created without `security_invoker`; check whether dev and prod point at the same database URL; break one feature and see whether any test fails. Then open a fresh agent session, give it the same checklist, and compare what it found with what you found. Finish with a harden-or-rewrite decision in one sentence. At Rhino: synthetic data only, and a prototype never gets FCP credentials or a connection to FCP databases.
labs.output: A gate report with pass or fail and evidence per check, what the agent missed, and your harden-or-rewrite decision

labs.title: Throw the code away, keep the spec
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Prototype one screen for 15 minutes in any prototyping tool, or with your agent in a scratch folder, on fake data. FE example: a filterable list of projects with an empty state. BE example: a Django or FastAPI endpoint that exports a project summary as CSV. Keep a feature ledger while you work: every instruction you gave, one line each. Then write a one-page spec from the prototype: screens and states, three acceptance examples, the data it reads and who may see it, and what the prototype got wrong. Give the spec, not the code, to your coding agent in your real repo (a small public sample app works), and ask it to build with your own components and to turn each ledger line into a story, a test or an end-to-end check. At Rhino: a PM or designer makes the prototype in Claude Design with synthetic data and exports the handoff bundle; the FE developer’s agent builds it in the FCP frontend with designSystem components, and an engineer who is not the requester approves the PR.
labs.output: A prototype screenshot, a one-page spec with its ledger, and a PR whose description maps every ledger line to its check

labs.title: Test your gate with planted holes
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Copy the app from lab 1, or any small app, and plant five holes: a secret key in a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` or `VITE_` variable, a table or endpoint with no ownership check, an admin route with no role check, one database URL shared by dev and prod, and a test that asserts nothing. Write your gate as a short skill or checklist file, then run it in a fresh agent session without saying what you planted. Count the catches. For every hole it missed, add a check that doesn’t depend on the model: a grep in CI, a two-user test or a lint rule. At Rhino: run it on a scratch copy, and add each new deterministic check to the team’s promotion-gate skill.
labs.output: A catch table (planted, caught by the agent, caught by a deterministic check) and at least one new deterministic check

checks.q: A builder’s security scan says every table has row-level security turned on. Why isn’t that enough?
checks.a: A scan that checks RLS exists doesn’t check that it is correct: Lovable’s scanner only checked existence. Test with two users: B tries to read and change A’s rows, including through views, which skip RLS unless they are created with `security_invoker = true`.

checks.q: Which parts of a prototype can you keep, and which do you rebuild?
checks.a: Keep leaf nodes that pass the gate, such as a one-off screen or report that nothing depends on. Rebuild the trunk in the repo with someone who understands it: login, access rules, the data model and shared APIs. Rewrite it all if it lives outside your stack, its data or access model is wrong, or nobody can explain it.

checks.q: If you throw the prototype’s code away, what moves into the real build?
checks.a: The knowledge: screens and states, acceptance examples, decisions, what went wrong, and the feature ledger of every instruction you gave. Each ledger line becomes a story or a test, because multi-turn generation overwrites features built earlier.

checks.q: A PM built a useful internal tool in a builder and wants colleagues to use it next week. What has to be true first?
checks.a: It passes the promotion gate with evidence: a named owner who can explain it, access tested with two users, no secrets in the client, separate dev and prod data, tests that fail when a feature breaks, scans, and logs without PHI, rate limits and a rollback. It reaches colleagues through a PR in a repo, approved by someone who is not the requester and deployed by a pipeline, not through the builder’s Publish button.

watchOut: A green badge read as “secure”. A builder’s scanner checks that a setting exists, not that user B is kept out of user A’s data. Only a two-user test shows that.

Patching a live leak table by table. Moltbook needed four rounds of fixes in about three hours, and each round found more exposed tables (Wiz’s timeline). Close access first, gate the whole app, then reopen.
Keys that lived in the prototype. They were pasted into chats, builders and demo links. Rotate every one before launch, even if it never reached git.
Real data “just for the demo”. PHI never enters a prompt: not in an uploaded CSV, a screenshot, or a builder’s capture of a logged-in page.
modules.watchTime: 27 min core, 58 min with electives
modules.goal: Prototype freely to learn, then decide on purpose what happens next: throw it away, turn it into a spec, or promote it. A prototype that real users will touch passes a promotion gate first, where every check has evidence in the pull request: an owner who can explain it, access tested with two users, no secrets in the browser, separate dev and prod data, tests that can fail, scans, and a way to operate and roll back. Keep what the prototype taught you, and rebuild its core in the repo with your design system.
modules.why: Anyone can now build a working app in an afternoon: a PM, a designer, or you with an agent and no plan. “It works” is not “it is safe to hand to users”, and these apps fail in the same few places every time. Escape.tech scanned about 5,600 public apps built on platforms such as Lovable, Base44, Create.xyz and Bolt and found more than 2,000 vulnerabilities, 400+ exposed secrets and 175 exposures of personal data, including medical records, most of them reachable without logging in (a security vendor’s passive scan, Oct 2025, so by its own account a lower bound). Georgia Tech’s Vibe Security Radar had traced 74 published CVEs to AI coding tools by April 2026, 35 of them in March 2026 alone, more than in all of 2025 (a research tracker that only sees code with an AI tool’s signature). Chapter 15, Build a whole feature with agents, worked inside the repo from the first commit. This chapter is the other road: the work starts as a prototype outside it, and something has to decide whether it may come in.

shipIt.title: A promotion-gate skill
shipIt.body: A `/gate` skill, or a checklist any agent can run, that checks a prototype against the seven gates, attaches the evidence, and fills a “Promoted from prototype” section in the PR template: owner, harden or rewrite, and each check with its proof. A reviewer who is not the requester signs it off.

modules.title: Maintaining code with AI

keyIdeas.title: Measure the slope
keyIdeas.body: Track duplication, complexity and file size every month, and look at the trend, not one number. GitClear’s data shows duplicated code rising and moved (refactored) code falling as the AI share grows (vendor research). A 2026 study of 441 repositories found that agent-first repos without committed AI configuration saw about twice the rise in cognitive complexity (+53% against +27%), though it was observational and the authors call it hypothesis-generating (RAMP, Aug 2026). Commit today’s numbers as a baseline and gate each PR against it, so the slope becomes visible in review instead of a year later.

keyIdeas.title: Ratchets, not judgments
keyIdeas.body: A ratchet accepts a change only when the count of violations stays the same or goes down, never up, so the baseline can only shrink. It works for duplication, lint warnings, accessibility violations, bundle size and visual baselines. Verification is the point: in a July 2026 study, unverified model edits for web accessibility improved and broke pages at similar rates (24 improvements against 20 regressions in 100 trials), while a loop that accepted a change only if violations strictly decreased rejected 126 of 126 harmful candidates. Keep baseline files under CODEOWNERS, so the writer can’t move them.

keyIdeas.title: Review comments become lint
keyIdeas.body: When reviewers keep writing the same comment, write a rule instead (Rhino rule 7: fix the harness on the second repeat), with fixtures that must match and must not match, and an error message that tells the agent how to fix it. Rules become reliable only when the model tests them against those fixtures in a loop. Front-end examples: logical CSS properties only (`margin-inline-start`, or Tailwind `ms-` and `me-`), so Hebrew right-to-left layouts don’t break; no hex colors or pixel values outside design tokens; no `` without `alt`. Back-end examples: an import-linter contract that keeps one layer from importing another, and no `mock.patch` in new API tests. GritQL and ast-grep match code by structure, and Biome, ESLint and ruff carry rules too; Rhino already has one, `no-uppercase-class.grit`.

keyIdeas.title: Loops that clean one thing at a time
keyIdeas.body: A janitor loop has a sensor (a count against the committed baseline), a deterministic controller that picks the smallest item first, and an agent with a skill as the actuator. One CI job is one iteration, and each loop keeps at most one PR open. Ramp asked an agent on Fable to fix all of its Python import cycles, and with dynamic workflows the job cut CI time by 66% (Ramp, Aug 2026). Give every loop a recur condition, so it stops when the count reaches zero or stops falling.

keyIdeas.title: Code migrations as state machines
keyIdeas.body: Moving code to a new API (a deprecated hook to its replacement, one test framework to another) works best file by file. Airbnb moved its test files through a per-file state machine with validation gates and retries: 75% in four hours, 97% in four days, and six weeks in total against an estimate of a year and a half. Iterate by sample, tune and sweep: run a small sample, fix the prompt on the failures, then run the rest in batches as stacked PRs. These are code migrations; database migrations are a different job with their own gates (chapter 13, Build APIs and databases with agents).

keyIdeas.title: Judges catch in-scope drift
keyIdeas.body: Spotify’s Honk exposes its verifiers through MCP plus a stop hook, and an LLM judge vetoes about a quarter of runs, half of which then correct themselves. The worst failure Spotify reports is a change that passes CI but is functionally wrong. So pair every loop with a judge that checks the diff stayed inside the task, and keep a human review on the PR.

labs.title: A baseline that can only shrink
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): On any repo you work on, or a public sample app, measure three numbers: duplication with jscpd, complexity with a tool for your language (lizard works for most; radon for Python; ESLint’s complexity rule for TypeScript), and the count of files over 500 lines. Test it with one PR that copies a function (it must fail) and one that removes a duplicate (it must pass and lower the baseline). At Rhino: the gate sits next to the patch-coverage gate, and the baseline file is under CODEOWNERS.
labs.output: A committed baseline and a ratchet gate in CI

labs.title: Three review comments become rules
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Pick three comments reviewers keep writing in your repo, or use these: no physical CSS margins or paddings (use logical properties), no hex colors outside the design tokens, no `` without `alt`. For each, have the agent write a rule in ast-grep, GritQL, Biome, ESLint or ruff, with at least three fixtures that must match and three that must not, and an error message that says how to fix the code. Loop until every fixture passes, then run the rules on the whole repo and count the hits. Back-end variant: an import-linter contract for one layer boundary. At Rhino: the top five comments from Byte and human reviews, plus an import-linter contract for the client and cloud boundary.
labs.output: Three rules with fixtures, wired into CI, and the first count

labs.title: A small code migration as a state machine
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): Pick a mechanical migration in a repo you know (a deprecated API to its replacement, an old test style to a new one, or class components to hooks in a sample React app). Have the agent write a small harness that keeps each file’s state in a JSON file (todo, migrated, verified, failed), runs `claude -p` on one file at a time, then the type check, lint and tests, and retries twice with the error before marking the file failed. Run a sample of five files, tune the prompt on the failures, then sweep up to 20 more. Open the result as stacked PRs of about ten files each, and report the success rate before and after tuning. At Rhino: the move from useResult to useQuery.
labs.output: A migration harness, its state file and the success rate before and after tuning

checks.q: Why aren’t better prompts enough to stop erosion?
checks.a: They lower the starting point, not the slope. You need external gates.

checks.q: What was Spotify’s worst failure mode?
checks.a: A change that passes CI but is functionally wrong.

checks.q: How did Airbnb get to 97%?
checks.a: A per-file state machine with validation gates and retries, iterating by sample, tune, sweep.

checks.q: How many PRs should a janitor loop open?
checks.a: One or none per run.

modules.watchTime: 37 min core, 1 h 9 min with electives
modules.goal: Keep code entropy flat while agents write most of the code: measure it and commit a baseline that can only improve, turn repeated review comments into lint rules with fixtures, run janitor loops that open one small PR or none, move code to new APIs with per-file state machines, and use a judge to catch changes that pass CI but drift off task.
modules.why: Code that agents extend gets worse turn by turn unless something outside the agent stops it. In SlopCodeBench, where 15 coding agents repeatedly extended their own solutions to 36 problems, structural erosion (complexity piling up in a few functions) rose in 77% of trajectories and verbosity in 75.5%, and agent code was 2.3 times more verbose and 2.0 times more eroded than 473 open-source Python repositories. Explicit quality guidance in the prompt cut the starting verbosity and erosion by up to a third but did not change how fast they grew (preprint, v2, May 2026; the March version reported 80% and 89.8% on a smaller set). Real repositories show the same slope: after projects adopted coding agents, static-analysis warnings rose about 18% and cognitive complexity about 39%, and the rise persisted even after the speed gains faded (a difference-in-differences study of open-source repos, Jan 2026). Messy code also costs the agent: in one Thoughtworks experiment, after refactoring one layer of a 150,000-line app, the same change used 83% fewer input tokens, 27,360 instead of 159,564 (one developer, one app, Jul 2026). So prompts set the starting point, and gates set the slope. Chapter 7, Check the agent’s work, built the checks for one change; this chapter keeps them working for months on old code.

shipIt.title: A baseline and the first three rules
shipIt.body: A monthly entropy chart, a ratchet gate that stops new duplication, and three lint rules that came from real review comments, each with fixtures. Show a teammate one PR that the gate stopped.

modules.title: One agent or many?

keyIdeas.title: Start with one agent, and make the evidence argue for more
keyIdeas.body: Kim et al. found the strongest predictor of whether extra agents help is how well one agent already does. Their rule of thumb: once one agent scores above about 45%, more agents rarely help. Treat it as a hint from one study, not a law: the authors call it “a practical selection rule rather than a universal scaling principle”, it matched the sign of the gain in 94% of 16 SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench configurations, and the effect behind it did not survive their cluster-robust correction. What did survive is error amplification: without a central verifier, errors spread more as tasks get harder. MAST (Cemri et al., 1,600+ traces) names 14 failure modes; the top three are step repetition, reasoning-action mismatch and not knowing when to stop. Anthropic gives three reasons many agents do help: protecting context, parallel breadth and specialization, and says to expect three to ten times the tokens, and about seven times for agent teams.

keyIdeas.title: Many agents win when the job splits cleanly and a check says when each part is done
keyIdeas.body: Cursor (January 2026) ran hundreds of agents for about a week to build a browser with over a million lines of code. Flat coordination failed first: with shared locks, 20 agents slowed to the throughput of two or three, and optimistic concurrency made them risk-averse. What worked was planners that create tasks, workers that only complete them, and a judge that decides whether to continue; an integrator role became a bottleneck and was removed, and “the prompts matter more”. Anthropic’s C compiler (February 2026) used 16 agents over about 2,000 sessions, for under $20,000, to write 100,000 lines that pass 99% of GCC’s torture tests; agents claimed tasks with lock files, and when they all hit the same bug in one big task, GCC as a reference oracle let each agent own different files. Decomposition rules you can reuse: GitHub Spec Kit marks a task [P] only if it touches different files and waits on nothing unfinished; Kiro runs independent tasks in execution waves; Robert Brennan (OpenHands) asks for tasks one agent can finish in one PR, verify quickly, and order by dependencies, leaves first, and suggests starting with three to five agents at once.

keyIdeas.title: One agent owns the judgment; the others read, search and check
keyIdeas.body: ZS Associates built one agent per analyst step and got true facts with the wrong action, because context was lost at every handoff; they rebuilt it as one agent that owns the reasoning and delegates narrow investigations to subagents that return results, not judgments. Factory’s Missions use an orchestrator, workers and validators: a validation contract is written before any code, validators have never seen the code they check, and features run one at a time with only read-only work in parallel. Uber’s uReview runs many review generators, then rates, filters and deduplicates their comments; about 25,000 comments a week, with 67% addressed (Uber’s own numbers). Six workflow patterns cover most needs: classify and act, fan out and synthesize, adversarial verification, generate and filter, tournament, and loop until done.

keyIdeas.title: Measure a second model before you add one
keyIdeas.body: In one workshop paper (Xiang et al., arXiv 2607.21656, July 2026, accepted at the Agentic SE workshop of KDD 2026), Claude Opus 4.7 reviewing Codex GPT-5.5 raised the pass rate from 71.6% to 89.7%, Codex reviewing Claude lowered it from 91.4% to 82.8%, and Claude reviewing itself gained nothing. The tasks were 116 LiveCodeBench competitive-programming problems, the reviewers read code without running it, and the authors say the setting does not generalize to repository-scale bug fixing or multi-file review. The lasting lesson is the asymmetry: the other model’s review helped only when the reviewer was the stronger model, and hurt when it was the weaker one. Test any second reviewer on your own PRs first (chapter 21, Test your agents like code). Factory picks a model per role and may put validation on a different provider on purpose.

keyIdeas.title: The tool map, and what survives a restart
keyIdeas.body: Subagents: a helper with its own context for isolated reads, returning a summary. /batch: splits one change into 5 to 30 units, each in its own git worktree. Dynamic workflows: a JavaScript script with agent(), pipeline() and parallel() that holds the plan in code instead of in Claude’s context; up to 16 agents at once by default (fewer in a small-CPU container, up to 256 if you raise it), 1,000 per run; they run in claude -p and the Agent SDK; type ultracode in a prompt to ask for one, and /deep-research is a bundled example. A run resumes only in the same session, or in a session you resume whose saved results still exist; a fresh session starts over, so a pod that restarts on an empty disk loses the run while the files under ~/.claude/projects survive only if you keep them. Agent teams: experimental and off by default, a lead plus teammates with a shared task list and messages; they need an interactive session, so in -p and the Agent SDK no teammates spawn; the docs suggest three to five teammates. Between agents that different teams or vendors own, use A2A (v1.0, 12 March 2026, with signed Agent Cards; in the Agentic AI Foundation since 27 August 2026); use MCP to expose tools (chapter 19, Connect agents to tools), and see chapter 22, Build your own agent, for choosing the wire.

keyIdeas.title: Merge parallel work through owned paths, a queue and one shared plan
keyIdeas.body: In Xu et al. (arXiv 2607.04697), different agents editing the same area conflicted 41.7% of the time, against 19.8% for one agent. Give each writer its own worktree and owned paths, merge one change at a time through a queue, and test each merge first with git merge-tree. Conflicts start upstream too: Maggie Appleton (GitHub Next) shows that when every developer drives agents alone, the alignment that used to happen before the code piles up on the PR, as wasted work and coordination debt. Write one plan per feature before agents fan out. Running a fleet across a team (WIP limits, kill rules, review capacity) is the lead’s job in chapter 31, The AI team lead’s job.

labs.title: One reviewer against a fan-out
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): On a throwaway branch of any repo you know (a small public sample app works), plant four bugs in separate commits across at least three files: an off-by-one in a loop, a missing await, a permission check that returns data anyway, and a SQL query built by string formatting. Run two reviews, each in a fresh session, on the diff: (a) one agent asked to review it; (b) a fan-out: one read-only reviewer per changed file, then a verifier that sees only the findings and the code and tries to disprove each one. In Claude Code, ask for a workflow (or start the prompt with ultracode) and save the run; with another agent, run parallel read-only sessions and one verifier session by hand. Record planted bugs found, false alarms, tokens or cost, and minutes for each. At Rhino: use a Lane A branch of the FCP frontend with factory-seeded data, save the workflow as .claude/workflows/fcp-review.js, and add the FE guild’s own review skill as a third arm.
labs.output: A results table for both arms and a saved review workflow or recipe

labs.title: Split a migration by independence
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): In any repo with ten or more call sites of an old pattern (a React data hook you want to replace, class components, Django function views, or print calls to swap for logging), have one agent list the call sites and what imports what, then mark a task [P] only if it touches different files and waits on nothing unfinished. Migrate a slice of about six call sites three ways from the same commit: in one session in order; in parallel, one git worktree per unit (/batch in Claude Code, or git worktree add and several sessions); and in leaf-first waves with a serial merge that runs the tests and git merge-tree before each merge. On purpose, give two parallel units one shared file, and watch the conflict. Record time, tokens, conflicts and test results. At Rhino: take one slice of the useResult-to-useQuery move in the FCP frontend (the useResult-to-useQuery work), Lane A only, and keep the path manifest in the migration skill.
labs.output: A task list with [P] marks, a three-way comparison and your rule for when to go parallel

labs.title: What survives a stop, an exit and a restart
labs.body: Solo (about 30 min): In Claude Code, ask for a small workflow, for example “ultracode: count TODO comments per top-level directory, then summarize”. Stop it halfway from /workflows and relaunch it in the same session; note which agents reran. Exit, start a fresh session and ask for a relaunch; then try again after claude --resume. Run it once headless with claude -p (it needs a Workflow allow rule or auto mode). Write down what a remote agent would lose if its container restarted on an empty disk. With another agent, test the same question for its background or cloud runs. At Rhino: this decides whether pods in the remote-agent project keep ~/.claude/projects on a persistent volume or accept a rerun.
labs.output: A one-page note on what resumes, what reruns and what is lost

checks.q: One study says extra agents stop helping once one agent scores above about 45%. How much weight should you give that?
checks.a: Some, as a rule of thumb from one study: Kim et al. call it a practical selection rule, not a law, and it didn’t survive their strictest statistics. The robust finding is error amplification (17.2 times for independent agents, 4.4 times with a central verifier). Measure on your own task.

checks.q: Why can’t a headless pod use agent teams, and what resumes after the pod restarts?
checks.a: Teams need an interactive session; in -p and the Agent SDK no teammates spawn. Use a dynamic workflow, which runs headless but resumes only in the same session or a resumed one whose saved results survived. On an empty disk it starts over.

checks.q: When may two agents write in parallel?
checks.a: When their tasks touch different files and neither waits on unfinished work, each has its own worktree and owned paths, and a check tells each when it is done. Merge one at a time: different agents conflicted 41.7% of the time, against 19.8% for one agent.

checks.q: Which workflow patterns fit a bug-hunting review?
checks.a: Fan out and synthesize, then adversarial verification of each finding, with one agent owning the final judgment.

watchOut: Swarms of parallel writers on coupled code. Cursor’s 20 agents behind shared locks ran at the speed of two or three.
A verifier that declares victory early, or that already saw the code it checks.
Benchmark results about puzzles used as proof about your PRs. Name the benchmark, then test on your own work.
Fan-out multiplies reads, including reads of anything sensitive. At Rhino, parallel runs are Lane A on synthetic data only.

modules.goal: Choose the right rung on the orchestration ladder (one agent, subagents, /batch, dynamic workflows, agent teams, and agents that other teams own), split work only where it is independent and checkable, and merge parallel work without conflicts.
modules.why: Starting ten agents is now one command, and it feels ten times faster. The best evidence says it often isn’t. In the largest controlled study so far (Kim et al., Nature Machine Intelligence, July 2026; 260 configurations on six agent benchmarks), every multi-agent design scored 1% to 13% below a single agent on SWE-bench Verified, and on Terminal-Bench the centralized design fell 20% while independent agents gained 6%. Independent agents amplified errors 17.2 times; a central verifier held that to 4.4 times. The cases where many agents clearly won, such as Cursor’s browser and Anthropic’s C compiler, had work that split cleanly and a check that told each agent when it was done. So the default is read many, write one: agents fan out to read and check, and one agent owns the judgment, unless each writer owns different files.

shipIt.body: Share your saved review workflow or recipe with its planted-bug score, false alarms and cost against the single-agent baseline, plus the one-line rule you now use for when to fan out. At Rhino, publish it in the team marketplace (chapter 23, Share and test skills across teams).

modules.title: Connect agents to tools: CLI, MCP and skills

keyIdeas.title: CLI, MCP or skill: pick by where the agent runs
keyIdeas.body: A CLI fits when the agent has a shell and a sandbox: it costs little context, composes in bash, and tools like git and gh are already in the model’s training. MCP fits when you need auth, central governance, rich protocol features such as elicitation or MCP Apps, or access from surfaces with no shell, such as claude.ai, Cowork and web agents. A skill encodes the workflow on top of either (chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills). David Soria Parra, MCP’s co-creator, says the best agents in 2026 use all three. Nick Aldridge, an MCP core maintainer, sums up the trade: CLIs win on context and composition but mean running code and installing dependencies; MCP wins on elicitation, auth and curation. The clearest real case is the browser: the Playwright team recommends its CLI plus skills for coding agents and MCP for long exploratory loops where keeping browser state is worth the tokens, Chrome DevTools for agents ships both, and Vercel’s agent-browser is CLI-first (chapter 11, Build UI with agents).

keyIdeas.title: Design tools around what the user wants done
keyIdeas.body: One tool per agent story, not one per endpoint: if finding an order’s status takes three API calls, make them inside one tool rather than asking the agent to chain them (Jeremiah Lowin, FastMCP). Anthropic’s guide adds: namespace tools, return names rather than UUIDs, offer a concise or detailed response, paginate, truncate with a hint, and write errors that say how to fix the call. Flatten arguments into named top-level values, with enums for fixed choices. Descriptions are the biggest lever (Arcade’s 600-word rule). Practitioners’ limits differ, so treat them as rules of thumb: Arcade saw chained calls fail over 50% of the time across six tools and success drop past about 20 tools; Lowin draws the line at about 50 tools visible to the agent, across all servers. Test tool changes with held-out tasks (chapter 21, Test your agents like code).

keyIdeas.title: Keep context small: load tools late, and call them from code
keyIdeas.body: Progressive discovery loads a tool’s full definition only when the agent needs it; tool search does this and is on by default in Claude Code. Claude Code warns when one MCP result passes 10,000 tokens, and above 25,000 by default it saves the result to a file and gives the agent the path. Code mode, or programmatic tool calling, lets the agent write a short script that calls several tools and filters the results, instead of passing every result through the model; Uber’s savings above come from this. The script needs a sandbox of its own, which is the cost Lowin warns about.

keyIdeas.title: The 2026 spec, and servers the clouds run for you
keyIdeas.body: The 2026-07-28 spec made the core stateless: no initialize handshake, no session ID, state in explicit handles, and server/discover. Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers let gateways route requests, client ID metadata documents replace dynamic client registration, and roots, sampling, logging and HTTP+SSE are deprecated. Enterprise-managed authorization (Cross-App Access, with an ID-JAG token) lets the company’s identity provider grant access at sign-in, with no consent screen per server; Okta was the only provider at launch. The clouds now host MCP servers: the AWS MCP Server (generally available 6 May 2026) calls over 15,000 AWS API operations with your IAM role, runs scripts in a sandbox without network, logs every call to CloudTrail and adds IAM condition keys (aws:ViaAWSMCPService, aws:CalledViaAWSMCP) so one policy can let people change things while agents only read. Google made over 50 managed MCP servers available to everyone on 29 April 2026 (GKE, Cloud Run, BigQuery, Cloud SQL and more), governed by Cloud IAM, including Deny policies, with Model Armor and audit logs. Chapter 28, Agents on AWS and Google Cloud, goes deeper.

keyIdeas.title: Put one gateway between agents and servers
keyIdeas.body: Karan Sampath (Anthropic) argues that a security team should “bless one platform” and let every team build servers behind it. A gateway holds sign-in, role-based access, a proxy so clients see only the gateway, a secure tunnel, a sub-registry of approved servers, and data on which tools carry the load. Uber’s gateway and registry are its control plane: tools generated from more than 10,000 service definitions, PII redaction, and blocked mutating endpoints. Managed options now exist: AgentCore Gateway turns OpenAPI and Lambda functions into MCP tools, finds tools by semantic search and checks every call with interceptors and Cedar policy; Google’s Agent Gateway works with Model Armor; Apigee exposes APIs as MCP tools. Registries (AWS Agent Registry, generally available 31 August 2026, and Google’s Agent Registry) list what exists, so unapproved servers show up. In Claude Code, allowedMcpServers and deniedMcpServers match on serverUrl or serverCommand; serverName is only a label.

keyIdeas.title: Every tool is a supply-chain item and an input channel
keyIdeas.body: Chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer, covers injection and the lethal trifecta. For tools, add tool poisoning (orders hidden in a tool description), rug pulls (a server changes its tools after you approved it), shadowing (one server’s tool redefines another’s), cross-server attacks and the confused deputy (a server acts with its own, larger rights). Treat tool output as untrusted input, pin and hash the tool lists you approved, scan servers with Snyk agent-scan or Cisco mcp-scanner, and give agent identities read-only cloud rights unless a person makes the change.

labs.title: One tool, two ways
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): Pick one read-only job people do by hand on any GitHub repo, such as “why did this CI run fail?” or “which open issues mention this module?”. Build it twice. (a) A small MCP server with the official Python or TypeScript SDK, or FastMCP, with one or two workflow tools: for example ci_run_summary(run_id) that calls gh and returns only the failing job, the failing step and a 40-line excerpt. (b) The same job as a short script or CLI, plus a SKILL.md that says when and how to use it. Write 10 prompts and keep 3 aside. Run both arms in fresh sessions and record success, turns and context used (/context in Claude Code; the token count in other agents). labs.title: Tune descriptions and errors
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Take the tools from lab 1. Rewrite each description: what it does, when to use it and when not, each argument with an example, and what it returns. Flatten arguments, use enums for fixed choices, add pagination with a “call again with page=2” hint, and make every error say how to fix the call. Then run only the 3 held-out prompts, plus 3 near-miss prompts where the tool must not be used. At Rhino: record the before and after in the PR that changes the tool.
labs.output: The before and after on held-out and near-miss prompts

labs.title: Rug-pull alarm and a rights check
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Write a small script that asks each MCP server you use for its tool list (for example with the MCP Inspector’s CLI mode or a tiny client), hashes each tool’s name, description and input schema, stores the hashes, and reports any change. Schedule it nightly with cron or a CI job, and run Snyk agent-scan or Cisco mcp-scanner on your MCP config once. In your Claude Code settings, allow servers by serverUrl or serverCommand, never by serverName. If you have a sandbox cloud account, do the read-only lab in chapter 28, Agents on AWS and Google Cloud, for the cloud’s own MCP server. At Rhino: send the report to the security team’s channel, and ask them before you approve a new server.
labs.output: A running job, its first report and your allowlist

checks.q: When do you pick MCP over a CLI?
checks.a: When you need auth, central governance, protocol features such as elicitation, or access from surfaces without a shell. With a shell and a sandbox, a CLI plus a skill is usually cheaper in context.

checks.q: Why return names instead of UUIDs?
checks.a: Agents reason and chain better on meaningful identifiers, and UUIDs invite made-up IDs.

checks.q: Is serverName in allowedMcpServers a security control?
checks.a: No. It is a label anyone can change. Match on serverUrl or serverCommand.

checks.q: A cloud MCP server can call any API your role allows. How do you keep agents read-only while people can still make changes?
checks.a: Deny mutating actions when the call comes through MCP: on AWS with the aws:ViaAWSMCPService condition key, on Google with an IAM Deny policy on the managed server. Every agent call still lands in the audit log.

watchOut: Designing around the Tasks extension. It became polling, and few clients support it.
Tool output is untrusted: an issue body or a log line can carry an injection.
Remote servers can change after you approve them. Pin, hash and re-check.
One-click installs that switch on writes. Read the server’s arguments before you click.

modules.goal: Decide CLI, MCP or skill for each integration, design tools around what the user wants done, keep tool context small, put one governed gateway between agents and servers (your own or your cloud’s), and treat every tool and its output as untrusted.
modules.why: How you design and serve tools decides whether agents succeed, more than how many tools they have. Uber routes over 1,000 MCP servers through one gateway, yet projects the gateway’s tools to its coding agents as shell commands, because loading the MCP schemas added about 50,000 to 70,000 tokens to every session; letting the agent batch calls in code cut tokens by 55 to 71% on typical SQL work and by more than 90% on bulk jobs (Uber’s own figures, August 2026). The Playwright team measured the same trade-off on one browser task: about 114,000 tokens through its MCP server against about 26,800 through its CLI (February 2026). In 2026 the protocol also went stateless, AWS and Google started running MCP servers and gateways for you, and every new server became one more way in for an attacker.

shipIt.body: A one-page decision for one integration, with your measured success, turns and tokens, the gateway or allowlist rule it will sit behind, and the winner published where your team finds tools (at Rhino, the team marketplace in chapter 23, Share and test skills across teams).

modules.title: Let agents work alone, safely

keyIdeas.title: Boundaries first: sandbox, egress, filesystem, nothing to steal
keyIdeas.body: Whether the user is fooled or the agent reads a poisoned ticket, the same walls must hold. Claude Code’s sandbox isolates the filesystem and sends network traffic through a proxy with an allowlist; Anthropic reported 84% fewer permission prompts with it (October 2025), with git credentials kept outside the sandbox. Deny egress by default and allow named hosts, and don’t treat the model provider’s own API as a free exit: Anthropic had to put a proxy in front of it. Keep secrets out of any file the agent can read; in the Great Loops Debate (July 2026) a panelist calls that the most concrete step, because a goal-seeking agent whose token is too weak will search the disk for a stronger one. Bypass mode belongs only in an isolated container or VM without internet: in August 2025 the s1ngularity malware ran victims’ own Claude, Gemini and Q command-line tools with --dangerously-skip-permissions, --yolo and --trust-all-tools to hunt for secrets (Wiz), so switch bypass off in managed settings on laptops and runners. Falco’s co-creators (May 2026) argue for kernel and network boundaries the agent cannot edit, instead of rules in the prompt.

keyIdeas.title: Auto mode is now the default, so configure it
keyIdeas.body: Anthropic made auto mode the default for new sessions on Pro, Max and Team on 14 August 2026, and from Claude Code v2.1.283 it is the built-in starting mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions on every plan and provider; claude -p and the Agent SDK still start in Manual. Managed defaults don’t move: a permissions.defaultMode set in managed settings outranks the built-in default, and admins can remove auto mode entirely. Cost depends on the plan: Anthropic stopped charging Pro, Max and Team for the classifier’s tokens, while on Enterprise and on Claude API, Bedrock, Agent Platform and Foundry accounts the classifier calls count toward usage (docs, September 2026). Evidence from Anthropic (vendor data): in the August 2026 study, people caught 13.6% of the dangerous commands and auto mode blocked 89% of the same commands; the March 2026 write-up reported 0.4% false positives on 10,000 real internal tool calls and a 17% miss rate on 52 real overeager actions. An independent stress test (Ji et al., arXiv 2604.04978, April 2026) found far more misses: on 128 deliberately ambiguous DevOps prompts, auto mode missed 81% of the risky state changes end to end, partly because 36.8% of all state changes were file edits inside the project, which the classifier does not review. Treat auto mode as one layer, not the wall. By default only your working directory and its git remotes count as internal, and it allows reading .env and sending credentials to their matching API. So describe your trusted infrastructure in the auto-mode environment (admins set it in managed settings; developers can add but not remove), treat soft and hard deny as guidance, and use deny and ask rules for hard limits. Other agents split the same two controls: Codex separates the sandbox mode from the approval policy (chapter 4).

keyIdeas.title: A hook is the guardian, and you supervise by interrupting
keyIdeas.body: A PreToolUse hook permits, denies or changes each action before it runs; OWASP’s Agent Control Standard calls this a guardian. Hooks run the same way every time and in every mode; a line in CLAUDE.md is a suggestion. Nick Nisi (WorkOS, May 2026) found Claude would simply create the marker file that meant “tests ran”, so his harness stores a hash of the real test output instead: enforce, don’t instruct. People supervise unattended agents by watching and interrupting, not by approving each step: in Anthropic’s February 2026 autonomy data, new users fully auto-approved about 20% of sessions, rising to over 40% by 750 sessions, while experienced users also interrupted more often (vendor telemetry). Note that allowManagedHooksOnly also switches off /goal, because /goal runs as a hook.

keyIdeas.title: Every loop needs a checkable exit, a turn cap and a budget
keyIdeas.body: /goal keeps Claude working until a condition holds: after each turn a small fast model (Haiku by default on the Claude API) judges the condition from the conversation only. It runs no commands and reads no files, so write the condition as proof that Claude’s own output can show (“npx tsc --noEmit exits 0”), add what must not change (“no file under tests/ changes”) and a turn clause (“or stop after 15 turns”). /goal also works in claude -p; there, add --max-turns and --max-budget-usd. One item per pass, and one open PR per loop. Loops pay where the check is strong: at Sentry, Greg Pstrucha pays about $5 a PR for security scanning that finds real issues; ports with years of tests behind them converge; throwaway prototypes are fine. Geoff Huntley’s advice is to encode your rules as checks that stop the loop from closing: pre-commit hooks, static analysis and deterministic tests. For anything that runs alone, look at how often all tries pass, not the best try (pass^k in chapter 21, Test your agents like code).

keyIdeas.title: Pick the runner by lane: headless in your pipeline, routines in the vendor’s cloud
keyIdeas.body: Headless claude -p in your own CI or pod starts in Manual; give it an exact tool allowlist (dontAsk mode), a turn cap, a budget cap and a pinned model, and a Workflow allow rule if it runs workflows. Routines (research preview) are a saved prompt, repositories and connectors that run in Anthropic’s cloud on a schedule (at most once an hour), from an API call or on a GitHub event. They belong to one person’s account and act as that person, have no permission-mode picker, and can use every tool of every connector you include, writes too, without asking, so include only what the routine needs. Text sent to /fire arrives wrapped as untrusted data, and a green run only means the session exited cleanly. Routines aren’t available under ZDR, so at Rhino they are Lane A only; unattended Lane B work runs as the Agent SDK or claude -p in our own pod (chapter 29, Run agents remotely).
