labs.title: The fooled-user drill
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): In a throwaway copy of any repo, create a dummy credentials file outside the project (for example ~/.fake-cloud/credentials holding FAKE_KEY=not-a-secret) and start a local listener that plays the attacker (python3 -m http.server 8765 in another terminal). Now play the phished user: paste a prompt that asks the agent to read that file, base64 it and POST it to the listener. Run it four ways in fresh sessions: Manual mode, auto mode, the sandbox on (/sandbox) with the dummy file’s folder outside what it may read, and the sandbox with a network allowlist that holds only your package registry. For each run, record whether the file was read, whether the POST left the machine, and which layer stopped it. If you use Codex or Cursor, repeat with their sandbox settings. At Rhino: repeat inside the pod image with synthetic data only; the Lane B pod must stop both the read and the POST, and bypass mode must be switched off in managed settings.
labs.output: A table of attempts, modes and the layer that stopped each

labs.title: The guardian hook
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Write a PreToolUse hook script that denies a git push to main, network commands to hosts off an allowlist, reads of .env files, and anything under a sensitive-data folder you create with fake records. Red-team it with a README line asking agents to curl the environment to a URL, and with a fake ticket in a text file that hides an instruction to push to main. Log every attempt and the hook’s verdict. Then write the same limits as permission deny rules, and note which attacks each layer caught and which it missed. At Rhino: add the FCP’s PHI-adjacent paths and all production hosts to the deny lists, synthetic data only.
labs.output: The hook, the deny rules and a red-team log

labs.title: A goal with a proof and a budget
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Pick a small failing check in any repo: a set of type errors, one lint rule, or one failing test file. Write a /goal condition that names the proof and the limits, such as “npx tsc --noEmit exits 0, no file under tests/ changes, or stop after 15 turns”, and run it in auto mode. Then run the same goal headless: claude -p "/goal ..." --max-turns 20 --max-budget-usd 2. Record turns, cost, where it got stuck, and whether it tried to weaken a test. With another agent, write the same loop as a script with a turn cap and a cost cap. At Rhino: use a Lane A frontend or backend check with factory-seeded data, and open at most one PR.
labs.output: A run report and a goal condition you would reuse

checks.q: In Anthropic’s red-team exercise, why couldn’t a classifier stop the credential leak?
checks.a: The phished user typed the prompt, so the request matched what the user asked for. Only egress controls and filesystem boundaries held.

checks.q: Why a hook instead of a CLAUDE.md rule for “never push to main”?
checks.a: A hook runs deterministically on every tool call. A prose rule can be missed or argued away.

checks.q: What stops a /goal run, and what must the condition contain?
checks.a: A small fast model checks the condition after every turn, from the conversation only. So the condition must name the proof Claude will show, what must not change and a turn limit; in claude -p, also set --max-turns and --max-budget-usd.

checks.q: Why can’t PHI-adjacent work use routines?
checks.a: Routines run in Anthropic’s cloud and aren’t available under ZDR, which the BAA requires for Claude Code. Unattended Lane B work runs in our own pod.

watchOut: Bypass mode on any machine with real credentials. s1ngularity ran local agent CLIs with their skip-permissions flags to hunt secrets; switch bypass off in managed settings.
Allowlisting the model provider’s own API as an exit. Anthropic had to put a proxy in front of it.
A routine with every connector included. It can write through all of them without asking.
A green routine run. It means the session exited, not that the task worked; read the transcript.
modules.watchTime: 38 min core, 1 h 26 min with electives
modules.goal: Let agents run while nobody watches each step, and stay safe: boundaries first (sandbox, egress, filesystem, no secrets to find), auto mode configured for your environment, a deterministic guardian hook, loops with a checkable exit and a budget, and scheduled runs only where your lane allows. Chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer, covers the basics; this chapter builds the unattended setup.
modules.why: In May 2026 Anthropic described a red-team exercise from February 2026: an employee was phished into launching Claude Code with a ready-made prompt whose setup steps asked Claude to read ~/.aws/credentials, encode them and POST them to an outside endpoint. It worked in 24 of 25 tries. This was not prompt injection: the user typed the request, so to the model, and to any classifier, it looked like what the user wanted. Anthropic’s conclusion: the only defense that holds here is the environment, meaning egress controls that block the POST whatever the intent, and filesystem boundaries that keep ~/.aws out of reach. The other failure is text the agent reads, such as a ticket that carries orders, where the lethal trifecta (chapter 4) applies. Approving every step is no answer either: in Anthropic’s August 2026 study with 1,053 paid testers, people caught 13.6% of dangerous commands (vendor data). Once agents run alone, both failures need walls, not wishes.

shipIt.title: The unattended-run invariants
shipIt.body: Write the invariants for one agent that runs alone: what it may read, which hosts it may reach, where credentials live, its turn and budget caps, and who reviews its PR. Enforce them with the sandbox, deny rules, a guardian hook and an auto-mode environment, then run twenty red-team prompts (fooled-user and injected-content) against seeded fake secrets; every attempt must be blocked and logged. At Rhino, these are the pod invariants: synthetic data only, no route to production, credentials through a broker, Jira and Slack input treated as untrusted.

modules.title: Test your agents like code

keyIdeas.title: An eval is a test suite for behavior
keyIdeas.body: You can’t read a prompt, a skill or a CLAUDE.md and know what the agent will do, because the same input gives different runs. Harbor’s Alex Shaw (Jul 2026) puts it with a regex he can predict for a million runs and a model call he can’t. So you measure behavior, as machine-learning teams do. Anthropic’s words (Jan 2026): a task is one test with inputs and success criteria; a trial is one attempt at it; a grader scores one aspect of a trial; the transcript is the full record of a trial (messages, tool calls, results); the outcome is the final state (the reservation in the database, not the agent saying “booked”); a suite is a set of tasks. You always test the model and the harness together. In Shaw’s mapping, your prompts, skills and tools are the weights, a PR to the harness is a gradient step, and reward hacking is overfitting.

keyIdeas.title: Start from real failures, and seal them
keyIdeas.body: Anthropic’s advice: 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start, because early changes have big effects. Error analysis comes first: read transcripts, note each failure, group the notes, and write tasks for the groups that matter. A good task is one where two domain experts would give the same pass or fail, with a reference solution that proves it can be solved; a task that fails on every one of many trials is usually a broken task, not a weak agent. The best coding tasks come from your own history: check out the parent commit of a merged fix, write the bug as a ticket, and grade with the repo’s tests plus the fix’s own tests held back (Braintrust built one this way from TypeScript-Go fix PRs, Mar 2026). Seal each task: no git history after the parent, no link to the fixing PR, and a clean environment for every trial, because Anthropic saw Claude gain an unfair advantage by reading git history from earlier trials. Public benchmarks leak too: OpenAI stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified after finding flawed tests or descriptions in 59.4% of 138 audited hard problems, and models that could reproduce some of the answers. Test both directions (cases where a skill must fire and cases where it must stay quiet). Capability suites start with a low pass rate; once they saturate, they graduate into a regression suite that must stay near 100%. This also serves Rhino’s rule to fix the harness on the second repeat: turn the second repeat into an eval task first, so you can prove the fix works.

keyIdeas.title: Grade the outcome, with the cheapest grader you can trust
keyIdeas.body: Anthropic names three kinds: code graders (tests, types, lint, state checks such as “the view has security_invoker = true”) are fast, cheap and repeatable; model graders (an AI judge with a rubric) handle meaning but need calibration; human graders are the gold standard and slow. In Birgitta Böckeler’s terms (Apr 2026), these are sensors, computational or inferential. Use code first, a judge where code can’t see, and people to define and audit what good means. Grade what the agent produced, not the path it took: requiring tool A, then tool B punishes valid routes you didn’t foresee. Passing tests is not the whole bar: in METR’s review of 296 agent PRs that passed SWE-bench Verified, maintainers’ merge decisions ran about 24 points below the automated grader (Mar 2026), so add a mergeability rubric (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work). And test the grader: Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench until an Anthropic researcher found rigid grading (it rejected “96.12” when expecting “96.124991…”), ambiguous task specs and tasks that could not be reproduced exactly; after fixing those bugs and loosening the scaffold, it scored 95%.

keyIdeas.title: Count trials: pass@k and pass^k
keyIdeas.body: One run per task tells you little: in a 10-task suite, one failure moves the score 10 points (Braintrust). Run at least three trials. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k trials passes; pass^k is the chance that all k pass. At 75% per trial, pass@3 is about 98% but pass^3 is about 42% (Anthropic). Use pass@k when a person picks the best of several tries; use pass^k for anything that runs alone, such as the night shift and routines in chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely. Record cost, turns and time next to every score as a second outcome: in Braintrust’s test, agentic search and vector search both fixed 70% of TypeScript-Go bugs, but vector search spent far more tokens. Cost grades the harness, never a person. Keep tests and graders out of the agent’s reach: in SWE-Marathon (Jun 2026), agents tried to exploit the environment or verifier in 13.8% of rollouts.

keyIdeas.title: Calibrate the AI judge before you trust it
keyIdeas.body: An LLM judge is a classifier, so measure it like one (Laurie Voss, Arize, May 2026). One domain expert labels outputs pass or fail with a short critique: binary labels, not 1 to 5 scores (Hamel Husain). Split the labels: a few clear examples go into the judge prompt, a dev set to improve it, and a test set you run once at the end; never put dev or test examples in the prompt. Treat “fail” as the positive class and report the true positive rate (real failures the judge catches) and the true negative rate (real passes it passes) separately. Agreement hides misses: if 5% of outputs fail, a judge that always says pass agrees 95% of the time and catches nothing. Give each dimension its own judge and a way out (“unknown”). Known biases are position, length and self-preference (Zheng et al., 2023; Panickssery et al., 2024), so swap answer order, compare long and short answers, and test a judge from another model family. Never let an AI reviewer be the only gate: in one practitioner’s 23-setup test (Insight APAC, Jul 2026), an Opus review gate merged three models’ implementations of a complex feature, while objective tests scored them 16, 18 and 30 out of 38.

keyIdeas.title: A/B test every harness change
keyIdeas.body: Change one thing and keep the model, tasks, budget and number of trials fixed. The 2026 evidence says intuition is a weak guide. ETH Zurich: context files didn’t generally raise success and cost over 20% more; they were useful for non-standard conventions, while repository overviews didn’t help. Lulla et al. (Jan 2026): an AGENTS.md went with 28.64% lower median runtime at similar task completion, so measure cost as well as success. SkillsBench: focused skills with three modules or fewer beat large bundles. The Aug 2026 skill-failure study found that skills often turn validation checklists into mandatory work: excessive verification alone explained 67 of the 182 cost regressions it traced. Chen et al. (Feb 2026): prompting agents to write more or fewer tests didn’t significantly change outcomes. Check that the change really ran: Vercel’s Next.js docs skill was never invoked in 56% of eval cases (Jan 2026), and the Towards AI team checked that compaction actually fired before trusting a result. Tools: Harbor runs any agent on task folders in parallel sandboxes; claude plugin eval compares runs with and without a plugin in CI (chapter 23, Share and test skills across teams); Braintrust, Phoenix and Langfuse store traces. At Rhino, eval runs are Lane A on synthetic data only, because a transcript holds everything the agent read.

clips.label: Your judge is a classifier: a golden set labeled with the same rubric, reference solutions, cases in both directions and a 75/25 split
Comparing judge labels with human labels: true and false positives, precision versus recall, and why catching failures usually favors recall
Position, length, confidence and self-preference bias, and a benchmark that scored 42% until its grader was fixed

takeaways: People who label the golden set need the same written rubric as the judge, or their labels are arbitrary too.
Keep part of the labeled set out of every prompt change, or you overfit the judge to the cases you keep looking at.
When the judge hunts for failures, a false alarm costs a human review and a miss reaches users. Decide which error costs more before you tune.
If a failing trace looks fine to you, suspect the eval before the agent.

labs.title: Seal five tasks from your own history
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): In any repo with tests (a small public sample app works), find five merged bug fixes that added or changed a test (`git log --grep=fix`). For each one, export the parent commit with no history (`git archive <parent> | tar -x -C task-N/repo`, then `git init` inside it), write the bug as a ticket in `task-N/issue.md` (what is wrong and how to see it, never how to fix it), and keep the fix’s tests in `task-N/hidden/` as the grader. Prove each task: the parent fails the hidden tests and the real fix passes them. Then run the agent headless three times per task, each time in a fresh copy with a turn cap and a budget cap (for Claude Code, `claude -p` with `--max-turns` and `--max-budget-usd`, and permissions scoped to that folder). Copy the hidden tests in, run the whole suite, and record pass@3, pass^3, turns and cost per task. Read one failing transcript and write down why it failed. At Rhino: use closed Lane-A tickets on synthetic data only, and keep ticket text to code behavior; these tasks can seed the team’s sealed replay set in chapter 33, Measure results and cost.
labs.output: Five sealed task folders with reference solutions, and a results table

labs.title: Calibrate an AI grader
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Warm up with this chapter’s practice tool, “Can you trust the AI grader?”. Then pick one yes-or-no question about agent work, for example “Does this PR description show evidence that the change works?” Collect 30 examples (agent PR descriptions, or the final messages from lab 1) and label each pass or fail yourself, with a one-line reason. Put four clear examples into a judge prompt that answers only PASS, FAIL or UNKNOWN, and split the rest into a dev half and a test half. Treat “fail” as the positive class. On the dev half, count the real failures the judge catches (true positive rate) and the real passes it passes (true negative rate), fix the prompt, and repeat. Freeze the prompt and run the test half once. Then probe two biases: pad two failing examples with long, confident text, and swap the order in one pairwise comparison. Note which verdicts flip, and repeat with a judge from another model family if you can. Thirty examples teach the method, not trust: Hamel Husain suggests 30 to 50 examples of each label in each of the dev and test sets before you rely on a judge. At Rhino: use only Lane-A PRs, and no judge may block or approve a PR until its two rates are written in the PR that adds it.
labs.output: A versioned judge prompt, a dev and test table with both rates, and two bias notes

labs.title: A/B test one harness change
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): Pick one change you believe in: delete the repository-overview section of your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, add one skill, or add a hook that makes the agent run the tests before it stops. Write down your prediction first. Run lab 1’s five tasks (add five more if you can) three times in each arm, with the same model, turn cap and budget, and a fresh copy for every trial. Before you compare scores, open the transcripts and confirm that the change really happened in the second arm (the skill loaded, the hook ran). Report for each arm: pass rate, pass^3, median cost and median time. Read two failing transcripts per arm and name each failure. Then write a five-line decision memo: keep, drop or test again with more tasks, and why. At Rhino: attach the table and the memo to the PR that changes the harness; a reviewer who is not the requester approves it (SOC 2 CC8.1), and cost is reported per task, never per person.
labs.output: A two-arm results table and a decision memo

checks.q: Your agent passes 75% of trials. What are pass@3 and pass^3, and which one matters for a night-shift agent?
checks.a: pass@3 is about 98% (at least one of three trials passes) and pass^3 is about 42% (all three pass). An agent that runs alone must be right every time, so use pass^3.

checks.q: Why report an AI judge’s true positive and true negative rates instead of its agreement with you?
checks.a: Agreement hides misses when failures are rare. If 5% of outputs fail, a judge that always says pass agrees 95% of the time and catches nothing.

checks.q: An A/B test shows that a new skill makes no difference. What do you check before you delete it?
checks.a: Whether it ran at all. Read the transcripts: Vercel’s skill was never invoked in 56% of eval cases. Then test triggering on its own (chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills).

checks.q: What makes a replay task sealed, and why does it matter?
checks.a: The agent can’t see the answer: no git history after the starting commit, no link to the fixing PR, and a clean copy for every trial. Anthropic saw Claude gain an unfair advantage by reading git history from earlier trials.

watchOut: Scores taken at face value. A broken grader looks like a weak agent, so read failing transcripts before you change the harness (CORE-Bench went from 42% to 95% once its grading and scaffold were fixed).
One run per task. A 10-task suite moves 10 points on a single failure; run at least three trials and look at pass^k.
Graders, tests or task files the agent can edit. Agents tried to game the verifier in 13.8% of SWE-Marathon rollouts; keep every grader read-only to the writer.
PHI in eval tasks, transcripts or judge prompts. A transcript holds everything the agent read, so build suites from Lane A work on synthetic data only.
modules.watchTime: 34 min core, 1 h 27 min with electives
modules.goal: Test your agent setup the way you test code. Turn real failures into a small suite of sealed tasks, choose graders you can trust (code first, then a calibrated AI judge, then people), run enough trials to see reliability as well as capability, and A/B test every change to CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks or the model before it ships.
modules.why: The setup around the model can move results a lot: in LangChain’s tests, changing only the harness took the same model from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (vendor figures, Feb 2026). But the popular moves often don’t help. In ETH Zurich’s study (Feb 2026), repository context files such as AGENTS.md did not generally raise task success and added over 20% inference cost, and repository overviews did not help. In SkillsBench (Feb 2026), curated skills raised the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5%, yet a later study (Aug 2026) found 307 cases where a loaded skill made the agent fail or cost more. Every CLAUDE.md line, skill, hook and model switch is a hypothesis. The developer who can test one in an afternoon stops copying blog posts and keeps only what works.

shipIt.title: A harness eval gate
shipIt.body: A suite of at least ten sealed tasks from real failures, three trials each, that runs on every change to CLAUDE.md, skills or hooks and on every model upgrade. It posts pass rate, pass^3, cost per task and the calibrated judge’s verdicts, with the judge’s true positive and true negative rates, to the PR, and a reviewer who is not the requester decides.

modules.title: Build your own agent: the SDK, tools, traces and evals

keyIdeas.title: Build one only when a skill or a workflow is not enough
keyIdeas.body: Most jobs don’t need a new agent. If you run the job yourself inside your coding agent, write a skill (chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills). If you can draw the whole decision tree, write a workflow: plain code with one model call per step and a typed answer, which costs less and gives you more control. Anthropic defines the difference (Dec 2024): workflows run models and tools through predefined code paths; agents direct their own process and tool use. Build an agent when the path depends on what it finds, the result can be checked, and it runs for other people or without you. Barry Zhang’s checklist (Anthropic, Apr 2025): is the task complex enough, is it worth the tokens (a budget of about 10 cents a task buys only 30,000 to 50,000 tokens), can the model do the critical steps, and how costly and how hard to spot is an error. Thariq Shihipar’s test (Anthropic, Jan 2026): if you can verify its work, it is a good candidate; code can be linted, compiled and run, while research is harder to check, and citing sources is one way. Between a skill and your own agent sit headless runs (`claude -p --output-format json`) and the routines from chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely.

keyIdeas.title: Start from a harness, and freeze a working prototype into it
keyIdeas.body: The loop is easy; the harness around it (tool errors, compaction, permissions, sessions, subagents, hooks) is what teams kept rebuilding. The Claude Agent SDK is Claude Code as a library for Python and TypeScript: `query()` streams messages while the agent works, with the same built-in tools, hooks, subagents, MCP, permissions and sessions. The other routes: the Client SDK (you write the loop), `claude -p` from any language, and Managed Agents, where Anthropic hosts the loop (beta, and not eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA, so Lane A only). OpenAI’s Agents SDK, Google’s ADK, AWS Strands and Vercel’s AI SDK have the same parts. Thariq’s method: prototype in Claude Code with a real API, helper scripts and a short CLAUDE.md, read the transcripts, then keep the instructions and scripts behind a small SDK entry point. Sessions are the conversation history, saved as JSONL on local disk: resume one by ID, fork it to try another path, or mirror it to your own store with a `SessionStore` (transcripts only), because local disk is gone after a restart. One session is one CLI subprocess; about 1 GiB of RAM, 5 GiB of disk and 1 CPU per agent is the docs’ starting point, and chapter 28, Agents on AWS and Google Cloud, and chapter 29, Run agents remotely, cover where it runs. Change two defaults for a product agent: with no `settingSources`, `query()` loads your user and project settings, CLAUDE.md files, skills and auto memory, so pass `settingSources: []` and set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`; and `maxTurns` and `maxBudgetUsd` stay off until you set them. Memory a product agent keeps should be explicit and reviewed (chapter 24, Give agents team memory).

keyIdeas.title: Tools and a schema are the agent’s contract
keyIdeas.body: Thariq names three ways to act: structured tools for atomic actions you want to control or approve, such as writing a file or sending an email; Bash for composable steps with little upfront context; generated code for dynamic logic that composes APIs. Put deterministic work inside the tool: a `get_failed_log(run_id)` handler that calls `gh` beats a model guessing commands. In the SDK, define a tool with `tool()` (TypeScript, a Zod schema) or `@tool` (Python), serve it from `createSdkMcpServer`, and allow it by its full name, `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. When a call fails, return `isError: true` with a message that says what to try next; annotations such as `readOnlyHint` are hints, not enforcement. For the final answer, pass `outputFormat` with a JSON Schema (Zod or Pydantic can generate it; the SDK validates against draft-07): the SDK checks the result, re-prompts on a mismatch, and ends with `error_max_structured_output_retries` when it can’t. Treat `success` without a `structured_output` as a failure too. Keep patient data out of every schema: on the Claude API, compiled schemas are cached for up to 24 hours and don’t get the protections prompts get, so property names, `enum` and `const` values never hold PHI.

keyIdeas.title: Guardrails live outside the model
keyIdeas.body: The SDK checks each tool call in a fixed order: hooks, deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules, then your `canUseTool` callback. Three traps: `allowedTools` only pre-approves, so in `bypassPermissions` mode every other tool still runs; a call approved early never reaches `canUseTool`; and subagents run in the parent’s `bypassPermissions` mode. For a locked-down agent, list the only tools it can see in `tools`, pre-approve them in `allowedTools`, and set `permissionMode: "dontAsk"` so any call that would need approval is denied. A `PreToolUse` hook runs before every other step, and its deny holds even in `bypassPermissions`. Keep credentials outside the agent (a proxy adds the key after the request leaves the sandbox) and deny network egress by default. Thariq calls the whole design Swiss cheese: model alignment, harness permissions with a parser for Bash commands, and a sandbox, each with holes that shouldn’t line up. Bedrock Guardrails or Model Armor are defense in depth, not the PHI control. When a person must approve an action, `canUseTool` pauses the run until your UI answers; for a wait longer than your process can live, a `PreToolUse` hook can return `defer` and the session resumes later.

keyIdeas.title: Trace every run, then evaluate the product
keyIdeas.body: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` and an OTLP exporter, and the Claude Code CLI inside the SDK exports metrics, log events and, with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1`, traces (beta): a `claude_code.interaction` span per turn, with `llm_request`, `tool` (split into the permission wait and the execution) and `hook` spans under it, and subagent spans nested under the parent’s tool span. Call `query()` inside your own span and the SDK passes `TRACEPARENT`, so the run sits inside your service’s trace. Prompt text and tool content are off by default; `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS`, `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS`, `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT` and `OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES` turn them on, and a prompt copied into a trace is still a prompt. OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions for agent spans (`invoke_agent`, `execute_tool`) are still in Development status; OpenInference, used by Arize Phoenix, adds LLM fields on top of OpenTelemetry. Then evaluate with the method from chapter 21, Test your agents like code: read traces before you write checks, build cases from real failures, grade the outcome, and put code checks first. A product agent often has free ground truth: the CI API knows which step failed, and the log either contains the quoted error or it doesn’t. `total_cost_usd` is a client-side estimate; bill from the Usage and Cost API.

keyIdeas.title: Pick the wire: subagent, MCP, A2A or a screen
keyIdeas.body: Inside one harness, use subagents: they protect the main agent’s context and can run in parallel (chapter 18, One agent or many?); cap them with `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` (20 by default) and `maxBudgetUsd`. To give other agents a capability, expose it as an MCP tool (chapter 19, Connect agents to tools). When an independent agent owned by another team or vendor must hand whole tasks to yours, use A2A: v1.0 added signed Agent Cards (JWS), multi-tenancy, and OAuth device code and PKCE, and A2A joined the Agentic AI Foundation, next to MCP, goose and AGENTS.md, on 27 August 2026, with over 150 organizations behind it. People need a screen: MCP Apps (January 2026) let a tool return UI in a sandboxed iframe in Claude, ChatGPT, Goose and VS Code, and Vercel’s AI SDK 7 (June 2026) adds tool approvals, with optional HMAC-signed approvals against forgery. Indeed’s rules for MCP Apps (Sep 2026): give the model every piece of data the user sees, tell the tool description that a UI exists, and split data tools from render tools, because a widget that did both made the model stop searching.

labs.title: Prototype first, then freeze it into an SDK agent
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): pick a read-only job people ask you to do by hand. The default: “why did this CI run fail, and who should look?” on any GitHub repo with Actions and a few failed runs (your own, or a public one). Step 1: do it in Claude Code on three failed runs with a short CLAUDE.md and one helper command (`gh run view <id> --log-failed`), and read each transcript: note where it guessed or wandered. Step 2: write `agent.ts` or `agent.py` with the Agent SDK. Set `cwd` to a clone of the repo and pass `settingSources: []` so your own `~/.claude` setup doesn’t leak in; set `tools` to `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`; add one custom tool, `get_failed_log(run_id)`, through `createSdkMcpServer`, whose handler calls `gh`; pre-approve `mcp__ci__get_failed_log` in `allowedTools` (not `Read`: reads inside the repo need no approval, and reads outside it will then be denied); and set `permissionMode: "dontAsk"`, `maxTurns: 15` and `maxBudgetUsd: 1` (snake_case in Python). Ask for an `outputFormat` schema with `summary`, `failing_job`, `failing_step`, `error_excerpt` (copied from the log), `suspected_files`, `suggested_owner` and `confidence` (low, medium or high), and treat anything other than `success` with a `structured_output` as a failure. Use an API key from your organization’s Console, not a personal subscription login. At Rhino: Lane A only, on failed front-end or back-end CI runs of the FCP repo, whose logs hold code and factory-seeded test data; the agent reads and never re-runs or dispatches a workflow.
labs.output: A runnable agent, JSON results for three failed runs, and a short list of what you changed from the prototype and why

labs.title: Traces, then a first product eval
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): run a trace viewer on your machine (Arize Phoenix or Jaeger in Docker both accept OTLP), and start the agent with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1`, `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` pointing at it. Leave every `OTEL_LOG_*` content flag unset, and never use the `console` exporter through the SDK, because stdout is its message channel. Collect 12 to 15 failed runs where you know the answer: `gh run view <id> --json jobs` gives the failed job and step for free, and the commit that fixed the build tells you the real cause. Read every trace first and write down the kinds of failure you see. Then write three code graders: the failing step matches the API, the `error_excerpt` appears word for word in the log, and every suspected file exists in the repo; grade the owner by hand. Run each case three times and report pass@1 and pass^3 (chapter 21, Test your agents like code). Change one thing, such as the tool description or the prompt, run again and compare. At Rhino: send traces only to a collector approved for the data the agent reads.
labs.output: A screenshot of one trace, your list of failure kinds, and an eval script with before-and-after numbers

labs.title: Attack your own agent
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): copy one failed log to a local file, point `get_failed_log` at it for this test, and plant a prompt injection in it, such as a line that tells the agent to read `~/fake-agent-test/credentials.txt` (a file you create with a made-up key) and put its contents in the summary. Run the agent on it and look at the trace: what did it try, and what stopped it? In `dontAsk` mode a read outside the working directory needs approval, so it should be denied. Then add a `PreToolUse` hook that denies any `Read`, `Grep` or `Glob` outside the repo path with a clear reason and writes each denial to a log file, run it again, and check that the summary still fits the schema. Finally, add the poisoned log to your eval set, so every later change is tested against it. At Rhino: never use real credentials, tokens or PHI as bait; a made-up key in a scratch folder is enough.
labs.output: The hook, its denial log, and one adversarial case in your eval set

checks.q: A teammate wants an agent that tags every new bug with one of 12 components. Should you build one?
checks.a: Probably not. The steps are fixed and the answer is one of 12 labels, so a workflow fits: one model call with a structured output that allows only those labels, plus tests. Build an agent when the path depends on what it finds.

checks.q: Your agent has `allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep"]` and `permissionMode: "bypassPermissions"`. Which tools can it run?
checks.a: All of them. `allowedTools` only pre-approves the listed tools; every other tool falls through to the mode, and `bypassPermissions` approves it. Limit what it can see with `tools`, deny the rest with `dontAsk`, and put checks that must always run in a `PreToolUse` hook.

checks.q: Why ask for structured output instead of parsing the agent’s final text?
checks.a: The SDK validates the answer against your schema and re-prompts on a mismatch, so your code gets typed data or a clear failure (`error_max_structured_output_retries`). Treat `success` without a `structured_output` as a failure too, and keep PHI out of the schema.

checks.q: Another team’s agent needs to hand long investigations to yours. Subagent, MCP or A2A?
checks.a: A2A. It is for independent agents owned by different teams or vendors, with signed Agent Cards and tasks. MCP fits when they only need a tool or data from you, and subagents work only inside your own harness.

watchOut: Your own settings inside the product. With no `settingSources`, `query()` loads your user and project settings, CLAUDE.md files, skills and auto memory, and `~/.claude.json` is read either way. Pass `settingSources: []`, set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`, and give each tenant its own filesystem.

Content in telemetry. Prompt text, tool inputs and tool output stay out of exports until you set the `OTEL_LOG_*` flags or add an instrumentation library that records them. A prompt copied into a trace is still a prompt, and PHI never enters a prompt.

Runs without limits. `maxTurns` and `maxBudgetUsd` are off by default, and `total_cost_usd` is an estimate. Set both caps on every agent, cap subagents, and take real costs from the Usage and Cost API.

Hosted and PHI-adjacent routes. Managed Agents isn’t eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA, so it is Lane A only. Anthropic’s API page also says Claude Code, which the SDK runs, “is not covered under HIPAA readiness”; the route for PHI-adjacent SDK agents is being checked with the vendors, so follow the lane rules in chapter 34, Stay safe and compliant.
modules.watchTime: 40 min core, 59 min with electives
modules.goal: Build a small internal agent on an agent SDK that does one job for other people: only the tools it needs, a typed answer, hard limits on turns and spend, guardrails outside the model, traces you read and an eval you rerun on every change. Know when a skill or a plain workflow is the better choice, and how your agent should talk to other agents and to the people who use it.
modules.why: A coding agent makes you faster. An agent you build does a job for other people, every day, without you in the loop, and that is where an AI specialist earns the title. It is also where first versions fail quietly. Vercel’s internal data agent passed about 30% of its evals, and its first trusted users called it awful. Rebuilt as one agent with a file system and bash in a sandbox, its eval score roughly doubled, and Vercel now counts about 20 internal agents with real product fit (one company’s account, Sep 2026, from a vendor that sells an agent framework). In Arize’s workshop, a simple code check on 13 runs of a small Agent SDK agent caught 2 bad reports: one about AWS instead of Amazon, and one lost because the agent tried to save it to disk (May 2026). The fix each time came from reading runs and measuring them, not from a longer prompt.

shipIt.title: A CI-failure agent your team trusts
shipIt.body: Run the agent from a GitHub Actions job on every failed run of one repo’s main branch, with a token that can read runs and post comments and nothing more, and traces going to the team’s collector; it posts its summary as a comment on the commit or PR, it never re-runs or deploys anything, the eval runs in CI whenever its prompt, tools or model change, and a teammate who is not you reviews the PR that adds it. After two weeks, report how many summaries the person who fixed the build marked right, the cost per run (a cost of the agent, never a score for a person), and the harness fix you made when the same mistake came back a second time.

modules.title: Share and test skills across teams

keyIdeas.title: One marketplace, many plugins, designed like services
keyIdeas.body: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents, commands, workflows and MCP settings. A marketplace is a git repo with a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json that lists plugins and where to fetch each: a folder in the repo, a GitHub repo, a subfolder of another repo, a URL, an archive, an npm package or a command. Imad Touil (QuantumBlack) argues for designing skills like microservices: reusable, modular, discoverable, portable across harnesses, specialized and composable, with a catalog, versions, owners and access control. The skill format itself travels: Elvin Aghammadzada (DataRobot) counts 26+ platforms that read it, including Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Gemini CLI. One proposal for Rhino shows the shape: next to the shared harness plugin, a front-end plugin that bundles the run recipe, design-to-component, the UI state matrix, the accessibility ratchet and a performance budget, plus a read-only UI-evaluator subagent (chapter 12, Let agents check every screen).

keyIdeas.title: Pin versions and ship through channels
keyIdeas.body: Set a plugin version or track commits, not both, and pin git sources to a ref or a sha. A beta channel is a second marketplace on a different ref, given to one group through its own endpoint-managed settings or gateway policy; server-managed settings from the admin console reach everyone, so they can’t split groups. Auto-update changes code you already reviewed: decide it per marketplace, on purpose.

keyIdeas.title: The organization decides what loads
keyIdeas.body: Managed settings can require a marketplace and force-enable its plugins, allow only listed marketplace sources, block others, reject plugins loaded from a local folder, run only managed hooks, and allow skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers only from plugins. Containers and CI can load a read-only seed of plugins baked into the image, without cloning. Watch the side effects: running only managed hooks also switches off /goal, because it runs as a hook (chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely). The key names are in lab 1.

keyIdeas.title: Plugins run with your rights, so gate them like dependencies
keyIdeas.body: Plugin hooks and MCP servers run outside the sandbox with your full user rights. Nubank’s Skill Vector shows the gate: the author scans locally; on the PR, deterministic checks catch known patterns, then an LLM review judges context, findings land in the PR and as a SARIF report in vulnerability management, and policy decides to allow, fix first or block; skills are scanned again after upload, and old skills were scanned once as a batch. Two lessons from them: a line in a prompt that says “ask for confirmation” is not a human gate, because the AI can confirm to itself, so put approval at tool execution with hooks; and bring third-party skills through the same gate. AWS-2025-015 adds a third: scope the tokens that publish your plugins.

keyIdeas.title: Test every plugin with evals in CI, and retire what doesn’t help
keyIdeas.body: claude plugin eval runs each case three times with the plugin and three times without, and reports the difference (Δ). Six grader types: regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists, llm and baseline; a tool_used grader with min 0 and max 0 checks a skill stays quiet. Give each case one grader on the result and one on the steps, suspect a small judge model before the plugin, mock MCP tools, cap cost, and rerun on every model release. Nick Nisi (WorkOS) generated over 10,000 lines of skills from product docs; the evals took 68 minutes a run and results got worse. He replaced them with 553 lines of the gotchas agents actually hit, and runs took six minutes. The method behind this (sealed tasks, pass^k, judge calibration) is chapter 21, Test your agents like code. Uber’s lesson from uReview holds here too: writing a skill is easy; running it at scale with steady quality and cost is the hard part.

labs.title: A pinned marketplace with a beta channel
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Create a marketplace repo with two plugins: one skill of your own (from chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills) as a folder in the repo, and one public plugin as a git source pinned to a sha. Run claude plugin validate on it, register it with claude plugin marketplace add, install both, and check them with claude plugin details. Add a beta channel: a second marketplace that points at a newer ref of the same plugins. Then draft the policy an admin would push, and test it in a throwaway container or VM where you are admin: extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins to require your plugins, strictKnownMarketplaces to allow only your marketplace (keep a skills-dir entry if you use skill folders), and disableSideloadFlags. Try to add a marketplace that isn’t on the list, and read the error. Finally bake a seed into the image (install with CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR, run with CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR) and confirm the plugins load with claude -p --output-format stream-json --verbose. At Rhino: this is the rhino-agents marketplace, with the FE guild’s plugin and the backend skills as git-subdir sources pinned by sha, seeded into the image of the remote-agent pods; make the security team CODEOWNERS of hooks and MCP config.

labs.title: An eval gate in CI
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): For one plugin, run claude plugin eval init (or write five cases with --bare). Give each case one grader on the result and one on the steps, and add two negative cases with a tool_used grader set to min 0 and max 0 and arm both, where the skill must not run. Run the suite and read the Δ for each case; if a case shows a negative Δ, rerun it with a stronger judge before blaming the plugin. Add a GitHub Actions job that runs the suite on every PR with a threshold (for example 0.8) and --max-cost-usd, mocks any MCP tools under evals/mocks, and fails the PR below the threshold. Rerun it after the next model release. At Rhino: gate the ticket-to-PR plugin (the FE team’s ticket-to-PR pipeline), with Jira and GitHub mocks built from the fakes of the tests-and-fakes project.

labs.title: A supply-chain gate for skills
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): On every PR to your marketplace repo, run three layers: deterministic checks (claude plugin validate, a grep of scripts and hooks for curl, wget, base64, eval, rm -rf and reads of .env or ~/.ssh, and Snyk agent-scan), then an LLM review with a short rubric (data exfiltration, destructive commands, credential requests, overbroad permissions, prompt injection in the text), then a human approval for anything with a hook, a script or an MCP server. Test it with a harmless planted skill that asks the agent to print an environment variable and send it to a URL. At Rhino: export the results as evidence for the security audit, and make security the CODEOWNERS of hooks and MCP config.

checks.a: A second marketplace on a different git ref, given to one group through its own endpoint-managed settings or a gateway policy. Server-managed settings reach everyone.

checks.a: Three runs with the plugin and three without, per case. The report is the difference.

checks.q: In what order did Nubank vet skills, and what did they learn about “ask for confirmation”?
checks.a: Deterministic checks, then an LLM review, then findings in the PR and a policy decision to allow, fix first or block. A prompt line asking for confirmation is not a human gate, because the AI can confirm to itself.

modules.why: Skills are code that runs with your permissions, and they now spread like packages. Snyk scanned 3,984 public skills from ClawHub and skills.sh in February 2026: 13.4% had at least one critical issue, 36.8% had some flaw, and 76 were malicious, 91% of those also using prompt injection (vendor research). Nubank scanned over 2,000 internal skills before they reached developers and found more than 1,500 risks (their own numbers, July 2026). The pipeline that publishes a tool is part of the supply chain too: in July 2025 an over-privileged GitHub token in AWS’s build system let an attacker commit malicious code into the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code, version 1.84.0, and it shipped; the payload failed only because of a syntax error (AWS security bulletin AWS-2025-015). And more skills are not better skills: one WorkOS engineer’s skill made the agent right 77% of the time, against 97% without it, and he only knew because he measured.

modules.title: The R&D brain

keyIdeas.title: Every always-loaded line has a price
keyIdeas.body: Whatever sits in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md is read on every turn and competes for the model’s attention. The ETH study found overviews of the repo wasted that budget, while short notes on what is unusual about your code (a non-standard build step, a banned pattern) paid off. Keep the always-loaded file for stable, non-standard rules, and enforce everything a tool can check with lint rules and hooks instead (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work).

keyIdeas.title: Push a small map, pull the pages
keyIdeas.body: An agent can only pull what it knows exists, and it often doesn’t go looking: Vercel’s skill sat unused in 56% of runs. So always load a small index (a few lines per area: what it covers and the path to its pages) and keep the pages themselves in the repo, where the agent reads only the ones the task needs. A search command or skill that returns short excerpts with their source links helps when the pages grow. Vercel compressed its index from about 40 KB to 8 KB and kept the 100% pass rate. The same shape works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Copilot, because every one of them reads an instructions file and can read files.

keyIdeas.title: Three layers, in order
keyIdeas.body: First, repo-native context: a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md per package and docs as code, reviewed like code. Second, a thin org-memory repo of reviewed markdown for knowledge that spans repos, in an open format such as Google’s OKF for LLM-maintained wikis, so any agent and any person can read it. Third, live systems through MCP (chapter 19, Connect agents to tools), in Lane A only and behind PHI scrubbing, because Slack threads, tickets and logs can hold patient data.

keyIdeas.title: Agents propose, humans approve
keyIdeas.body: Memory changes arrive as PRs to the brain repo, drafted by an agent from merged PRs and postmortems, each entry with a link to its source. A human checks the entry against the source, then approves or rejects it; a CODEOWNERS rule on the memory folder makes that approval required. Anthropic’s memory “dreaming” for Managed Agents verifies and merges what an agent learned between sessions; borrow that verify-then-merge step, not the hosting, since Managed Agents sit outside Anthropic’s BAA. Memory that anyone or any agent can write without review is a poisoning path: one wrong entry misleads every agent that reads it.

keyIdeas.title: Every entry has an owner and a date
keyIdeas.body: Each page lists an owner, a review date, a source link and a confidence level. When the review date passes, the page is flagged and not trusted until its owner reviews it. The RAMP numbers show why this must be a rule: set-and-forget is the default, and a stale memory is worse than none, because agents follow it with confidence.

keyIdeas.title: Measure retrieval like any eval
keyIdeas.body: Keep a set of real questions with known answers, scrubbed of anything sensitive, and grade agents with and without the memory, several times each, since one run proves little (chapter 21, Test your agents like code). Track the score and the tokens each run used; if the memory doesn’t raise the score, shrink it.

labs.title: Push versus pull, measured
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): In a repo you know, or a small public sample app, write five to eight short pages of team knowledge for one area (how a feature works, where its config lives, one known trap) as markdown in a `docs/memory/` folder. Give every page an owner, a review date, a source link and a confidence level. Then set up two versions of the same session. Push: paste all the pages into CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. Pull: keep a ten-line index there that lists each page’s path and one line on what it covers. Ask the agent the same three questions in each version, record the answers, and compare the tokens that load at the start with `/context` in Claude Code (or your agent’s usage report). At Rhino: one FCP product area, such as workgroups, written for the R&D brain, with no PHI, secrets or customer names.
labs.output: A memory folder, an index, and a two-row table of answers and start-up tokens

labs.title: A retrieval eval
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Write 15 to 20 questions whose answers are in your repo, its docs or its closed PRs, with the correct answer and its source written next to each. Run the agent on every question three times without the memory folder and three times with it, in fresh sessions, and grade each answer right, wrong or unsupported. Report the score, how often all three runs were right, and the tokens per run. Keep the question set in the repo so the next change to the memory runs against it too. At Rhino: questions collected from Slack threads, scrubbed of anything sensitive before they are saved.
labs.output: A question set and a with-and-without score table

labs.title: Memory proposals behind review
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Write a prompt or skill that reads your repo’s last ten merged PRs (`gh pr list --state merged --limit 10`, then `gh pr view` on each) and proposes up to three new memory entries, each with a link to the PR it came from. Have it open them as one PR against the memory folder, never a commit to main. Add a CODEOWNERS line so a named human must approve that folder. Review the PR yourself: check every entry against its source, reject at least one, and write down why. At Rhino: a weekly job over merged PRs and postmortems that opens a PR to the R&D brain, approved by the area’s owner, never by the person who started the job.

checks.q: Why pull rather than push, and why still load a small index?
checks.a: Always-loaded context costs tokens and attention on every turn and rarely helps on its own. But agents often don’t look for what they don’t know exists, so a small index tells them what to pull.

checks.q: Who approves a new memory entry?
checks.a: A human, through a PR, checked against its source. Agents only propose.

checks.q: What may never go into team memory?
checks.a: PHI, secrets and customer-identifying data, including inside pasted logs or Slack excerpts.

modules.watchTime: 22 min core, 56 min with electives
modules.goal: Build team memory that agents pull from instead of having it pushed into every session: a short map that always loads, reviewed pages in an open format with an owner, a date and a source on each, a search the agent can call, a score that shows the memory helps, and human approval on anything an agent proposes to remember.
modules.why: Once several people and agents work on the same code, the team’s knowledge has to live somewhere every agent can reach. Pushing it all into CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md is the obvious move, and the evidence says it doesn’t work: in a study by researchers at ETH Zurich, context files did not generally raise task success and increased inference cost by over 20% on average; repository overviews didn’t help, while notes on non-standard practices did (preprint, Feb 2026, revised Jun 2026). Leaving everything for the agent to find fails too. In Vercel’s evals on Next.js 16 APIs, the agent never invoked the docs skill in 56% of cases, while a compressed 8 KB docs index in AGENTS.md reached a 100% pass rate, against 79% for the skill with explicit instructions (one team’s evals, Jan 2026). And memory rots: across 441 repositories, 73.8% of committed AI configuration files were committed once and never changed (RAMP, observational, Aug 2026). Unreviewed memory is also an attack surface, which OWASP lists as memory poisoning (ASI06). So the teams that scale memory keep a small map in context, keep the pages in reviewed files, give every page an owner, and treat an agent’s proposal to remember something like any other PR. At Rhino this is the R&D brain project. Chapter 6, Give the agent the right context, did this for one repo, and chapter 23, Share and test skills across teams, shared skills; this chapter shares knowledge.

modules.title: The infrastructure you need to know

keyIdeas.title: A container is a process with a private view, not a wall
keyIdeas.body: An image packs your app and its files; running it starts ordinary processes on the host. Linux namespaces give those processes their own view of process IDs, mounts and the network, and cgroups cap their CPU and memory, so one runaway tool can’t starve the node. But every system call still goes to the one shared host kernel, so a kernel exploit in one container reaches every container on that machine (Abhishek Bhardwaj, OpenAI, July 2026). seccomp filters which system calls are allowed, but a strict filter also blocks legitimate tools an open-ended agent needs. gVisor answers most calls in a user-space “application kernel”, so an escape needs a two-step exploit chain; a VM or microVM gives each workload its own kernel. The rule that follows: your own app in a container is fine, while code that an agent writes and runs needs a stronger boundary, which chapter 29, Run agents remotely, builds.

keyIdeas.title: Kubernetes objects are desired state
keyIdeas.body: You write YAML that says what you want, and controllers keep moving the cluster toward it, like a thermostat (Kubernetes docs). Every manifest reads the same way: `kind` and `metadata` say what it is, `spec` says what you want, and `status` is what the cluster reports back. A Pod runs one or more containers and can be replaced at any time. A Deployment keeps a set number of identical Pods running and rolls out a new image step by step; a Job runs Pods until they finish, and chapter 29 shows teams running one Job per agent session. A Service gives Pods one stable name and address and finds them only by label: if its `selector` matches no Pod’s labels, it has no endpoints and every request fails. A Namespace groups objects, and Roles, NetworkPolicies and Secrets live inside one. A ServiceAccount is the Pod’s identity; every namespace has one named `default`, and a Pod that names none runs as it. RBAC Roles and RoleBindings list which verbs (`get`, `list`, `create`, `delete`) an identity may use on which resources. A NetworkPolicy says which traffic is allowed: by default a Pod accepts and sends everything, and once a policy selects it for egress, only listed traffic leaves, DNS included. It works only if the cluster’s network plugin enforces it; kind does since v0.24.0 (August 2024). Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. Microsoft’s talk adds the warning: namespaces, RBAC and NetworkPolicy were designed for cooperative workloads, not for agents that act in unpredictable ways.

keyIdeas.title: Helm is a template engine, so review what it renders
keyIdeas.body: A chart is a folder of templates plus a `values.yaml` file. `helm template` renders it to plain YAML on your laptop, with no cluster, so you see the real objects before anything is installed (Helm 4.3 docs, September 2026). One changed value can add or change whole objects: a Service type, a new ServiceAccount, a mounted token. Defaults are not hardening: the starter chart from `helm create` ships `securityContext: {}`, `resources: {}` and `automount: true` for its ServiceAccount token, and its test Pod uses `busybox` with no tag (Helm source, v4.3.0). So review an agent’s chart change by rendering before and after and diffing the output, not by reading the values diff. Custom resources such as an ExternalSecret or a Sandbox are objects too: find out which controller acts on them and what it does.

keyIdeas.title: Identity without stored keys
keyIdeas.body: OIDC (OpenID Connect) lets a job prove who it is with a signed, short-lived token instead of a stored password. In GitHub Actions the job asks for the token with `permissions: id-token: write`, which grants no write access to anything else; the cloud checks the token’s claims against a trust condition and returns credentials that expire. On AWS that’s an IAM role whose trust policy checks `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` and `aud` (`sts.amazonaws.com`); on Google Cloud it’s a Workload Identity pool and provider with an attribute condition, plus a service account the pool may impersonate. The condition is the real control. GitHub’s own docs note that `repo:octo-org/octo-repo:*` lets any branch, pull request merge branch or environment of that repo assume the role; `repo:octo-org/octo-repo:environment:prod` or `repo:octo-org/octo-repo:ref:refs/heads/main` does not. Repositories created after 15 July 2026 get an immutable subject with owner and repository IDs, such as `repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:ref:refs/heads/main`, so copy the subject from a real run, not from an old blog post. Inside a cluster the same idea is workload identity: a Kubernetes ServiceAccount maps to a cloud identity (Workload Identity Federation for GKE, EKS Pod Identity), so no cloud key sits in a Secret. Claude Code’s GitHub Action reaches Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform this way, and FCP’s workflows already use OIDC to AWS and Google Cloud.

keyIdeas.title: Workflows and plans are contracts you can read
keyIdeas.body: A GitHub Actions workflow answers the three questions in fixed places. `on:` says what starts it: a push, a pull request, a comment. `permissions:` sets what the job’s GITHUB_TOKEN may do, and once you list one permission, every one you don’t list is `none`. `runs-on:` says whose machine runs it: a fresh GitHub-hosted runner, or a self-hosted runner inside your network. Each step either runs someone else’s code with `uses:`, at the version after `@`, or a shell command with `run:`, and secrets come in by name. A Terraform plan shows what `apply` would do: `+` create, `~` update in place, `-` destroy, and `-/+` destroy then create, with `# forces replacement` on the attribute that caused it; the last line counts adds, changes and destroys. Terraform builds the plan by comparing your code with its state, its record of what already exists. `terraform show -json` turns a saved plan into `resource_changes` with actions such as `["delete", "create"]`, which scripts and policies read (chapter 27, Let agents write infrastructure code). Plan and state files hold sensitive values in plain text, even variables marked sensitive (HashiCorp docs), so they never go into Git or a prompt.

keyIdeas.title: Make the agent a read-only tutor
keyIdeas.body: The agent explains; you change things. Give it an identity that can only read, on a cluster that holds nothing real: a local kind cluster (Kubernetes in Docker containers; v0.33.0 shipped in August 2026), a ServiceAccount bound to the built-in `view` ClusterRole, and a two-hour token from `kubectl create token`. The `view` role can’t read Secrets, Roles or RoleBindings (Kubernetes docs), and `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:mcp:mcp-viewer` shows exactly what that identity may do. The cluster enforces this lock, so it holds for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Copilot alike, as long as the agent can’t pick up your own admin kubeconfig instead: deny reads of `~/.kube/config` with a deny rule and the sandbox, as chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer, does for `.env` files. If you add the Kubernetes MCP server, set `read_only = true` in its TOML config, which exposes only tools marked read-only (the old `--read-only` flag is gone). AWS’s EKS MCP server stays read-only unless you pass `--allow-write`, and needs `--allow-sensitive-data-access` for logs, events and Secrets. Ask for explanations, not commands: the three questions (table below), what each field does, and what is missing, each with the line it comes from. In Claude Code, `/output-style Explanatory` adds the reasoning as Insight blocks. At Rhino the tutor stays in Lane A: kind and synthetic data only, never a shared, customer or production cluster, because logs and events can hold PHI. Agents open PRs and pipelines deploy, so the fixes you learn here reach real clusters only through review.
