labs.title: Break and fix a local cluster with a read-only tutor
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): Install Docker and kind, then run kind create cluster. Give the agent its own identity before anything else: follow the Kubernetes MCP server’s setup guide to create an mcp-viewer ServiceAccount bound to the view ClusterRole, mint a two-hour token with kubectl create token, and write it into a separate kubeconfig file. Start the agent with only that file (for example KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/mcp-viewer.kubeconfig claude), or add the MCP server with read_only = true and the same file. Deny the agent reads of your admin file, ~/.kube/config, with a deny rule and the sandbox. Ask it to delete a Pod, and keep its refusal or the Forbidden error as proof. Then, in your own admin context, deploy two nginx replicas behind a Service plus a small busybox Pod to test from, and break one thing at a time: a container command that exits at once (CrashLoopBackOff), a Service selector that matches no Pod label, and a default-deny egress NetworkPolicy that also blocks DNS. For each one, give the agent only the symptom, ask for the object at fault and the smallest fix with the line it comes from, apply the fix yourself, and write it down. If you also use Codex, Cursor or Copilot, point it at the same kubeconfig: the lock is in the cluster, not in the tool. At Rhino: this is Lane A work; never point the tutor at a shared, customer or production cluster.
labs.output: A three-entry runbook (symptom, object, fix) and the agent’s Forbidden error

labs.title: Map a Helm chart before anything is installed
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Run helm create demo, then helm template demo ./demo > rendered.yaml; you need no cluster. Before you ask the agent anything, write a table with one row per object: kind, name, what runs, which ServiceAccount, and what it can reach. Then hunt for what is missing: an empty securityContext, empty resources, a ServiceAccount token mounted automatically, an image with no tag, no NetworkPolicy. Now ask the agent to check your table and your gaps against rendered.yaml, citing the line for every claim. Last, render again with --set service.type=LoadBalancer and diff the two outputs to see what one value changes. At Rhino: render client/.devops/charts/rhino-agent the same way (it asks for cloudEnvName, and the error message suggests qa-on-prem), list every object, and write down each verb and resource its ClusterRole grants and which workload uses it. Render and read only; never install it.
labs.output: An object table with its gaps, and a before-and-after diff for one value

labs.title: Follow one identity from workflow to cloud
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): In a throwaway GitHub repo you own, add a workflow that runs on push, pull_request and workflow_dispatch, with permissions set to contents: read and id-token: write. Ask the agent to write one step that fetches the job’s OIDC token and prints only its decoded claims, never the token itself. Run it from main, from another branch and from a pull request, and copy each run’s sub, ref and event_name into a table (a repo created after 15 July 2026 shows the immutable format with IDs). Then write two trust conditions that accept only main, matching the format you saw: an AWS condition on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub with aud sts.amazonaws.com, and a Google Cloud attribute condition on assertion.sub. Mark which runs each would accept, and which runs repo:your-name/your-repo:* would accept instead. You need no cloud account. At Rhino: pick one FCP workflow step that uses aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials or google-github-actions/auth, and draw the chain: trigger, job permissions, token claims, cloud role or service account, and what that role can do. Ask the platform owner for the real trust condition instead of guessing it.
labs.output: A claims table, two trust conditions and a one-page identity diagram

checks.q: Two containers share a node. Why isn’t that enough isolation for code an agent writes and runs?
checks.a: Namespaces and cgroups give each a private view and resource limits, but both send their system calls to the same host kernel, so a kernel exploit in one reaches the other. gVisor puts an application kernel in between; a VM or microVM gives each its own kernel.

checks.q: Why give the tutor agent a view-only ServiceAccount instead of telling it not to change anything?
checks.a: The cluster enforces RBAC for every tool and every mode, while a prompt is only a request. Write access is also bigger than it looks: anyone who can create a Pod or a Deployment in a namespace can read every Secret in it, and the view role can’t read Secrets at all.

checks.q: A role’s trust policy allows repo:acme/api:*. What can assume it, and what would you use for a deploy role?
checks.a: Any branch, pull request merge branch or environment of acme/api. For deploys, name one environment (repo:acme/api:environment:prod) or one branch (repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main), and copy the exact subject format from a real run.

checks.q: A plan shows -/+ with # forces replacement on a database. What will apply do?
checks.a: Destroy the database and create a new one, so the data goes unless it is backed up or moved first. Stop and find out why that attribute changed.

watchOut: Your own kubeconfig. An agent uses whatever context is current and can read any file you can, so give it its own KUBECONFIG with one local cluster and a view-only token, and deny it reads of the file that also reaches staging or production.

One-click installs that switch writes on. The EKS MCP server is read-only by default, but the install buttons and examples in its README pass --allow-write and --allow-sensitive-data-access. Read the arguments before you click.
Cluster output is untrusted data. Logs, events and describe output can carry PHI and prompt injection, so only a practice cluster with synthetic data goes into a prompt.
Plan and state files. They hold sensitive values in plain text, even variables marked sensitive. Keep them out of Git and out of prompts; share the counts and a redacted summary instead.

extras.title: Three questions for any infrastructure file
extras.note: use it in the labs and the Ship it
lines: | File | What runs | As whom | What it can reach |
| Dockerfile | The FROM image and the CMD or ENTRYPOINT | The USER line; usually root if there is none | Nothing yet: it is the recipe for an image |

| Pod or Deployment | The image and command of each container | serviceAccountName; the namespace’s default if missing | The Secrets it mounts, the Kubernetes API if its token is mounted, any address unless a NetworkPolicy limits it |
| Service | Nothing: it routes traffic | Not an identity | The Pods whose labels match its selector; outside the cluster if its type is LoadBalancer |
| Rendered Helm chart | Every object it renders | The ServiceAccounts and RBAC it renders | Whatever those objects reach; one value can change all three answers |

| GitHub Actions workflow | Every uses: action at its version and every run: command | The GITHUB_TOKEN with its permissions, plus secrets and any OIDC role | The runner machine, and whatever the token, secrets and role can reach |
| Terraform plan | The apply that the pipeline will run | The pipeline’s cloud role | Every resource marked +, ~, - or -/+ |
| Cloud trust policy | Nothing: it decides who may take a role | Whoever matches the sub and aud conditions | Whatever the role’s permissions allow |

modules.watchTime: 38 min core, 1 h 56 min with electives
modules.goal: Read the infrastructure an agent writes for you well enough to approve or reject it: what a container does and doesn’t isolate, the Kubernetes objects (Pod, Deployment, Service, ServiceAccount, RBAC, NetworkPolicy), a Helm chart rendered to plain YAML, cloud identity through OIDC trust and workload identity, a GitHub Actions workflow and a Terraform plan. Learn it with the agent as a read-only tutor on a local kind cluster, asking three questions of every file: what runs, as whom, and what it can reach.
modules.why: Agents now write the Dockerfile, the Helm values, the workflow and the Terraform in the same PR as your React or Django code, and you own every line you merge. A single line in those files can matter more than a whole feature: in Kubernetes, anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace, even indirectly through a Deployment, can read every Secret in that namespace (Kubernetes docs). These are also the parts every agent platform is built from. Microsoft’s platform for hundreds of engineers’ agents, presented in a CNCF talk in September 2026, uses a VM with its own kernel per agent, a unique cloud identity per agent through OIDC federation, NetworkPolicy that blocks the cloud metadata endpoint, and admission policy against exec (talk abstract). The agent is the best tutor you have for this: Anthropic’s security engineers paste Terraform plans into Claude Code to ask “what’s this going to do? Am I going to regret this?”, which made their approvals faster, and its Data Infrastructure team found pod IP address exhaustion during an outage with Claude, saving 20 minutes (Anthropic’s own report). Chapters 26 to 30 assume every word in this one.

shipIt.title: Explain one real infrastructure change
shipIt.body: Pick one change that touches a workflow, a manifest, a Helm value or Terraform (an agent’s PR, or one from your labs) and post a five-line note on it: what runs, as whom, what it can reach, what the rendered diff or plan counts show, and the one question you need answered before anyone approves. Link the rendered YAML or plan output behind every line.

modules.headlineSrc: 20 min · saved when Claude diagnosed a Kubernetes outage

modules.title: Keep CI safe when agents run in it

keyIdeas.title: Anything a stranger can type is input to your agent
keyIdeas.body: The attacker controls issue titles and bodies, PR titles and descriptions, commit messages, branch names and comments, and there are three ways that text becomes action. Classic script injection: `${{ github.event.issue.title }}` inside a `run:` block is pasted into the shell before it runs; GitHub’s fix is to pass it through an intermediate environment variable. Prompt-to-agent (P2A, the study’s term): the text reaches the agent’s prompt, and the environment variable no longer helps, because the model still reads the attacker’s words and can’t reliably tell your instructions from the text it reads; in Aikido’s words, environment variables “do not protect against prompt injection.” Prompt-to-script (P2S): the model’s output flows into a later shell step or `gh` call, so an injected answer becomes a command. PromptPwnd was P2A: an issue that said “The login button does not work!” carried a fake “additional GEMINI.md instruction”, and the agent ran `gh issue edit` with both tokens in the body, using only the tools and secrets the workflow gave it. The text doesn’t even have to be in the prompt: an agent that can run `gh issue view` or read comments pulls the attacker’s words in by itself. So design every agent job as if the attacker wrote its prompt, then limit what that prompt could make it do (chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer, and chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely, explain the lethal trifecta behind this).

keyIdeas.title: The agent thinks, a small job writes
keyIdeas.body: Permissions are the blast radius. Set the workflow default to `permissions: contents: read` (or `{}`) and grant writes per job. Keep the agent job read-only, with no deploy secrets and no write token. It produces data, such as a JSON file with the label or comment it proposes, and a separate job with no model in it checks that data against an allowlist (known labels only, a length limit, no links) and makes the one write with the one scope it needs. That is how Google fixed Gemini CLI: the model now runs on untrusted input with no GitHub token and almost no tools, and the privileged action (applying labels) moved to a separate non-LLM step that parses and validates the model’s output. GitHub’s gh-aw builds the same design in: the agent job is read-only, its writes are buffered as safe outputs, a threat-detection job with no write access must pass them, and only then do small jobs with scoped permissions create the issue, comment or PR; egress goes through a Squid proxy with a domain allowlist, each MCP server runs in its own container, and compiling a workflow runs actionlint, zizmor and poutine (gh-aw is still below 1.0: v0.89.21 on 23 Sept 2026). Keep the tool list short as well: in claude-code-action’s automation mode Claude has no shell or GitHub API access until you grant it with `--allowedTools`, so grant `Bash(gh issue view:*)`, never plain `Bash`, and cap the run with `--max-turns`. Never splice model output into `run:`; treat it like any other untrusted input.

keyIdeas.title: Know each CI agent’s guardrails, and the switch that removes them
keyIdeas.body: claude-code-action (v1.0.235, 25 Sept 2026) runs only for users with write access, rejects bots unless you list them in `allowed_bots`, strips HTML comments and invisible characters from what Claude reads, opens no PR by itself, and on pull requests restores `.claude/`, `.mcp.json`, `CLAUDE.md` and a few other config paths from the base branch. It doesn’t restore `package.json`, lockfiles or the Makefile, so a base-branch hook that runs `npm run` executes code the PR supplied. The Copilot cloud agent never sees comments from users without write access, pushes to one branch only, can’t mark its PR ready, approve it or merge it, blocks the person who asked from approving it, holds CI until someone with write access clicks “Approve and run workflows”, filters hidden characters, restricts internet access with a firewall and stops at a hard 59 minutes. Codex cloud blocks internet access during the agent phase by default (setup scripts still have it) and can limit requests to GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; codex-action defaults to `safety-strategy: drop-sudo`, and even its `read-only` mode leaves the OpenAI key readable if Codex can reach process memory. The switches that turn these protections off are the ones to search for in review: `allowed_non_write_users: "*"` (Aikido: with it, leaking a privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` is “almost always possible”), `allowed_bots: "*"`, codex-action’s `allow-users: "*"`, `safety-strategy: unsafe`, and `show_full_output` or Actions debug mode on a public repository, which prints tool output that can contain tokens.

keyIdeas.title: Close the old doors: privileged triggers, moving tags and shared runners
keyIdeas.body: `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` run with the base repository’s secrets, write token and cache, so checking out a fork’s code in them hands your secrets to its author (a “pwn request”), and so does pasting a PR title into a shell command there. GitHub’s advice for privilege separation: run the PR’s code in a plain `pull_request` workflow with no secrets, do the privileged step in a `workflow_run` workflow that checks out nothing from the PR, and treat artifacts from the first run as untrusted. s1ngularity came in through the second kind of mistake, and deleting the workflow from master wasn’t enough, because it still lived on older branches. actions/checkout v7 (18 June 2026, backported to supported major versions on 20 July 2026) refuses fork PR head and merge checkouts in these triggers unless you add `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout`. It doesn’t cover `issue_comment` triggers, which is where `@claude` mentions arrive, or a `run:` step that fetches the PR with git or gh, and a checkout pinned by SHA gets the block only when you upgrade it. Workflow execution protections (generally available 17 Sept 2026) let you allowlist who and which events may start each workflow, with an evaluate mode first; public repositories get a default rule that disables `pull_request_target`, enforced from 2 Nov 2026, and private ones must write their own. Pin every action by full commit SHA, “currently the only way to use an action as an immutable release” (GitHub): in March 2025 attackers pointed every tag of tj-actions/changed-files, used by about 23,000 repositories, at one malicious commit that dumped CI credentials into build logs. Since August 2025 an organization can enforce SHA pinning and block actions by policy; Dependabot keeps SHA pins current but raises no vulnerability alerts for them, so also run zizmor’s online audits (known vulnerable actions, impostor commits). Self-hosted runners “should almost never be used for public repositories” (GitHub): Shai-Hulud 2.0 registered runners named SHA1HULUD with a workflow that ran `echo ${{ github.event.discussion.body }}`. Run agent jobs on GitHub-hosted runners or on ephemeral just-in-time runners that take one job and are removed. zizmor finds most of these mistakes (template-injection, excessive-permissions, dangerous-triggers, unpinned-uses, artipacked, cache-poisoning, self-hosted-runner), but it doesn’t judge what an agent will do with text, so every prompt and the tools behind it still get a human review.

keyIdeas.title: No long-lived keys in the pipeline
keyIdeas.body: OIDC lets a job trade a short-lived, GitHub-signed token for cloud access, and it now covers the model too: the Claude Code GitHub Action supports workload identity federation to the Claude API (`anthropic_federation_rule_id`, a Claude Console service account and `id-token: write`), and Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry all work through OIDC (chapter 28, Agents on AWS and Google Cloud). If you keep a static secret shared across repositories, Anthropic recommends an API key over a subscription OAuth token, because the OAuth token is tied to the subscription of the person who ran `claude setup-token`. Watch the GitHub side as well: installing the official Claude GitHub App grants its whole permission set, including Actions, Workflows and Repository hooks write, and GitHub doesn’t let you accept a subset; a custom GitHub App with only Contents, Issues and Pull requests covers the Action. Commits made with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` don’t trigger other workflows, which stops agent loops but also means an agent’s push with that token runs no CI. Keep deploy credentials in a GitHub environment, whose secrets stay locked until a required reviewer approves the job, and never in the agent’s job.

keyIdeas.title: Make “nobody approves their own agent’s work” a setting
keyIdeas.body: Rhino’s rules (SOC 2 CC8.1): the requester never approves their own agent’s PR, and agents open PRs while pipelines deploy. GitHub stops a PR’s author from approving it, and it blocks the requester only for the Copilot cloud agent, which by default also needs one extra approval when its PR isn’t attributed to a person. When another agent opens a PR under a bot identity, the person who asked is not the author, so GitHub lets them approve. Close that gap: let the requester open the PR (claude-code-action’s default for `@claude` requests, since it only posts a link to create one), or record the requester as co-author and add a required check that fails if that person approved. Add a ruleset with “Require approval of the most recent reviewable push” (approval from someone other than the last person to push) and an empty bypass list, since GitHub’s docs note that repository owners and administrators can merge a pull request without an approving review. Give each deploy an environment with required reviewers (up to six) and “Prevent self-review”, so whoever started a deployment can’t approve it. Add a concurrency group per PR (`group: agent-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true`) so one agent run works on a PR at a time. On Free, Pro and Team plans, environment reviewers work only on public repositories, so check your plan, and keep screenshots of each setting as audit evidence (chapter 34, Stay safe and compliant). A CI agent is Lane A work: code and synthetic data only, never PHI in a prompt or in a log it reads.

videos.title: Hijacking Google’s CI/CD Through Prompt Injection: The New Era of AI-Based Exploits
videos.speaker: Mackenzie Jackson, Aikido Security
videos.desc: The PromptPwnd story from the team that found it: how one issue made the Gemini CLI workflow publish its own tokens, how Google fixed it, and a five-question threat model for any agent in CI.

clips.label: Where agents sit in CI today, and the Gemini CLI triage workflow that puts the issue title and body into its prompt
The agent’s shell tools, the hidden “additional GEMINI.md instruction”, and the live run that writes both tokens into the issue
How Google fixed it: no GitHub token and almost no tools for the model, and the label step moved into a separate non-LLM step that validates the output
Threat-modelling an agent (who can trigger it, what it reads, which model, which tools, which secrets) and three defences: limit the agent, treat its output as untrusted, shrink the blast radius

takeaways: An environment variable stops shell injection, not prompt injection. The model still reads the attacker’s text.
The fix was architectural: the step that reads untrusted text holds no token, and a deterministic step does the one write.
Ask five questions of every agent workflow: who can trigger it, what it reads, which model reads it, which tools it can call and which secrets sit in its environment.
videos.tryAtRhino: Answer the five questions for Byte, Rhino’s review bot, and for any other agent job in fcp, and keep the answers as a comment at the top of each workflow file.

videos.title: GitHub Actions Security: From CI Nightmare to Supply Chain Sentinel
videos.speaker: Niek Palm
videos.desc: The classic CI attacks that every agent workflow inherits, each followed by its fix: moving tags, script injection, `pull_request_target`, broad tokens and long-lived secrets.

clips.label: A tag-pinned tj-actions/changed-files turns malicious, and the fix: pin by SHA, keep pins fresh with Dependabot, grant minimal privileges
Script injection: a discussion body echoed on a self-hosted runner, and the intermediate environment variable that fixes it

labs.title: Break and fix an agent triage workflow
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Create a private scratch repository that holds nothing real, and add a repository secret named `CANARY` with a made-up value. First build the unsafe version on purpose: on `issues: opened`, one job with `issues: write` and `CANARY` in its environment, running an agent whose prompt contains `${{ github.event.issue.title }}` and `${{ github.event.issue.body }}` and which may edit issues (with claude-code-action: a `prompt` input, `--allowedTools "Bash(gh issue edit:*)"` and `--max-turns 5`; any other CI agent works the same way). Run `zizmor .github/workflows` and write down what it flags and what it misses. Open an issue that reports a small bug and hides an instruction to copy `$CANARY` into the issue body, and record what the agent does. Then fix it in three steps, repeating the attack after each: give the prompt only the issue number and a read-only `gh issue view` tool; split the work into a read-only agent job (`contents: read`, `issues: read`, no secrets) that saves its chosen label as a JSON artifact, and a writer job with no model that accepts only labels from a fixed list and applies it with `issues: write`; finally add a concurrency group per issue and pin every action by full SHA. The agent still reads the attacker’s text in the end; what changes is what that text can reach. Delete the repository when you finish. At Rhino: do this in a personal scratch repository, never in the RhinoHealth organization and never with a Rhino secret.
labs.output: The unsafe and fixed workflows, zizmor output for each, and a table of what the injected issue reached after each step

labs.title: A zizmor baseline and one clean-up PR
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Install zizmor (`brew install zizmor`, `pipx install zizmor` or `uvx zizmor`) and run it on a repository you work on, or on a clone of any public repository with a few workflows: first `zizmor .` offline, then with `GH_TOKEN` set so the online audits for known vulnerable actions and impostor commits run too. Sort the findings into fix now, accept with a written reason, and false positive. Fix the biggest class in one PR: a top-level `permissions: contents: read` with writes granted per job, actions pinned by full SHA with the version in a comment, any `${{ }}` of untrusted text moved out of `run:` into `env:`, and a Dependabot `github-actions` update so the pins stay current. Add zizmor to CI with zizmorcore/zizmor-action, and make it a required check the second time a finding comes back. At Rhino: run it on your team’s `.github/workflows`. Look for workflows with no top-level permissions block, actions pinned by tag or branch instead of a commit SHA, and jobs on self-hosted runners, and check that those runners are ephemeral before any agent job runs there. Have someone other than you approve the PR.
labs.output: A triaged finding list, one clean-up PR and a zizmor job in CI

labs.title: Settings that stop self-approval
labs.body: Solo (about 40 min): On Free, Pro and Team plans, environment reviewers work only on public repositories, so use a public scratch repository with no secret of value. Add a ruleset on the default branch that requires one approval and “Require approval of the most recent reviewable push”, with an empty bypass list. Create an environment named `production` with yourself as the only required reviewer, turn on “Prevent self-review”, and store a fake secret in it. Add a deploy job that uses the environment and prints only whether the secret is set, start it yourself and try to approve it; then open a PR yourself and try to approve and merge it. Add a per-PR concurrency group to your agent workflow from lab 1. For each block, take a screenshot and write one line on which Rhino rule it enforces, including the gap it doesn’t close: a PR opened by a bot, where the requester isn’t the author. At Rhino: an admin applies the same settings to the release path, and the screenshots become SOC 2 CC8.1 evidence in Vanta, Rhino’s compliance tool.
labs.output: A repository whose settings block self-approval, with a screenshot and a one-line rule for each block

checks.q: A triage workflow moves `${{ github.event.issue.body }}` into an environment variable, as GitHub advises for scripts, and passes it to the agent’s prompt. Is it safe now?
checks.a: Only from shell injection. The model still reads the attacker’s text, which is exactly how PromptPwnd made the Gemini CLI workflow leak its tokens. Limit what an injected agent could do: no write token or secrets in its job, few tools, and writes in a separate job that validates its output.

checks.q: Why keep the agent job read-only when the task ends with a label or a comment?
checks.a: An injected read-only job can only produce bad output. A separate deterministic job checks that output against an allowlist and writes with one scoped permission. That is how Google fixed Gemini CLI and how gh-aw’s safe outputs work.

checks.q: actions/checkout v7 refuses fork PR checkouts in `pull_request_target`. Name two ways a workflow can still run untrusted code with your secrets.
checks.a: Any two of: an `issue_comment` trigger, which checkout v7 doesn’t cover and where `@claude` mentions arrive; a `run:` step that fetches the PR with git or gh; an older checkout pinned by SHA that was never upgraded; the `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout` opt-out; a `${{ }}` expression of untrusted text inside `run:`.

checks.q: Your scheduled agent opened a PR under its bot account, and GitHub lets you approve it. You asked for the change. May you approve it?
checks.a: No. You are the requester, and Rhino’s rule (SOC 2 CC8.1) is that the requester never approves their own agent’s PR. GitHub blocks PR authors, and requesters only for Copilot, so make it mechanical: let the requester open the PR, or record them as co-author and add a required check.

watchOut: Deleting a bad workflow from the default branch only. An attacker can still reach a copy that lives on an older branch, as s1ngularity showed. Remove it from every branch, or block the trigger with execution protections.
A star in an allowlist. `allowed_non_write_users: "*"`, `allowed_bots: "*"` or codex-action’s `allow-users: "*"` lets anyone’s text, or any GitHub App, drive your agent with your token.

Debug logs on public repositories. Turning on Actions debug mode also turns on claude-code-action’s full output, which can include tool output with tokens, and the logs of a public repository are public. GitHub masks the secret values it knows, but a token printed in another form, such as encoded or inside JSON, can slip through, and deleting logs afterwards is late: s1ngularity’s leaked data was public for about 8 hours, long enough to be copied (Wiz).

“zizmor is clean” read as “the agent is safe”. zizmor checks workflow mistakes; it doesn’t know what your agent will do with an issue body. Review every prompt, the tools it can call and the secrets in its job.
modules.watchTime: 34 min core, 53 min with electives
modules.goal: Run agents in GitHub Actions (claude-code-action, the Copilot cloud agent, Codex, the Gemini CLI action or gh-aw) so that text in an issue, a pull request or a comment can’t become a leaked secret, a push or a deploy. The agent job reads with a read-only token and holds no long-lived secret; a small deterministic job checks its output and does the one write it needs; every action is pinned by full commit SHA; privileged triggers never run untrusted code; cloud and model access comes through OIDC; zizmor checks every workflow change; and repository settings make sure nobody approves their own agent’s work.
modules.why: An agent in CI does what any CI job does, with one difference: it reads text that anyone can write and then decides what to run. In a May 2026 study, researchers scanned 13,392 agentic workflows in 10,792 repositories and confirmed 496 exploitable injection flaws (95.6% precision), 343 of them unknown before; of the 187 they reported, maintainers answered 26 (Wang et al., arXiv 2605.07135). In December 2025 Aikido showed, on a private fork with test credentials, that one GitHub issue with a hidden instruction made the issue-triage workflow of Google’s own Gemini CLI repository write its GEMINI_API_KEY and GITHUB_TOKEN into the issue body; the same pattern affected at least five Fortune 500 companies, and Google patched it in four days. The classic CI attacks never stopped either. s1ngularity (August 2025) started from a `pull_request_target` workflow with an unsanitized PR title and ended with over 1,000 valid GitHub tokens leaked and over 5,500 private repositories made public (Wiz). Shai-Hulud 2.0 (November 2025) backdoored 796 npm packages and registered self-hosted runners on infected machines as a command channel (Datadog); Aikido reports that it was first seeded with credentials stolen from AsyncAPI and PostHog through a GitHub Actions flaw. GitHub answered with new defaults in 2026: actions/checkout v7 in June and workflow execution protections in September. At Rhino the pipeline builds and deploys a healthcare platform, so a leaked write token or cloud key is a production incident, not a lab result. Chapter 25, The infrastructure you need to know, taught you to read a workflow and an OIDC trust; this chapter makes that workflow safe with an agent inside it, and chapter 27, Let agents write infrastructure code, hands the same pipeline your infrastructure.

shipIt.title: A hardened agent workflow
shipIt.body: A reusable workflow for agent jobs in one repository: a read-only agent job with SHA-pinned actions and OIDC or federation instead of stored keys, a writer job that accepts only an allowlist, a concurrency group and a turn cap, and zizmor as a required check. Show a teammate the injected issue from lab 1 failing against it, and have that teammate, not you, approve the PR.

modules.title: Let agents write infrastructure code

keyIdeas.title: Valid is not secure, and prompts cap out
keyIdeas.body: In an August 2026 preprint benchmark (seven models, 17 AWS scenarios, every output scanned by Checkov and Trivy), WizardCoder-33B wrote Terraform that passed `terraform validate` 77.8% of the time and never passed Checkov. The best model, Claude Opus 4, reached 23.1% Checkov compliance and a 92.5% Trivy pass rate, and only with a prompt that listed the exact check IDs to satisfy. Given its own scanner output once, Claude Opus 4’s Checkov rate rose only from 8.5% to 20.8%, because the missing pieces were design decisions that one revision doesn’t make: adding encryption resources, IAM (identity and access management) and logging. The authors’ conclusion: “prompt engineering alone is insufficient.” Infrastructure is also harder than it looks: in IaC-Eval (NeurIPS 2024), GPT-4 solved 86.6% of Python tasks but only 19.36% of Terraform tasks. So `validate` and a clean `plan` prove only that the code is well formed. Scanners and policies decide whether it is safe, on every change.

keyIdeas.title: Verifiers in the loop, policies in the context
keyIdeas.body: A May 2026 single-author preprint on 186 Terraform tasks (IaC-Eval v2) split every failure into three verifier stages: `terraform validate`, `terraform plan` and `opa eval`. Retrieval of current docs (a ReAct agent with an MCP server or a docs index) raised a small open model, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, from 14.0% to 45.7%, mostly by cutting validate failures from 144 tasks to 66. Its main failure was invented attributes, and repair alone can’t fix those: the error says what is wrong, not what is right, so the cure is current docs. Feeding verifier output back for repair reached 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o), and convergence was binary: 83% of GPT-4o’s tasks passed within one or two attempts, and 16% used up all four. The finding that matters most: 79% of the policy failures left after repair were information gaps that disappeared once the policy text was in the prompt, and with the policies visible GPT-4o reached 93.0%. So give the agent the checks as tools and hooks. Locally it runs what needs no credentials (`terraform fmt`, `validate` after `init -backend=false`, `tflint`, Checkov, Conftest on the `.tf` files); for the plan, it pushes and reads the plan and policy results that CI posts on its PR. Put the policies themselves in its context through a skill or a linked file (chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills), and hand the task to a person after two failed attempts instead of looping. For current docs, the Terraform MCP server (v1.3.0, 26 Aug 2026) serves registry docs for providers, modules and policies; its default toolset is the registry, and tools that need explicit approval stay off unless `ENABLE_TF_OPERATIONS` is set. HashiCorp Agent Skills (Feb 2026) and Anton Babenko’s terraform-skill package style, testing and scanning practice for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Copilot. HashiCorp’s own advice for its server: “Always validate before doing any write changes.”

keyIdeas.title: The plan is the contract
keyIdeas.body: Build the path so the plan is the thing everyone agrees to. The agent edits code on a branch and opens a PR; it holds no state file and no cloud credentials. CI signs in with OIDC, runs `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, and writes `terraform show -json tfplan` for the policy engines. Conftest or OPA scores that JSON, and scanners such as Checkov and Trivy check the code and the plan; on HCP Terraform, Sentinel, OPA or the new HCL-based tfpolicy (public beta, Jul 2026) run between plan and apply, and on Pulumi, CrossGuard policy packs check the preview. Vendors now build their own agents this way: Pulumi’s Neo runs previews, checks policy and opens PRs, with human approvals (Sep 2025). A read-only agent writes a five-line summary: what is created, changed, replaced and destroyed, any IAM or network change, and what you might regret. A person who isn’t the requester approves the protected environment, and the pipeline applies that saved file and nothing else. The order matters because Terraform “interprets the act of passing the plan file as the approval”: whoever can run `apply tfplan` has already approved it. Anthropic’s security engineers built the same habit by hand: they paste Terraform plans into Claude Code and ask “what’s this going to do? Am I going to regret this?” (Anthropic, one team’s practice). Atlantis (plan and apply output as PR comments) and HCP Terraform run this loop for you, and OpenTofu (CNCF Sandbox since 23 Apr 2025) has the same commands. Two traps. The summary is a reading aid, not the gate, so read every destroy and replace (`-/+`) line in the raw plan yourself. And `terraform show -json` prints sensitive values in plain text, so treat the plan JSON as a secret: give the summarizer the human-readable plan, which masks values marked sensitive, or a redacted JSON.

keyIdeas.title: Blast radius as a number, deletes as their own question
keyIdeas.body: OPA’s Terraform tutorial turns a plan into a score. Each resource type gets a weight per action (in its example, deleting an autoscaling group counts 100, creating one 10, changing one 1), the counts are multiplied and added, and the plan passes only if the score stays under 30 and nothing touches IAM. Copy the shape, then set your own weights: deletes and replacements of anything that holds data (databases, buckets, disks, keys) count most, and any change to IAM, RBAC (Kubernetes role-based access control) or public network exposure needs a platform owner whatever the score. A rename that forces a replacement is a delete in disguise; a `moved` block tells Terraform it is the same resource. Back the score with guards that don’t depend on review: `prevent_destroy` in the resource’s lifecycle, deletion protection in the cloud itself, remote state with locking, and backups outside the same blast radius. The 2026 incidents failed exactly there. At DataTalks.Club the state lived on one laptop and the snapshots were deleted with the database. At PocketOS (April 2026, as the founder reported it), a Cursor agent running Claude Opus 4.6 found a Railway API token in the codebase with the right to delete volumes, and deleted the production database and the backups stored with it in 9 seconds; the newest recoverable backup was three months old. An agent can’t delete with a credential it can’t reach.

keyIdeas.title: Git is the only door to the cluster
keyIdeas.body: GitOps makes “agents open PRs, pipelines deploy” mechanical. Desired state lives in Git, and a reconciler inside the cluster, Argo CD or Flux, pulls it and keeps the cluster matching (the OpenGitOps principles from chapter 25). The agent never holds cluster credentials, a rollback is a `git revert` that goes through the same review, and drift becomes a PR: a nightly `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` (exit code 2 means changes) can wake an agent that explains the drift and proposes the fix, never applies it. Agents help most at reading. The open-source Argo CD MCP server (v0.9.0, Aug 2026) lets an agent inspect applications, resource trees, events and logs to explain a failed sync. Its tools also include sync, create and delete, and all are on by default, so run it with `MCP_READ_ONLY=true` and have the agent turn its diagnosis into a PR. Its log tool reads workload logs, so keep it away from any cluster whose logs can hold PHI (chapter 30, Agents after release). Each PR can get its own preview: the Argo CD ApplicationSet Pull Request generator creates an Application for each PR with a chosen label, at that PR’s `head_sha`, and removes it when the PR closes or loses the label. It polls every 30 minutes by default, so add the webhook. Request-level sandboxes (Signadot) and preview deployments for front ends do the same job, and the agent runs its checks against the preview URL and posts the evidence (chapter 12, Let agents check every screen). Where experts disagree: Akuity lets its agents act freely in development, such as raising resource limits or patching manifests, and escalate for approval in production (Feb 2026), and Azure SRE Agent offers Review and Autonomous modes. Rhino’s rule stays: no agent holds deploy credentials.

keyIdeas.title: Cluster policy is the last net
keyIdeas.body: Review and CI see only what comes through the PR. Admission policy runs in the Kubernetes API server and rejects any object that breaks the rules, whoever sent it: Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, or ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, built into Kubernetes since v1.30. Viktor Farcic calls these policies “blast doors” once agents create resources at machine speed (KubeCon NA 2025). Start with rules that catch what agents commonly get wrong: no privileged containers, no hostPath volumes, no `latest` image tags, resource limits set, and no `exec` into agent pods. Run the same rules twice: in CI on the rendered manifests (`helm template` into Kyverno CLI or Conftest), so the agent sees the failure while it can still fix it, and in the cluster, in audit mode first and then enforce. Keep every policy file, Rego rule and scanner config under CODEOWNERS, out of the writer’s reach (chapter 7, Check the agent’s work). At Rhino, the FCP repo has no Terraform today. Its infrastructure code is the GitHub Actions workflows and the rhino-agent Helm chart, which runs in customers’ own networks and includes a ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding. Agents may propose chart changes in a PR; no agent installs or upgrades it anywhere.

labs.title: Scan what the agent writes, then let it repair
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): In an empty folder, with no cloud account needed, ask your agent for a Terraform or OpenTofu module and give it no security hints: a storage bucket for file uploads (Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage), a role or service account that can read it, and one more resource of your choice. Write three Conftest rules in Rego for your own basics, such as no public access, no `*` in IAM actions and a required owner tag, and run them on the `.tf` files (Conftest parses HCL). Now give the agent the scanner output and the rule files, let it repair for at most three rounds, and record what is left after each round. labs.output: A table of validate, Checkov, Trivy and Conftest results per round, and your three rules

labs.title: A plan gate with a blast-radius score, on your laptop
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Use a local kind cluster (chapter 25) and Terraform’s Kubernetes provider, so the plan is real and needs no cloud. Have the agent write a module that creates a namespace, a deployment and a service account, and apply this first version yourself (it is your own local cluster). Write the gate as one script: `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, `terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json`, then `conftest test plan.json` with a Rego policy adapted from OPA’s Terraform tutorial: a weight per resource type and action, a threshold, a hard deny for any change to a role or role binding, and a hard deny for deleting a namespace. Add a summarizer: a fresh agent session with no write tools that reads `terraform show tfplan` (the human-readable plan) and turns it into five lines (created, changed, replaced, destroyed; RBAC changes; the one line you could regret). Plant three changes, one at a time: rename the deployment so it must be replaced, bind the service account to cluster-admin, and delete the namespace. For each, record the score, the verdict and whether the summary mentioned it. At Rhino: render `client/.devops/charts/rhino-agent` with `helm template` and add a Conftest rule that lists the verbs its ClusterRole may grant and fails on anything else.
labs.output: A gate script, a policy file and a three-row table of score, verdict and summary per planted change

labs.title: Git is the only door: GitOps, a policy net and a read-only diagnosis
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): On the same kind cluster, install Argo CD (or Flux) and point it at a public repo you own that holds a small app’s manifests or Helm chart. From now on, change the cluster only through PRs: have the agent open one that raises the replica count, merge it and watch the sync. Install Kyverno with three policies in Audit mode (no privileged containers, no `latest` tag, resource limits required), then ask the agent for a change that breaks one. Catch it twice: first with `kyverno apply` on the rendered manifests in a pre-commit hook or CI job, then, after you switch the policy to Enforce, by the cluster refusing the object when you try to apply it by hand, the path that skips review. Finally, start the Argo CD MCP server with `MCP_READ_ONLY=true`, break a sync on purpose with a typo in an image tag, and let the agent diagnose it and open the revert PR. Optional: add an ApplicationSet with the Pull Request generator and a `preview` label, so each labelled PR gets its own app.
labs.output: A repo where every change arrived by PR, a Kyverno policy report, and the agent’s diagnosis with its revert PR

checks.q: The agent’s Terraform passes `terraform validate` and gives a clean plan. Why isn’t that enough?
checks.a: Validity and security are largely unrelated. In an August 2026 benchmark, one model validated 77.8% of the time and never passed Checkov, and the best model passed Checkov only 23.1% of the time, even with the check IDs in its prompt. Scanners and policies must gate every change.

checks.q: Why does the pipeline apply the saved plan file, and why must the approval come before apply?
checks.a: The saved file is exactly what policy scored and the person approved. Terraform treats passing the plan file as the approval, so nobody may apply anything else, and the approval gate has to sit in front of apply.

checks.q: CI enforces the policies anyway. Why put the policy text in the agent’s context too?
checks.a: In one study, 79% of the policy failures left after repair were information gaps that disappeared once the policy text was visible. The agent can fix only rules it can see; CI still has the final say.

checks.q: Review, CI and GitOps are all in place. What does admission policy add?
checks.a: It checks every object at the Kubernetes API server, whoever sends it, so it catches what review missed and anything that bypassed the PR path. Run the same rules in CI first, so the agent sees the failure early.

watchOut: The summary as the gate. An agent’s five-line summary helps you read. Read every destroy and replace line in the raw plan yourself.

State and credentials in reach. A stale state file turned a cleanup into the loss of a production database (DataTalks.Club, Mar 2026), and a found API token deleted a database and its backups in 9 seconds (PocketOS, Apr 2026). Keep state remote and locked, credentials only in CI, and deletion protection on.
`-auto-approve` and applies from a laptop. Both skip the contract. Only the pipeline applies, and only the plan that was approved.

Plan JSON in a prompt, and policies the writer can edit. `terraform show -json` prints sensitive values in plain text, so redact it before a model reads it, and keep Rego, Kyverno and scanner configs under CODEOWNERS.
modules.watchTime: 34 min core, 1 h 17 min with electives
modules.goal: Let an agent write Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi or Kubernetes manifests while nothing it writes reaches a cloud or a cluster without passing a gate. The agent iterates against validate, plan and policy checks, with the policies in its context. CI turns each change into a saved plan that policy scores and a person who isn’t the requester approves. Only the pipeline applies that exact plan, a GitOps reconciler is the only thing that changes a cluster, and admission policy stops what everyone else missed.
modules.why: In March 2026 Alexey Grigorev, who runs DataTalks.Club, let Claude Code clean up duplicate resources while he moved a small site onto the AWS setup of his course platform. Claude had advised keeping the two separate; he shared the setup to save money. He had also switched laptops without moving his Terraform state, and the agent unpacked an old archive that replaced the current state file. It then proposed `terraform destroy` as the cleaner way to remove the duplicates, he let it run, and it removed the platform’s production database, VPC, ECS cluster, load balancers, bastion host and all automated snapshots. AWS Business Support restored the database 24 hours later. His fix, in his own write-up: “Agents no longer execute commands. Every plan is reviewed manually.” Benchmarks say the same from the other side: Terraform that validates is rarely secure (key idea 1). Yet infrastructure is the best place to delegate, because Terraform shows every change as a plan before it happens, and policy can score that plan. A developer who owns a feature end to end owns its bucket, queue and chart too. Chapter 25, The infrastructure you need to know, taught you to read a plan; chapter 26, Keep CI safe when agents run in it, set up OIDC and protected environments. This chapter connects them into one path that an agent can’t skip.

shipIt.title: An infrastructure PR that proves itself
shipIt.body: Make every agent-written infrastructure PR carry the same evidence: the plan or the rendered chart diff, the policy and scanner results, the blast-radius score, the five-line summary and a link to the pipeline run that will apply that exact plan. Show a teammate one such PR, approved by someone other than the requester and applied only by the pipeline.

modules.title: Agents on AWS and Google Cloud

keyIdeas.title: Who processes the data decides the lane
keyIdeas.body: On AWS there are three ways to reach Claude, and what separates them is who processes the data. Claude in Amazon Bedrock (the Mantle endpoint, which speaks the Anthropic Messages API, open to all Bedrock customers in 27 regions since 16 April 2026) and the older Bedrock Invoke and Converse APIs are run by AWS, and AWS is the data processor. Claude Platform on AWS (launched 11 May 2026) is run by Anthropic and only billed through AWS Marketplace. It has the full Claude API, including skills and Managed Agents, but Anthropic’s HIPAA-ready program is not available on it, and Anthropic’s own docs tell regulated industries that need HIPAA-ready compliance to use Bedrock. On Google Cloud, Claude is a Partner Model on Agent Platform, run by Google, with prompt logging off by default and data residency, CMEK and VPC Service Controls supported. Anthropic’s ZDR and HIPAA arrangements don’t apply on Bedrock or Agent Platform; the cloud’s own terms do. The vendors’ lists are the starting point, never the finish: AWS’s HIPAA-eligible list (updated 3 Sep 2026) includes Bedrock, AgentCore and Kiro (excluding Kiro Web) but not Amazon Q Developer, and Google’s BAA page (updated 17 Sep 2026) covers Agent Platform, Model Armor, Cloud Run, GKE, Gemini Code Assist and Antigravity in Gemini Enterprise, and says Pre-GA offerings must not be used with PHI. Google’s BAA names products, not models, so Claude’s coverage needs a written answer. Covered Models (Fable 5.1, Fable 5 and the Mythos models) need 30-day retention wherever they run; on the clouds that data stays in the provider’s environment. At Rhino, Lane B today is Claude Code CLI or Desktop local under the BAA with ZDR, or the Agent SDK in our own pod, with no connectors. A Lane B route through Rhino’s own Bedrock or Agent Platform account is being checked with AWS, Google and Anthropic; it is not policy. Claude Platform on AWS can’t carry Lane B work while it has no HIPAA readiness.

keyIdeas.title: Claude Code through your own cloud: pin it, route it, close the side doors
keyIdeas.body: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` (or run `/setup-bedrock`, a wizard that writes your settings) for Bedrock, or `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1` with `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID` and `CLOUD_ML_REGION` for Agent Platform, where model access approval may take 24 to 48 hours. Both Claude Code guides recommend a dedicated AWS account or GCP project for cost tracking and access control. Pin every alias before a team rollout: unpinned, `opus` resolves to Opus 5.5 on Bedrock, and from v2.1.207 a deployment that doesn’t pin its primary model is billed at the Opus rate. Point each team’s settings at its own application inference profile ARN (with `modelOverrides` when a team needs several versions), so cost lands per team. Know what you give up: on Bedrock and Agent Platform there are no cloud sessions, routines, Code Review, Remote Control, fast mode, analytics dashboard or server-managed settings; Bedrock has no web search; auto mode works only with Sonnet 5, Opus 4.7 or later and Fable. Two things still reach Anthropic on every provider: session-quality surveys (`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY=1`) and the WebFetch hostname check to `api.anthropic.com` (`skipWebFetchPreflight: true`). For a whole team, use the Claude apps gateway. It ships inside the `claude` binary (v2.1.195 or later, with Postgres 14 or later) and boots fail-closed. Developers sign in with corporate SSO, the gateway alone holds the cloud credential, IdP groups map to model allowlists and managed settings, and it enforces per-user and per-group spend limits, stamps OTLP telemetry with identity and fails over between Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Agent Platform and Foundry. Its data plane sends nothing to Anthropic unless the Anthropic API is a configured upstream. It doesn’t support Mantle as an upstream and turns web search off. In CI, `claude-code-action` reaches Bedrock and Agent Platform through OIDC only (chapter 26, Keep CI safe when agents run in it), and it doesn’t run on Claude Platform on AWS.

keyIdeas.title: Climb down the hosting ladder only for a reason
keyIdeas.body: Both clouds now sell the parts teams used to build badly themselves: session isolation, memory, identity and tracing. Start at the top rung and step down only when you must. (1) An agent from config: AgentCore Harness (GA 17 June 2026) takes a model, a system prompt and tools, runs each session in a microVM with a filesystem and shell, and exports to Strands code, with the Claude Agent SDK listed as “coming soon”; Google’s Agent Studio is no-code and exports to ADK. (2) A managed runtime for your own code: AgentCore Runtime gives each session a dedicated microVM that is terminated and wiped when the session ends, runs sessions for up to 8 hours (14 days on Instances), serves HTTP, MCP, A2A and AG-UI, and typically doesn’t bill CPU while the agent waits on the model (AWS says agents spend 30 to 70% of their time in I/O wait, a vendor figure; Runtime v1 costs $0.0895 per vCPU-hour). Google’s Agent Runtime (formerly Agent Engine) adds Sessions, Memory Bank, a code sandbox and Agent Identity, for Python agents only, and Google’s guide says it can’t host custom MCP servers. (3) Serverless containers when you need another language, your own image or an existing deploy pipeline: ECS on Fargate, or Cloud Run, which scales to zero but caps a request at one hour; Lambda durable functions for workflows that wait for days (suspend up to a year, no compute charge while waiting). (4) Kubernetes for high, steady volume or an agent that must live inside an existing cluster: EKS with the open-source agent-sandbox and Pod Identity, or the managed GKE Agent Sandbox (gVisor, warm pools typically under a second). Google’s own guide warns that GKE’s control “introduces significant operational overhead and complexity”. Chapter 29, Run agents remotely, builds that rung. Frameworks travel between rungs: Strands, ADK (Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin, with Claude through LiteLLM) and the Claude Agent SDK.

keyIdeas.title: Every agent is its own principal, with nothing worth stealing
keyIdeas.body: The pattern is the same on both clouds: each agent gets its own workload identity, uses short-lived credentials bound to where it runs, acts for a user only through a flow that logs both identities, and never holds a long-lived key. On AWS, AgentCore Identity treats agents as workload identities, checks inbound JWTs and keeps outbound OAuth tokens and API keys in a vault; on EKS, Pod Identity hands each pod temporary role credentials. On Google Cloud, Agent Identity gives each agent on Agent Runtime a SPIFFE-based principal with an auto-provisioned x509 certificate, which Google calls “a more secure principal than service accounts”. A Google-managed Context-Aware Access policy binds its tokens to mTLS, so a stolen token can’t be replayed outside its runtime, and delegated calls log both the user and the agent. Its API is still `v1beta1`, so check GA status before PHI-adjacent use. Then write “humans change things, agents read” into IAM, not into the prompt. The AWS MCP Server (GA 6 May 2026) runs any of 15,000+ AWS API operations through one `call_aws` tool, and its `run_script` sandbox has no network. The IAM condition keys `aws:ViaAWSMCPService` and `aws:CalledViaAWSMCP` let one Deny statement block mutating actions whenever the call comes through an AWS MCP server, while the same person can still make the change directly. Google’s 50+ managed MCP servers sit under Cloud IAM, including Deny policies. Chapter 25, The infrastructure you need to know, explains roles and OIDC trust.

keyIdeas.title: Policy lives in the gateway; guardrails are the second layer
keyIdeas.body: Put deterministic policy where every tool call passes. AgentCore Gateway turns OpenAPI, Smithy and Lambda functions into MCP tools, fronts existing MCP servers, finds tools by semantic search, and runs AgentCore Policy (GA 3 Mar 2026): rules written in plain language compile to Cedar and are checked on each tool request before it runs. Google’s Agent Gateway is MCP- and A2A-aware and applies central IAM policy and Model Armor. Bedrock Guardrails and Model Armor detect prompt attacks and personal data, but detection is probabilistic, so they are defense in depth and never the reason PHI may enter a prompt; the control is still synthetic data, lanes and egress rules. Between agents that different teams own, use A2A: v1.0 (12 Mar 2026) added signed Agent Cards and multi-tenancy, and on 27 Aug 2026 A2A joined MCP and AGENTS.md in the Agentic AI Foundation, with 150+ organizations behind it. Use MCP for tools and subagents inside one harness (chapter 18, One agent or many?). Registries (AWS Agent Registry, GA 31 Aug 2026, and Google’s Agent Registry) list which agents exist, so shadow agents show up.

keyIdeas.title: Quota, region and pins are cost controls
keyIdeas.body: On Bedrock each output token counts 10 times against your tokens-per-minute and tokens-per-day quota for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5 and Fable 5.1, 15 times for Claude 4.8 and 5 times for 4.7 and earlier, and input plus `max_tokens` is deducted when the request starts. You pay only for real tokens, so a fleet that asks for 32,000 output tokens and uses 1,500 hits its quota long before the bill looks high. AWS’s own example: 1,000 input and 100 output tokens on a 5x model use 1,500 quota tokens and bill 1,100. Set `max_tokens` near real output. Region is a price and a promise: geographic cross-Region inference (`us.`, `eu.`, `apac.`) keeps processing inside that geography, `global.` routes to any commercial region for about 10% less, and CloudTrail’s `additionalEventData.inferenceRegion` shows where each request ran. On Google Cloud, regional and multi-region endpoints also cost 10% more than global. Attribute every dollar: a dedicated account or project, one inference profile per team, gateway spend limits, and AgentCore Payments (agents paying for APIs and MCP servers) off or capped. Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens on the Claude API and on both clouds (launched 22 Sep 2026). Chapter 33, Measure results and cost, turns these into team numbers.

labs.title: Claude Code through your own cloud, pinned and proven
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): In a personal or sandbox AWS account with a budget alert, enable one Claude model in Bedrock (submit Anthropic’s one-time use case form if asked). Run `/setup-bedrock`, or set `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` by hand. Pin `opus` and `sonnet` to exact model IDs with the `us.` or `eu.` prefix, and give your identity only the four actions the Claude Code docs list (`bedrock:InvokeModel`, `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`, `ListInferenceProfiles`, `GetInferenceProfile`) on those profile ARNs, plus the two marketplace actions. Add `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY=1` and `skipWebFetchPreflight: true`, run `/status`, and let the agent do one small task on a public sample repo. Then find your requests in CloudTrail and read `additionalEventData.inferenceRegion`. Send one more request with the `global.` prefix and compare where it ran and what it cost. Google Cloud variant: a project of its own, `roles/aiplatform.user`, `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1`, and `CLOUD_ML_REGION=us` against `global` (request model access a day or two ahead). At Rhino: a sandbox account and code without PHI only; the PHI-adjacent cloud route is being checked with the vendors.
labs.output: A settings file with pins and opt-outs, a minimal IAM policy, and a two-row table of where each request ran

labs.title: One small agent on a managed runtime
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): Write a tiny read-only agent with the Claude Agent SDK, Strands or ADK. It reads a synthetic failed-CI log from a file and returns a three-line summary and a likely owner from a CODEOWNERS file. Run it locally, then deploy it with the AgentCore CLI (`agentcore dev`, then `agentcore deploy`), or to Cloud Run as in the elective video. Record the cold-start time, the cost of one session at the published price, what one trace shows, which identity the agent runs as, and how you would revoke it. If you have both accounts, repeat on the other cloud with the same test log. Delete everything at the end and check that nothing still bills. At Rhino: synthetic logs only, because the rule that PHI never enters a prompt covers logs too.
labs.output: A comparison table (start time, cost per session, trace, identity, revoke path) and a teardown checklist

labs.title: Humans change, agents read
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): In a sandbox AWS account, create an S3 bucket with one test object and a role that may read and write it. Add a Deny statement on `s3:DeleteObject` and `s3:PutObject` with the condition `"Bool": {"aws:ViaAWSMCPService": "true"}`; the IAM condition keys reference shows this exact pattern. Connect Claude Code to the AWS MCP Server with a profile for that role, and ask the agent to list the bucket (allowed) and then delete the object (denied). Delete it yourself with the AWS CLI and the same role (allowed), and find all three calls in CloudTrail. Google Cloud variant: try the same idea with an IAM Deny policy on a Google-managed MCP server.
labs.output: A two-statement policy, and CloudTrail entries that show the agent’s delete denied and yours allowed

checks.q: Claude Platform on AWS and Claude in Amazon Bedrock are both billed through AWS. Why can only one of them ever be a candidate for PHI-adjacent work?
checks.a: Who processes the data. On Claude Platform on AWS, Anthropic is the processor and HIPAA readiness is not available. On Bedrock, AWS is the processor and Bedrock is on AWS’s HIPAA-eligible list. Even so, at Rhino the Bedrock route for Lane B is still being checked with the vendors.

checks.q: Your night-shift agents on Bedrock hit the tokens-per-minute quota while the bill stays low. What two things do you check?
checks.a: The output burndown (10x for Opus 5.5) and `max_tokens`, which is reserved in full when each request starts. Set `max_tokens` close to real output.

checks.q: Why aren’t Bedrock Guardrails or Model Armor the PHI control?
checks.a: Their detection is probabilistic, so some data can slip through. They are defense in depth. The control is that PHI never enters a prompt: synthetic data, lanes and egress rules.

checks.q: An agent must read cloud resources and a person must change them. How do you enforce that without trusting the prompt?
checks.a: Give the agent its own identity and a Deny on mutating actions when the call comes through MCP (`aws:ViaAWSMCPService` on AWS, IAM Deny policies on Google-managed MCP servers). The audit log then shows who did what.

watchOut: Unpinned models. The `opus` alias now resolves to Opus 5.5 and an unpinned deployment bills at the Opus rate. Pin every alias, and route teams through their own inference profiles.
`global.` as a default. It is about 10% cheaper, but a request can run in any commercial region. Use a geographic profile when residency matters, and prove it with `inferenceRegion` in CloudTrail.

Pre-GA features and “may store your content”. Google says Pre-GA offerings must not be used with PHI, and Agent Identity’s API is still `v1beta1`. AgentCore’s docs say it “may use and store your content to improve your service experience or performance”, for your own use and not for other customers. Ask the vendor in writing before any PHI-adjacent use.

Cloud dev tools are a supply chain, and they move. In July 2025 an over-privileged GitHub token in CodeBuild let an attacker ship malicious code in the Amazon Q Developer VS Code extension 1.84.0; the payload failed only because of a syntax error (AWS-2025-015). Q Developer IDE plugins reach end of support on 30 Apr 2027, with Kiro as the replacement, and Gemini CLI stopped serving free and AI Pro or Ultra users on 18 June 2026 in favour of Antigravity CLI. Teach the principle, and pin the tool version.
modules.watchTime: 40 min core, 52 min with electives
modules.goal: For every agent workload, choose where it runs on AWS or Google Cloud and prove the choice is safe: who processes the data, in which region, under which identity, behind which policy, and at what cost. Then run Claude Code through your own cloud account with pinned models, host one small agent on a managed runtime, and write “agents read, humans change” into IAM instead of into a prompt.
modules.why: Rhino runs on both clouds. The FCP hides AWS and GCP behind `StorageService` and `SecretsManager`, it has separate AWS and GCP integration-test workflows, and its CI already authenticates to both (`aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`, `google-github-actions/auth`, `get-gke-credentials`). In 2026 both clouds rebuilt their agent stacks: Vertex AI became Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform at Cloud Next on 22 April, and Bedrock AgentCore now lists 13 services, from Harness and Runtime to Identity, Gateway, Policy and Registry. On AWS alone there are three ways to call Claude, and they differ in the one thing a healthcare company can’t get wrong: who processes the data. The other traps are quiet and expensive. An unpinned `opus` alias now bills at Opus rates, a `global.` profile trades data residency for about 10% off, and on Bedrock each Opus 5.5 output token drains your quota ten times faster than it shows on the bill. A developer who wants to be a whole team has to make these calls on purpose and write them down, so a reviewer who isn’t the requester can check them.

shipIt.title: The cloud route record
shipIt.body: For one real agent workload, write a one-page record: the endpoint and who processes the data, the region and how you proved it, the agent’s identity and what it may not do, the gateway policy, `max_tokens` and the quota math, the spend limit, and the BAA status with the vendor contact who confirmed it in writing. A platform owner who is not the requester signs it off, and the record lives next to the code.

modules.title: Remote agent infrastructure

keyIdeas.title: Brain, hands and session log
keyIdeas.body: Anthropic’s Managed Agents design splits an agent into three replaceable parts: a durable, append-only session log, a stateless harness (the loop that calls the model, the brain) and a sandbox where tools run (the hands), reached through one execute call. If the harness dies, a new one reads the log and continues; if the sandbox dies, the harness asks for a new one. Devin’s and Open-Inspect’s builders describe the same shape: run the loop in a control plane, and give the sandbox only the requester’s own scoped credentials, never one shared GitHub App for everyone (Latent Space, May 2026). Decide early whether a sandbox is a disposable job per task (HubSpot’s one Job per execution) or a long-lived session, and remember that a restarted pod doesn’t resume an in-memory agent run: only your session log does.

keyIdeas.title: Buy, rent or build, and the lane decides
keyIdeas.body: Buy: hosted cloud agents (the Copilot cloud agent, Codex cloud, Cursor cloud agents, Devin) or Claude Code self-hosted environments launched as Kubernetes Jobs, which add web, mobile and routines but need an org without ZDR (zero data retention). Rent the sandbox: a managed runtime runs your harness for you. AgentCore Runtime gives each session a dedicated microVM that is wiped when the session ends, for up to 8 hours (14 days on Instances), with a filesystem that persists across stop and resume; the managed GKE Agent Sandbox add-on runs gVisor sandboxes with warm pools and pod snapshots; chapter 28 compares these rungs. Build thin: the Agent SDK or `claude -p` in your own pod, with your own Postgres session log. At Rhino, a remote agent for Lane B (PHI-adjacent) work may use only the build-thin path in our own pod, under the BAA with ZDR and with no connectors; self-hosted environments aren’t available under ZDR. A Lane B route through Rhino’s own Bedrock or Agent Platform account is being checked with the vendors; it is not policy.

keyIdeas.title: A kernel of its own for every agent
keyIdeas.body: Chapter 25 showed that containers share the host kernel, so code an agent writes and runs needs a stronger wall: gVisor (a kernel in user space) or a VM kernel per agent (Kata Containers, or a Firecracker microVM). Microsoft’s platform gives each agent a Kata VM with its own kernel, a unique cloud identity through OIDC federation that reaches only its owner’s data, NetworkPolicy that blocks the instance metadata service (IMDS) and lateral movement, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that stops `exec` into agent pods, and blast-radius limits with full audit logs (talk abstract, Sep 2026). OpenAI’s sandbox engineer adds the next two pillars after isolation: persistence (disk snapshots, so a long task survives and restarts fast) and fleet orchestration (AI Engineer, Jul 2026). On Kubernetes, the open-source agent-sandbox project (SIG Apps, v1.0.4 on 24 Sep 2026) gives you Sandbox, SandboxTemplate, SandboxClaim and SandboxWarmPool objects; v1.0.0 (28 Aug 2026) removed the old `v1alpha1` APIs, so update older manifests.

keyIdeas.title: Nothing to steal
keyIdeas.body: Real credentials never enter the sandbox. The pod holds placeholders, and a broker outside it (Infisical’s Agent Vault, Envoy’s credential injector, or an egress gateway) swaps in real, short-lived values on the way out. Alibaba Cloud moved token replacement and LLM request audit into one internal gateway instead of a sidecar per sandbox, because DNS changes, first-packet timing and short-lived sandboxes break static allowlists (KubeCon China talk abstract, Sep 2026). The clouds now sell brokers and agent identities: AgentCore Identity keeps outbound OAuth tokens and API keys in a vault, EKS Pod Identity hands each pod temporary role credentials, Workload Identity Federation for GKE swaps a Kubernetes token for a short-lived cloud token, and Google’s Agent Identity binds tokens to mTLS so a stolen one can’t be replayed (its API is still `v1beta1`). GitHub App installation tokens last an hour and can be scoped to one repo. Deny egress by default and block raw instance metadata; on GKE with Workload Identity, the GKE metadata server is the credential path, so allow it only for the pod’s own service account. And after PocketOS: no production database URL and no broad cloud token anywhere in the image, the repo or the environment.

keyIdeas.title: Fast, disposable environments
keyIdeas.body: Environment setup is the hard part, so bake it into a prebuilt image (rebuilt every 30 minutes in the remote-agents design), keep a warm pool of ready sandboxes, and give each task its own database cloned with `CREATE DATABASE … TEMPLATE` from synthetic seed data. Agents already work this way: Databricks says agents create 97% of database branches on Neon (vendor, 2026). One documented trap: setting `spec.env` on a SandboxClaim makes it start cold instead of using the warm pool (documented behavior since agent-sandbox v0.5.6, not a bug). For front-end tasks, put Chrome for Testing and isolated browser profiles in the image so screen checks (chapter 12, Let agents check every screen) run inside the sandbox. CI has the same shape: Actions Runner Controller runs ephemeral self-hosted runners, one job per pod, which can share the agents’ isolated node pool.

keyIdeas.title: What it costs
keyIdeas.body: A small container is about $0.05 an hour; tokens are the real cost. The Agent SDK has no session timeout, so always set a turn cap (`maxTurns`, or `--max-turns` for `claude -p`) and a token budget. Managed runtimes bill differently: AgentCore Runtime v1 costs $0.0895 per vCPU-hour and doesn’t bill CPU while the agent waits on the model, which AWS says is 30 to 70% of an agent’s time (vendor figure). Measure cost per merged PR, not per session (chapter 33, Measure results and cost).
