labs.title: One task, one sandbox, green tests
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): Pick one route. Local: a kind cluster from chapter 25 with the agent-sandbox controller (v1.0.4); kind has no gVisor, so this proves the flow, not the isolation. Google Cloud: a small GKE cluster with the managed Agent Sandbox add-on (gVisor). AWS: EKS with agent-sandbox and Pod Identity, or one AgentCore Runtime session per task, deployed with the AgentCore CLI as in chapter 28. Build an image with a small public sample app that has tests (a Next.js app, a Django app or both), its runtimes and Postgres. Create a template at 2 CPU and 4 GiB and a warm pool of two, then claim a sandbox and run `claude -p "<one small task>" --max-turns 30` inside it until the app’s tests pass. Use a low-budget key you revoke at the end; lab 2 takes it out of the sandbox. Measure claim-to-ready time from the warm pool, once cold, and once with `spec.env` set on the claim, plus time to green and cost per session. Delete everything and check that nothing still bills. At Rhino: the remote-agents image with the monorepo, Python 3.13, Node, Playwright and Postgres 17, a per-task database from TEMPLATE seeded_synthetic, gVisor on GKE, and a comparison with shared QA and its four-request ceiling.
labs.output: A working sandbox and a table of its start, test and cost numbers

labs.title: Nothing to steal, red-teamed
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Take the real key out of lab 1’s sandbox. Run a broker outside it (Infisical Agent Vault, or Envoy with a credential injector), give the sandbox only a placeholder and an `HTTPS_PROXY` that points at the broker, and add a NetworkPolicy that denies egress except DNS, the broker and your package mirror, with raw instance metadata (169.254.169.254) blocked. Create a GitHub App on a scratch repo and mint an installation token with only `contents: write` and `pull_requests: write`; it expires in an hour. Add a ruleset that requires one approving review. Then attack it: plant a README line that tells the agent to print its environment and send it to an outside URL, and ask the agent to push straight to main. Every attempt must fail and leave a log line, and `env` inside the sandbox must show only placeholders. At Rhino: an `agent/*` ruleset that requires a reviewer other than the requester, FQDN egress rules where the network plugin supports them, and on GKE with Workload Identity the metadata server allowed only for the pod’s own service account.
labs.output: A red-team log with every attempt blocked and every secret a placeholder

labs.title: A webhook to a PR, resumable and budgeted
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): Have the agent write a small intake service: it accepts a webhook (a Slack slash command, or a plain `curl`), wraps the text as untrusted input, writes a row to an append-only session log (a Postgres or SQLite table) and starts a sandbox or a `claude -p` job with a turn cap and a token budget. Stream each step to the log and post a short status back to the caller. Kill the job halfway, then start a new one that reads the log and continues from the last finished step, and write down what was lost. Add an idle TTL that stops a silent job, and send OpenTelemetry traces to a local collector tagged with the task ID. At Rhino: Slack and Jira triggers, traces to Langfuse tagged by ticket and team, and scale-to-zero at night.
labs.output: A session log with one resumed run, and cost, time to PR and outcome for each run

checks.q: Where do credentials live in a well-built sandbox?
checks.a: Outside it. The sandbox holds placeholders; a broker or gateway outside swaps in real, short-lived values on the way out.

checks.q: What happens if you set spec.env on a SandboxClaim?
checks.a: The claim starts a cold sandbox instead of taking one from the warm pool. The project documents this, so put per-task settings somewhere else.

checks.q: Is a container a security boundary for code an agent writes?
checks.a: No. Containers share the host kernel. Use gVisor, or a VM kernel per agent with Kata or a microVM, as Microsoft does.

checks.q: Which path keeps PHI-adjacent work under the BAA?
checks.a: The build-thin path: the Agent SDK or claude -p in our own pod, with ZDR. Self-hosted environments aren’t available under ZDR, and a cloud-account route is still being checked.

watchOut: Read-only production database or log access for triage. At Rhino that is a PHI path.
One shared GitHub App identity for every session.
A production database URL or a broad cloud token anywhere the agent can read, as at PocketOS.
agent-sandbox manifests written for `v1alpha1`: v1.0.0 removed those APIs.

extras.title: Reference architecture for remote agents
lines: - **Triggers:** Slack, Jira, GitHub comments, cron.
- **Control plane:**
- Intake API, wrapping every payload as untrusted
- Queue
- Append-only Postgres session log
- Policy: who can dispatch, repo scope, token budget, TTL
- GitHub App token minter: one identity per session, one repo, one hour
- Credential broker (Agent Vault or Envoy), or the cloud’s own: AgentCore Identity, Pod Identity, Workload Identity Federation
- Notifier to Slack, Jira or the PR
- SandboxClaim and SandboxWarmPool, or one AgentCore Runtime session per task
- **Data plane:**
- “agents” namespace: egress denied by default, raw instance metadata blocked, admission policy against exec
- One pod per task on gVisor or Kata (GKE Agent Sandbox, or EKS with agent-sandbox), or one AgentCore microVM per session
- Harness: claude -p or the Agent SDK with a turn cap, writing to the session log
- Prebuilt image, rebuilt every 30 minutes, with Chrome for Testing
- Postgres 17 sidecar: a database per task from TEMPLATE seeded_synthetic
- Django with IS_TEST_ENV, Next dev server, Playwright, and the in-memory test fakes from Rhino’s tests-and-fakes project
- HTTPS_PROXY to the broker; placeholder tokens only; no production URL or broad cloud token
- Egress only to the model, the broker and the package mirror
- **Observability:** OTel collector, Langfuse or SigNoz, Prometheus.

modules.watchTime: 39 min core, 1 h 41 min with electives
modules.goal: Design a place where agents run away from your laptop, the way HubSpot, Stripe, Microsoft and Cognition did: the agent’s brain (the harness loop) outside the sandbox, one disposable sandbox with its own kernel per task, one identity per agent, credentials that never enter the sandbox, a per-task database from synthetic data, and triggers from Slack, Jira or a webhook. Then build one on Kubernetes or on a managed runtime on AWS or Google Cloud, with nothing inside worth stealing. Chapters 25 to 28 are the foundations this chapter stands on: Pods, NetworkPolicy and OIDC (chapter 25, The infrastructure you need to know), CI with agents inside it (chapter 26, Keep CI safe when agents run in it), infrastructure changes through a plan gate (chapter 27, Let agents write infrastructure code) and the cloud hosting ladder (chapter 28, Agents on AWS and Google Cloud).
modules.why: Remote agents are how one developer runs several tasks at once without handing them a laptop full of secrets. HubSpot runs every agent execution as its own Kubernetes Job on its own infrastructure, and in six months merged over 7,000 fully AI-generated PRs and had agents review over 50,000 human PRs (HubSpot’s own numbers, Jan 2026). Stripe’s Minions produce more than 1,000 merged PRs a week, and humans still review the code (Stripe, Feb 2026). Microsoft runs agents for hundreds of engineers on one shared cluster, for daily development and on-call, and found that standard Kubernetes multi-tenancy “was designed for cooperative workloads, not for autonomous agents” (KubeCon China talk, Sep 2026). The sandbox is now a product too: GKE Agent Sandbox went GA on 21 May 2026 and allocates 300 sandboxes a second per cluster, 90% of them in 200 ms (Google’s figures), and AgentCore Runtime gives each session its own microVM for up to 8 hours (AWS docs). The failures are just as clear. In April 2026 a Cursor agent running Claude Opus 4.6 found an unrelated API token in a file and deleted PocketOS’s production database and its backups in 9 seconds (the founder’s report). Every team that got this right separated the agent’s brain from its hands, and left nothing in the hands worth stealing. At Rhino this is the remote-agent project: agents that start from a ticket or a Slack thread and open a PR, instead of sharing the QA environment, whose cloud API serves only four requests at a time per pod.

shipIt.body: Brain inside or outside the pod, a kernel per task, credentials injected per trigger through a broker, one identity per session, egress rules, and the per-task synthetic database. Plus lab 1 passing end to end, reviewed by someone who is not you.

modules.title: Production: deploy verification and incidents

keyIdeas.title: OODA for incidents
keyIdeas.body: Observe, orient, decide, act (John Boyd’s loop). Agents are superhuman at observe: they read logs, metrics, traces and alerts faster than any person. They are weak at orient, where they confuse correlation with causation, and the numbers agree: SREGym’s scores fall hardest on unfamiliar failures, and in the OpenRCA analysis the evidence was there but the reasoning missed it. So let the agent gather and summarize, and keep a human on “what is really happening” and “what do we do”.

keyIdeas.title: Choose the autonomy level on purpose
keyIdeas.body: The SAE levels for self-driving cars work for on-call: at Level 3 the agent drives, and a human must be ready to take over at any moment. Today’s products expose the dial. AWS DevOps Agent is advisory: it investigates and recommends, and humans approve. Azure SRE Agent runs in Review or Autonomous mode, with allow, ask or deny per tool and hooks on its actions. HolmesGPT (a CNCF Sandbox project, v0.42.0 in Sep 2026) and kagent (CNCF Sandbox, v1.0.0-alpha4) run agents inside Kubernetes. Experts disagree on direct action: Akuity lets its agents act freely in development and escalate in production, and Azure offers Autonomous mode. Rhino’s call stays: no agent holds deploy credentials, and production tools are read-only.

keyIdeas.title: Durable supervisor, stateless hypotheses
keyIdeas.body: PagerDuty’s incident agent is a long-lived supervisor that spawns short-lived subagents, each testing one hypothesis; its main failure mode is context rot as the incident drags on. incident.io runs parallel checks across its data sources, then builds and refines hypotheses. Either way, keep the evidence in a record outside any one context window, so a fresh subagent can start clean.

keyIdeas.title: Score it on your own past incidents
keyIdeas.body: A time-travel eval replays a closed incident and grades each of the agent’s claims against the postmortem (incident.io’s method). Vendor claims only count after your own replay: AWS says its DevOps Agent preview showed up to 75% lower time to resolution and 94% root-cause accuracy, and customer stories report resolution falling from about 2 hours to 28 minutes (vendor figures). SREGym is the reminder that a score on familiar faults doesn’t carry over to new ones.

keyIdeas.title: Fix, don’t deploy
keyIdeas.body: The alert agent may find and write the fix; it opens a PR, and the normal pipeline takes it from there. Vendors now build the same way: AWS DevOps Agent hands fixes to coding agents as specs, and HolmesGPT’s operator mode opens PRs. The release side is agent work too: after each deploy to QA, an agent-written smoke check runs in CI or a routine and posts pass or fail with evidence to the release thread, so a bad deploy is caught before production.

keyIdeas.title: PHI first, and let the agent read its own traces at dev time
keyIdeas.body: Alerts, logs and error events can carry patient data. Audit every signal source and scrub it before any of it reaches a prompt; at Rhino, check whether Sentry is initialised at all before planning labs with Seer, Sentry’s AI root-cause tool. The safe place to build the habit is dev time: logs written to files with trace IDs, OpenTelemetry through Django and Celery (or your Node server) to a local collector, and synthetic data only. Give the agent telemetry it can query: in Pydantic’s comparison of seven observability tools on the same 400 spans, query-backed MCP servers answered in 2 SQL calls where object-based ones needed 9 or more (vendor, Jul 2026). Then extend to production signals only read-only, scoped to one project and after the PHI audit.

labs.title: Deploy verification with evidence
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Take a small sample app you can deploy to a preview or staging environment, or “deploy” locally with Docker Compose. Have the agent write five smoke checks for the main paths (the home page renders, sign-in works with a test user, one API call returns the right shape, a health endpoint answers, a key page loads in under a set time). Run them as a plain script, with no model in the loop, in a CI job or scheduled routine that triggers after each deploy and posts pass or fail with evidence (status codes, timings, one screenshot) to the PR or a chat webhook. Break the app on purpose once and check that the post says fail. At Rhino: a Lane A routine or CI job after each QA deploy, posting to the release thread, with factory-seeded QA data only.
labs.output: A smoke-check job that posts evidence after every deploy, and one caught failure

labs.title: A PHI-safe signal map, and a trace the agent can read
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): For an app you know, list every signal an agent might read: logs, error events, traces, metrics, alerts and dashboards. For each, write what fields it holds, whether it could carry personal data, who can read it today and how you would scrub it (a logging filter, the error tracker’s scrubbing rules, dropping request bodies). Then add OpenTelemetry to the local dev stack (Django, Express or FastAPI), export to a local collector or a local tracing UI, seed only synthetic data, and ask the agent why one endpoint is slow, from the trace alone. At Rhino: treat every production source as PHI-adjacent until audited, check whether Sentry is initialised at all, and have the list signed off before any agent reads production signals.
labs.output: A signal table with a scrub plan per source, and one answer the agent found in a local trace

labs.title: A time-travel eval for an incident agent
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): Turn three closed incidents into replay packs: your own, or public postmortems that many companies publish. Each pack holds the first alert, a timeline of synthetic logs and metrics, and the true root cause kept in a separate file the agent can’t read. Run a read-only agent on each pack (Claude Code in plan mode, or a small Agent SDK agent with file-read tools only) and have it list its claims with the evidence for each. Grade every claim right, wrong or unsupported against the postmortem. Then apply Palcuie’s five patterns from the video to your prompt or harness and score all three again. At Rhino: five past incidents, synthetic data only, and an agent that may only open draft PRs.
labs.output: A claims-accuracy table before and after the patterns

checks.q: Where in the OODA loop are agents strongest and weakest?
checks.a: Strongest at observe, gathering signals fast. Weakest at orient, where they mistake correlation for causation.

checks.q: A vendor says its ops agent cuts time to resolution by 75%. How do you check?
checks.a: Treat it as a vendor figure and run a time-travel eval: replay your own closed incidents and grade each claim against the postmortem, including failures unlike the ones it was shown.

checks.q: The alert agent found the fix. Who deploys it?
checks.a: Not the agent. It opens a PR and the normal pipeline takes over.

checks.q: What must happen before alerts reach a prompt?
checks.a: A PHI audit of every signal source, and scrubbing.

watchOut: Engineers losing on-call skill because the agent always investigates first.
Vendor claims like “2x faster” or “75% lower time to resolution” without your own replay.
An ops agent in an autonomous mode with write access to production. At Rhino, no agent holds deploy credentials.
modules.watchTime: 25 min core, 1 h 11 min with electives
modules.goal: Use agents after release where they are strong: checking every deploy with evidence and gathering signals fast in an incident. Choose each ops agent’s autonomy level on purpose, keep humans on orienting, deciding and deploying, and score any ops agent, bought or built, by replaying your own past incidents before you trust it.
modules.why: Your code isn’t done when it merges, and agents now reach into the stages after it. Alex Palcuie of Anthropic’s AI reliability team rates Anthropic’s own AI incident response at SAE Level 3: the agent drives, and a human must be ready to take over at any moment. Claude is superhuman at gathering signals and bad at causation: during a KV-cache outage it kept calling for more capacity (InfoQ talk, Sep 2026). Benchmarks now show the same shape with numbers. In SREGym, 90 failure scenarios on live cloud-native systems, Claude Code on Sonnet 4.6 solved 60.7% end to end without background noise and 53.7% with it; on the 13 problems whose failures are unique to SREGym it fell to 28.2%, from 60.8% on the 34 problems ported from older benchmarks, and Codex on GPT-5.4 fell from 57.8% to 15.4% (preprint, May 2026, revised Jul 2026). An analysis of the OpenRCA benchmark found the evidence for the root cause was present in most failures; the bottleneck was the model’s reasoning over it (preprint, Jul 2026). Meanwhile ops agents became products with autonomy dials: AWS DevOps Agent (GA 31 Mar 2026) investigates and recommends while humans approve, Azure SRE Agent has Review and Autonomous modes, and the open-source HolmesGPT can run as an operator that opens PRs. The chapters before this one built the platform (chapters 25 to 29); this one runs it after release, with Rhino’s rule intact: agents open PRs, and pipelines deploy.

keyIdeas.title: Review capacity is the first plan
keyIdeas.body: Across 10,000+ developers, teams with high AI adoption completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more PRs, while review time rose 91%, average PR size 154% and bugs per developer 9%, and the gains did not show up at company level (Faros AI, vendor telemetry, Jul 2025). In the CMU and Stanford “2x mandate” study, automated review overtook human review while merge and revert rates held steady (Jul 2026). AI-generated PRs wait 4.6x longer before anyone reviews them, then get reviewed 2x faster (LinearB, vendor, 8.1M+ PRs, 2026), and median PR size nearly doubled while the AI-generated share of code rose to 52%, from 34% a quarter earlier (DX, vendor, 500+ organizations, Jul 2026). So before you add agent output, do the arithmetic: PRs arriving per day times review minutes per PR, against the review hours your people really have. When arrivals beat capacity, the queue grows every day and the oldest PRs go stale and start to conflict. The levers: smaller PRs and stacks (chapter 15, Build a whole feature with agents), a risk tier so low-risk changes get a lighter review, bots for the first pass on style, lint and tests, a limit on open agent PRs per person, and more trained reviewers. The Claude Code team lets Claude handle style, lint, PR feedback and adding tests, and keeps humans where expertise matters: legal risk, trust boundaries and security-sensitive code, and product sense and taste; Fiona Fung re-checks that split with each new model (May 2026, one team’s practice). Set a review SLA (a promise such as a first review within one working day) and watch the age of the oldest PR, not only the count. Two things are never levers: letting the requester approve their own agent’s PR, and merging on a bot’s approval alone.

keyIdeas.title: Lead from the harness, not the ticket queue
keyIdeas.body: Leads are back in the code. LeadDev’s Engineering Leadership Report 2026 found hands-on technical work among engineering managers up from 20% in 2025 to 35% in 2026, and 41% of tech leads and 44% of CTOs spent more time on hands-on coding and code review than the year before (survey, Aug 2026). On the Claude Code team, every manager starts as an IC (individual contributor) and ships before leading (Fiona Fung). But the same LeadDev piece warns that the goal is not to become another engineer on the team; Bloomberg’s Paul Williams suggests taking non-critical-path work. Meetings split your attention, so an urgent ticket on your desk makes the team wait for you. Put your hands-on time where it multiplies everyone. First, the harness: context lines, skills, hooks, lint rules, review bots and routines, which is Rhino rule 7 (fix the harness on the second repeat) at team scale. Second, prototypes that settle debates: “in technical debates, code wins” when you can generate three PRs and compare them, with a team rule that the last person to push does not win the argument (Fiona Fung). Third, deleting processes that quietly stopped working: her team has explicit permission to kill old processes, and a stand-up spreadsheet became a stand-up skill. Plan just in time: her six-month roadmap was out of date by month three.

keyIdeas.title: A human owns every agent run
keyIdeas.body: Accountability does not delegate, and the tools now say so. In Linear you can delegate an issue to an agent, but “the assignee remains responsible for the work, while the agent contributes on their behalf”, and triage rules can delegate automatically (Linear docs). Zapier’s hiring rubric puts it as “With AI, you can delegate the work, but not the accountability” (Mar 2026). DX counts agent PRs toward the team that directs them and expects developers to be “measured the way managers are measured today” (DX, May 2026). At Rhino this is rules 3 and 5, and it covers everyone who starts an agent: a PM or designer who delegates a ticket owns that PR and cannot approve it either. Owning means answering for it: the owner can explain every line, or it does not ship (Addy Osmani, from chapter 1, Your first hour with a coding agent). Watch for the polished-output trap: in 9,830 Claude.ai conversations, when Claude produced an artifact such as code, a document or an app, people were less likely to spot missing context (−5.2 points), check facts (−3.7) or question the reasoning (−3.1) (Anthropic AI Fluency Index, Feb 2026, correlational). “Who made this change?” is now a weak question, because Claude assisted every PR; ask what you really need to know (who caused the regression, who is the expert, what was the context) and let Claude answer what it can (Fiona Fung). The audit question “who approved it?” must still have a person’s name.

keyIdeas.title: Design the team around who checks, not who types
keyIdeas.body: In McKinsey’s survey, teams added tools but kept 8- to 10-person teams, two-week sprints and old roles. Top performers were six times more likely to have AI-native roles, such as one-pizza pods of three to five people with consolidated roles, and seven times more likely to use AI in four or more parts of the lifecycle, not only in coding or code review; one bank split its squads by workflow, one for small bug fixes and one for new features (consultants’ survey and client cases, Dec 2025). Anthropic describes the engineer’s value moving to system design, agent coordination, quality evaluation and breaking problems down (2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report), and its own staff use Claude in about 60% of their work but can fully delegate only 0 to 20% of it (132 surveyed, Dec 2025). So give every code surface one accountable reviewer (a CODEOWNERS entry), put domain experts on security, contract and PHI-adjacent code, and let PMs prototype and write evals, designers review product taste, and QA own the verification contracts from chapter 7, Check the agent’s work. The Claude Code team hires two profiles, creative builders with product sense and deep systems experts, and weighs raw throughput less, because “the models handle that” (Fiona Fung, Jun 2026). Agree the plan before agents fan out, so alignment happens before the code and not on the PR (Maggie Appleton, chapter 15).

keyIdeas.title: Run the agent fleet like a queue
keyIdeas.body: Put every run on one board with its state. In Claude Code, `claude agents` opens agent view: one screen for all your background sessions, grouped as Needs input, Ready for review (the session has an open PR), Working and Completed, with each PR number colored by its status, and `claude agents --json` gives the same list to a script (research preview; each session uses your quota). Agent view shows one person’s sessions on one machine, so the team’s shared board is your tracker or the PR list, with one column per state, whichever agent people use. Then limit work in process the way DORA teaches for any team: a WIP (work-in-progress) limit per column set by capacity, never raised because people are idle, and counting invisible work. The column that matters most is “ready for review”, and its limit is your review capacity. Per person, keep one agent in front and at most two behind (chapter 10, Your workday with an AI agent). Addy Osmani’s rule for agent teams is “Don’t run more agents than you can meaningfully review”, with 3 to 5 as the sweet spot (Mar 2026). Write kill rules: stop and reassign a run stuck 3 or more times on the same error, pause at a budget line (Osmani pauses an agent at 85% of its token budget and notifies the lead), and cap headless runs with `--max-budget-usd` (chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely). Shopify replaced its token leaderboard with a usage dashboard and circuit breakers that catch runaway agents and flag abnormal daily spend spikes (DORA, Jun 2026). At team scale the night shift needs three more rules: every run names its owner and reviewer before launch, morning reviews come before new launches, and runs nobody claims by a set time are closed. For scale: Stripe’s agents produce more than a thousand merged PRs a week, and humans still review the code (Stripe, Feb 2026).

keyIdeas.title: Hire and grow people who can judge agent work
keyIdeas.body: Interviews now take three stances. Canva expects front-end, back-end and ML candidates to use AI on realistic, ambiguous problems, and found that candidates with little AI practice often struggled because they lacked the judgment to guide it, not because they couldn’t code (Jun 2025). Meta, since October 2025, makes one of two coding rounds AI-enabled: a multi-file codebase and three phases (fix a bug, build a feature, handle bigger inputs), graded on problem solving, code quality, verification and communication (candidate reports collected by Hello Interview). Anthropic allows no AI in live interviews unless it says otherwise. Zapier scores AI mindset, strategy, building and accountability, looks at the slope of a candidate’s growth rather than a snapshot, requires managers to show their team adopted AI, and says a rough result with strong reasoning beats a polished one with no visible process (Mar 2026). Keep hiring juniors on purpose. Employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below trend, mainly through fewer hires (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, revised Aug 2026), and 62% of leaders expect fewer junior hires (LeadDev AI Impact Report 2026). Yet supervising agents needs the very skills that AI overuse can stop from forming, what Anthropic calls the “paradox of supervision” (Dec 2025), and novice-rated Claude Code sessions reached verified success 15% of the time against 28 to 33% for intermediate and above (Anthropic, ~400,000 sessions, Jun 2026). So grow understanding, not only output: the learning style and comprehension checks from chapter 10, pairing (in Shopify’s own analysis, engineers who paired more had higher impact), and time on the calendar for questions to seniors, because juniors now ask Claude first. In performance reviews, count orchestration, review and harness work as engineering work, and never tokens (rule 6). Meta dropped AI dashboards and token counters from reviews in September 2026 and now judges the quality, speed and complexity of the work (The Decoder, citing The Information).

labs.title: Your team’s review budget
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): pick any repo with steady PR traffic that you can read, your team’s or a busy public project. Pull the last 200 merged PRs with `gh pr list --state merged --limit 200 --json number,author,additions,deletions,createdAt,mergedAt,reviews,commits`, and have your agent compute, per week: PRs merged, median lines changed, hours from opening to first review, and distinct reviewers. Mark agent-written PRs by bot authors or `Co-Authored-By` trailers in the commits. Time five real reviews of your own to estimate minutes per PR, multiply out the review hours needed, and compare them with the hours your team really has. Model what happens when agent PRs double, in this chapter’s practice tool (Can your team review it all?) or a spreadsheet, then write down the SLA you would set and three levers with numbers: a size cap, a risk tier, a WIP limit, a bot first pass or more reviewers. At Rhino: the Lane B org runs with Zero Data Retention (ZDR), where Claude Code’s analytics show usage only and no contribution metrics, so use the co-author trailers there; report team totals and never rank people.
labs.output: A one-page review-capacity plan with an SLA and three levers

labs.title: Fleet rules, tested on yourself
labs.body: Solo (about 75 min): write a FLEET.md for one repo with the starting set from this chapter: an owner and reviewer per run, WIP limits, the kill rule, a budget cap and what happens to unclaimed runs. Pick three small, independent tasks with a machine-checkable done, such as a failing test to fix, a missing Storybook story or a test for a Django endpoint, and dispatch them as background sessions: `claude agents` in Claude Code, or one worktree and one terminal per task with any other agent. Cap any headless `claude -p` run with `--max-budget-usd`. Check the board every 15 minutes and log each run’s state, and apply your kill rule for real when a run loops. At the end, record keep, fix or discard for each result, your supervision minutes, and the rule you had to change. At Rhino: Lane A tasks on synthetic or factory-seeded data only, and a teammate who is not you approves any PR.
labs.output: A tested FLEET.md and a run log with keep, fix or discard for each task

labs.title: An AI-enabled interview round
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): build a 60-minute round from this chapter’s template on a small public sample app or a synthetic repo you create. Plant one real bug and a test that exposes it, write one small feature task (a React component for a front-end role, a Django endpoint for a back-end role), pick the three lines you will ask about, and write a scorecard with 1-to-4 anchors for reading code, verification, breaking the task down, directing the agent, answerability and judgment. Run the round on yourself with a timer and your own agent, save the transcript and score yourself honestly. Then write what a weak run and a strong run look like in each part, so a second interviewer would score it the same way. At Rhino: the repo is public or synthetic, never the FCP codebase, and holds no PHI.
labs.output: An interview kit (repo, tasks and a scorecard with anchors) and your own scored run

checks.q: Agents doubled your team’s PR inflow and the review queue keeps growing. What do you plan first, and which fixes are off the table?
checks.a: Review capacity: compare PRs arriving times review minutes with the review hours you have, then cut PR size, tier by risk, let bots take the first pass and cap open agent PRs per person. Letting requesters approve their own agent PRs (SOC 2 CC8.1) or merging on a bot’s approval alone are off the table.

checks.q: A PM delegates a ticket to an agent, and the agent opens a PR. Who owns it, and who approves it?
checks.a: The PM who delegated it owns it and must be able to explain it, as the human assignee does in Linear’s model. Someone other than the PM approves it.

checks.q: Name three fleet rules to write down before the night shift runs at team scale.
checks.a: A named owner and reviewer for every run, a WIP limit on “ready for review” set by review capacity, and a kill rule: stop and reassign after 3 stuck tries on the same error or when a run hits its budget. Runs nobody claims get closed.

checks.q: What do you score in an AI-enabled interview, and what do you never score?
checks.a: How they read the code, break the task down, direct the agent, verify its output, catch its mistakes and explain every line. Never how much code the agent produced.

watchOut: Taking critical-path tickets yourself. Meetings split your attention, so the team ends up waiting on you. Take prototypes, harness work and non-critical-path fixes.
Per-person token views. Claude Code’s Team and Enterprise analytics include a top-10 leaderboard; don’t share it (rule 6).
Agent runs with no named owner or reviewer. They turn into PRs nobody wants to review.
A team that stops hiring juniors. In three years, who will be able to review the agents?

modules.watchTime: 34 min core, 1 h 52 min with electives
modules.goal: Run a team of people and agents as one system: plan review capacity before you add agent output, shape the roles around who checks the work, run the agent fleet with owners, WIP limits, kill rules and budgets, hire and grow people who can judge agent work, and keep a weekly rhythm that fixes the harness and reports outcomes, never tokens.
modules.why: Code got cheap; judging it did not. Fiona Fung, who leads the Claude Code and Cowork teams at Anthropic, says coding “is rarely the slow part anymore”, and the bottlenecks moved to verification, review, cross-functional partners and security (May 2026). The data agrees. In a CMU and Stanford study of a company that mandated doubling merged PRs per engineer (802 developers, 196,212 PRs, Jul 2026), output per developer reached 2.09x, each reviewer’s load roughly doubled, and the share of PRs with any human review fell from 89% to 68%. Most companies have not redesigned for this: in McKinsey’s survey of about 300 companies, the average company-level gain was 5 to 15%, and about 70% had not changed their roles at all (a consultants’ survey, Dec 2025). So the lead’s job has moved from handing out tickets to running a system of people and agents in which review hours, shared plans and verification are the scarce resources. At Rhino this is a hard limit, not a preference: every agent PR needs a human approver who is not the requester (SOC 2 CC8.1). Chapter 30, Agents after release, finished the stages an agent touches; this chapter is the weekly job of running them all as one team, and the chapters after it give you the tools: chapter 32, Agents in code review and merging, for the review flow; chapter 33, Measure results and cost, for the scorecard; chapter 34, Stay safe and compliant, for the audit; chapters 35 and 36 for the company-wide plan and rollout.

shipIt.title: The lead’s operating page
shipIt.body: One page your team can see: the week’s rituals, the review SLA and capacity plan from lab 1, the fleet rules from lab 2, the interview kit from lab 3, and the three signals you will report each month, plus the one you never will (tokens per person). Run it for two weeks, then change one thing and say why.

modules.headlineSrc: +91% · review time when merged PRs nearly doubled

modules.title: The review and merge flow for agent work

keyIdeas.title: The review queue obeys Little’s law
keyIdeas.body: In any stable queue, the average number of items waiting equals the rate they arrive times the average time each one waits. If 20 agent PRs arrive a day and each waits a day and a half, about 30 are open at any moment; halve the wait or the arrivals and the pile halves. The law holds only while reviewers keep up: when PRs arrive faster than they are cleared, the wait grows every day, the oldest PRs go stale and start to conflict. So watch arrivals per day, pickup time (open to first review) and the age of the oldest PR, not just the count. There are only four levers: fewer arrivals, smaller PRs, more review done per hour (a bot first pass, a lighter lane for low-risk PRs) and more trained reviewers. Letting the requester approve their own agent’s PR is never one of them (SOC 2 CC8.1). Chapter 31 turns these numbers into a capacity plan.

keyIdeas.title: Small PRs are the cheapest capacity
keyIdeas.body: PRs are growing: in Faros AI’s telemetry from 10,000+ developers, average PR size rose 154% and review time 91% in high-adoption teams (vendor, Jul 2025), and DX found median PR size nearly doubled in one quarter (vendor, Jul 2026). Size also changes what review finds: Anthropic’s Code Review found issues in 84% of PRs over 1,000 lines, averaging 7.5 each, against 31% of PRs under 50 lines, averaging 0.5 (vendor, Mar 2026). Working in small batches is one of DORA’s capabilities for AI adoption. So set a size cap that a reviewer can read in one sitting, have CI label PRs above it, and ask the agent to split a big change into a stack: migration, then service, then UI, then flag, each reviewed on its own. GitHub’s native stacked PRs are in public preview (30 Jul 2026) with the gh-stack CLI and an agent skill (chapter 15, Build a whole feature with agents). You still own every line you merge, so never file a PR you haven’t read.

keyIdeas.title: A computed tier sets the review depth
keyIdeas.body: Ona’s rule: a PR is low-risk only if all six hold: fewer than 1,000 lines changed, and no protobuf, database migration, infrastructure or CI configuration, authentication or authorization, or audit-logging and monitoring changes. An agent reviews every PR; low-risk ones get the agent’s approval and all others go to a human, and a person always clicks merge, which is the traceable approval event for SOC 2. The tier is computed from the paths a PR touches, so no engineer can label their own PR low-risk. Start in shadow mode: compute and log the tier for weeks before it changes anything, and backtest it against past PRs and reverts. Rhino adds its own exclusions: common/ protos, migrations, .github, .devops/charts, permissions and PHI paths. Tiers need a way down as well as a way in. One proposal from the research: a path class drops one tier only after its deterministic gates (squawk for migrations, a migration rehearsal, buf for protos, oasdiff for API contracts, a permission-matrix test) have passed for a quarter with no escapes. At Rhino that graduation rule is being checked, not policy.

keyIdeas.title: Bots do the first pass, and you measure them
keyIdeas.body: Every major tool now reviews PRs: Rhino’s own review bot Byte (Claude Code in CI), Anthropic’s managed Code Review (billed by tokens, about $15 to $25 a review on average, never approves a PR, and not available under ZDR), Copilot code review and Codex automatic reviews. Judge any of them by its addressal rate: the share of its comments that led to a code change. Atlassian’s RovoDev reviewer reached 38.70% over a year and cut PR cycle time by 30.8% (one company’s numbers, Jan 2026). In a study of 54,791 agent review comments across 342 Python repos, an inline code suggestion was the strongest predictor that a comment got resolved, long and complex comments were ignored, and the most common reasons for ignoring one were incorrect suggestions and intentional design decisions (Jul 2026). Give each bot a REVIEW.md with a severity threshold and a cap of five nits, and keep humans on what bots can’t judge: intent, trust boundaries, PHI paths and product sense.

keyIdeas.title: Security and screenshots are review lanes too
keyIdeas.body: Since 9 June 2026, GitHub runs CodeQL, a dependency check against its Advisory Database and secret scanning on code from third-party agents such as Claude and Codex before the PR is finalized, on by default and without an Advanced Security license. Treat it as a floor, not a review: in SWE-chat’s 6,000 real sessions, agent-written code introduced more security vulnerabilities than human-written code and only 44% of it survived into commits (Apr 2026), and Veracode measured a 56% average security pass rate across 100+ models (vendor, Jul 2026). UI changes need their own lane. A visual baseline update is an approval, so the requester can’t approve their own agent’s new screenshots either. Storybook 10.4 (May 2026) added new, modified and related filters to its sidebar so a reviewer can go straight to the stories an agent’s change touched (chapter 12, Let agents check every screen).

keyIdeas.title: Keep main green: queues, flakes and upgrades
keyIdeas.body: A merge queue tests each PR against the latest main plus the PRs ahead of it and merges them in order; required workflows need a `merge_group` trigger or the queue stalls. Agents make this matter more: across 61,837 workflow runs triggered by agent PRs, Copilot and Codex PRs passed CI about 93 to 94% of the time, and repos with more frequent agent PRs had lower CI success (MSR 2026 study). Flaky tests get re-run in isolation, confirmed, and marked fixme with a ticket, never deleted, and retries that hide flakes get turned off. Dependency majors go one PR or none: an upgrade agent that is allowed to do nothing, and says why, beats one that always opens something.

labs.title: Queue math on a real repo
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): Pick a busy public repo, or your team’s. Pull the last 30 days of PRs with `gh pr list --state all --limit 300 --json number,createdAt,mergedAt,closedAt,additions,deletions,reviews,author` and have your agent compute: arrivals per day, the average time from opening to first review and to merge, and Little’s law’s prediction of how many PRs are open (arrivals times average time open). Compare the prediction with the real count of open PRs today, and explain any gap. Then bucket the PRs by size (under 200 lines, 200 to 1,000, over 1,000) and compare time to first review and review comments per bucket. Write down the size cap you would set and what you expect it to change, and check it again in a month. At Rhino: team totals only, never a ranking of people; it builds on chapter 31’s review budget.
labs.output: A one-page queue report with arrivals, wait, open PRs and a proposed size cap

labs.title: Risk tiers in shadow mode
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Have the agent write a script that computes a tier for a PR from its changed paths and size: Ona’s six criteria plus the sensitive paths of your own repo. Backtest it on the last 100 merged PRs of a repo you know: how many would have been low-risk, and did any of those get reverted or need a fix within a week (search for “Revert” and linked follow-up PRs)? Then wire it into a GitHub Actions workflow that only adds a label and a one-line comment explaining the tier, with no approve permission at all. At Rhino: add Rhino’s exclusions (common/ protos, migrations, .github, .devops/charts, permissions, PHI paths) and run it four weeks in shadow mode before anyone proposes an agent approval lane; the requester still never approves.
labs.output: A tier script, a backtest table and a label-only workflow

labs.title: Measure a review bot and cap its nits
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): Pick a public repo whose PRs get comments from a review bot (Copilot, CodeRabbit, Claude or Codex), or turn one on in a scratch repo for a week of your own PRs. Pull 30 to 50 of its comments with `gh api` and label each resolved (the next commit changed that code), ignored or wrong. Compute the addressal rate overall, for inline suggestions against prose, and for short against long comments. Write a REVIEW.md that sets a severity threshold, caps nits at five and asks for inline suggestions, and note what you expect to change. At Rhino: do it for Byte over two weeks of PRs, and compare with managed Code Review only if the org isn’t on ZDR.
labs.output: An addressal-rate table and a REVIEW.md

checks.q: 24 agent PRs arrive a day and each waits two days. About how many are open, and what can you change?
checks.a: About 48, by Little’s law. Cut arrivals or PR size, get more review done per hour with a bot first pass and a low-risk lane, or add trained reviewers. Never let the requester approve.

checks.q: May an engineer label their own PR low-risk?
checks.a: No. The tier is computed from what the PR touches. It sets how deep the review goes; at Rhino, a human who isn’t the requester still approves and merges every PR.

checks.q: What predicts that a bot’s review comment gets resolved?
checks.a: An inline code suggestion. Long, complex comments get ignored.

checks.q: A test is flaky. What may the agent do?
checks.a: Re-run it in isolation, confirm it repeatedly, and open a fixme PR with a ticket. Never delete it.

modules.goal: Run the review and merge flow for a team whose agents write more PRs than people can read: do the queue math before the queue grows, cap PR size and stack big changes, compute a risk tier from what each PR touches, let measured bots do the first pass, keep a human who is not the requester on every merge, and keep main green with a merge queue and a flaky-test process.
modules.why: Review is now where agent speed is won or lost. In a CMU and Stanford study of one company’s “2x” mandate (802 developers, 196,212 PRs, Jul 2026), PR volume grew 3.1x while the pool of reviewers grew 1.5x, so each reviewer’s load roughly doubled. The share of PRs with any human review fell from 89% to 68% while AI review rose from about 19% to 84%, and the human review that remained thinned: substantive review fell from about 39% to 21% of PRs while silent approvals stayed near 50%. Merge and revert rates held steady, so nothing looked broken. Across 8.1 million PRs, AI-generated PRs waited 4.6 times longer before anyone picked them up (LinearB, vendor, 2026). A well-designed flow changes this. Ona let an agent approve PRs that met six low-risk criteria, with a human still clicking merge; over four-week windows, median time to first approval fell from 2 h 49 min to 3.8 minutes and median lead time from 4.1 to 1.1 hours (Ona’s own figures for its human-authored PRs, Apr 2026). Anthropic reports that after it ran its Code Review product on nearly every internal PR, the share of PRs with substantive review comments rose from 16% to 54%, and engineers marked under 1% of its findings as incorrect (vendor data about its own product, Mar 2026). Chapter 31, The AI team lead’s job, plans the review hours; this chapter builds the flow those hours run through. Chapter 26, Keep CI safe when agents run in it, already made the pipeline safe with agents inside it.

modules.title: Measurement and FinOps

keyIdeas.title: Start with the frameworks leaders already use
keyIdeas.body: DORA’s five delivery metrics split into throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate). SPACE (Forsgren and others, 2021) names five dimensions, satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, and efficiency and flow, and its lesson is that no single metric is enough. DX Core 4 folds DORA, SPACE and DevEx into four counterbalanced dimensions (speed, effectiveness, quality and business impact) and uses diffs per engineer only next to a counter-metric, never as a target. DX’s AI measurement framework adds three layers on top: utilization, impact and cost (DX, May 2026, a vendor’s framework). Measure teams and services, never individuals.

keyIdeas.title: Add AI-specific measures, each next to a guardrail
keyIdeas.body: Useful ones: the share of merged PRs written by agents, tasks assigned to agents, human-equivalent hours (HEH) of agent work and the “agent hourly rate” (HEH divided by AI spend) from DX; time from ready to first review; the share of PRs with a commented human review, not only an approval; revert rate; first-run test pass rate; and the innovation ratio, the share of time on new work. Two warnings from the data. In the CMU and Stanford study, commented reviews stayed flat while silent approvals roughly doubled. In DX’s Q2 2026 data (500+ organizations, vendor), developers saved 4 to 6 hours a week but the innovation ratio stayed flat, so saved time does not become new work unless you plan it. Agent PRs count toward the team that directs them (DX). Keep a sealed replay set of closed tickets as the scorecard’s quality check on the harness; chapter 21, Test your agents like code, teaches the method.

keyIdeas.title: Weigh the evidence before you repeat a number
keyIdeas.body: Give every number its source, month and strength: a randomized study, a large observational study, a survey, a vendor figure, or one company’s numbers. Self-reports run high: in METR’s survey of 349 technical workers (May 2026), the median self-reported speed-up was 3x but the self-reported value gain only 1.4x to 2x, and in METR’s 2025 study people overestimated AI’s effect on their time by about 40 percentage points. Count releases and outcomes, not commits, because the NBER chain shrinks from commits to releases. Booking.com (4,000 engineers, 8,000 repos) spent four years building an event store of its delivery pipeline that separates keep-the-lights-on work from feature delivery, and warns that a static dashboard creates the metric it shows (one company’s account, Jul 2026). DORA’s ROI report (Apr 2026) plans for the “productivity dip” of a new rollout, so don’t judge a tool in its first weeks.

keyIdeas.title: Tokens are a cost line, never a performance line
keyIdeas.body: DORA (Jun 2026): “company-wide aggregates are meaningless, and individual scores are harmful”. Token leaderboards invite “productivity theater”, with reports of developers running agents on nonsense projects to stay above average. Shopify replaced its leaderboard with a usage dashboard and “circuit breakers” that catch runaway agents and flag abnormal daily spend spikes. Meta dropped token counters from reviews (Sep 2026). In LeadDev’s AI Impact Report 2026 (a survey of engineering leaders), 58% said token usage metrics are ineffective. Two Rhino specifics: Claude Code’s Team and Enterprise analytics include a built-in leaderboard, so don’t share that view (rule 6); and contribution metrics are not available in orgs with ZDR, so the Lane B org shows usage only and its agent PRs are found by co-author trailers.

keyIdeas.title: Count dollars per merged feature, review included
keyIdeas.body: Per developer, Anthropic’s figure is about $13 per active day and $150 to $250 a month, with 90% of users under $30 a day, and agent teams use about seven times more tokens when teammates run in plan mode (Claude Code docs, Sep 2026). Per feature: $3 to $33 to merge the same OAuth device-flow feature across 23 model and harness setups, where the harness alone moved cost about 2.5x and, with the cheapest coding models, the review gate was up to 97% of the bill (Veli-Matti Vanamo, 29 runs, Jul 2026, one practitioner); $29.41 for a 4.5-hour port of an HTML5 parser (Simon Willison, Dec 2025); $124.70 and 3 h 50 min for a digital audio workstation (Anthropic, Mar 2026); under $20,000 for a C compiler written by 16 agents (Anthropic, Feb 2026). Add people’s review minutes to the bill. Spend is growing fast: DX saw median quarterly AI spend per organization go from about $1.5K to about $44K over four quarters (Jul 2026, vendor).

keyIdeas.title: Caps and forecasts before the spend
keyIdeas.body: Set limits before anything runs unattended: a workspace spend limit and alert, a budget cap on every headless run, per-user and per-group limits in the Claude apps gateway, and model pins so an alias can’t move you to a pricier model. Clouds add their own mechanics (chapter 28, Agents on AWS and Google Cloud): on Bedrock, each output token counts 10 times against your quota for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5 and Fable 5.1 and 15 times for Claude 4.8, the full output limit you ask for is reserved when a request starts (lab 3), regional endpoints cost 10% more than global ones, and application inference profiles tag spend per team. Switch off autonomous spend channels, such as AgentCore Payments, which lets agents pay for APIs. For telemetry, Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry export redacts prompt content unless you turn logging on, and Langfuse offers a HIPAA region. Ramp sets no token budgets for engineers and Uber caps each tool; both are choices, so write yours down.

In a CMU and Stanford study of a company that mandated doubling merged PRs per engineer (802 developers, 196,212 PRs, Jul 2026, a large observational study), raw output reached 2.09x, but the within-developer gain was 1.46x to 1.72x. Each reviewer’s load roughly doubled, the share of PRs with any human review fell from 89% to 68% while automated review rose from about 19% to 84%, and merge and revert rates held steady. modules.title: Governance, compliance and security

keyIdeas.title: What Anthropic’s BAA covers today
keyIdeas.body: The Claude Code CLI and Desktop local mode, with ZDR. Not cloud or web sessions, managed Code Review, Claude Code Security, Remote Control or MCP connectors. Fable models are Covered Models that need 30-day retention, so they are Lane A only. Two points are being checked with Anthropic. Its API data page says Claude Code “is not covered under HIPAA readiness” for the API arrangement, which Rhino must reconcile in writing with the account team. And Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (1 Sep 2026) plans ZDR on Fable 5 and 5.1 for eligible customers “later this fall”. Until this chapter’s matrix changes, Fable stays in Lane A.

keyIdeas.title: Two orgs, two lanes, and one route being checked
keyIdeas.body: A HIPAA-ready org and a ZDR org can’t be the same org. Lane A (code only, synthetic data) lives in the non-ZDR org, with cloud features. Lane B (PHI-adjacent) lives in the ZDR org: the CLI, Desktop local mode or the Agent SDK in our own pod, with no connectors. A third Lane B route is being checked with AWS, Google and Anthropic: Claude Code or the Agent SDK on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, in a dedicated Rhino account behind the Claude apps gateway. On those platforms Anthropic’s ZDR and HIPAA terms don’t apply; the cloud provider is the data processor and its BAA governs. The route would lose cloud sessions, routines and Code Review, which Lane B can’t use anyway. It is not policy until the vendors confirm in writing (chapter 28, Agents on AWS and Google Cloud).

keyIdeas.title: Every vendor and every surface, with a date
keyIdeas.body: A vendor’s own list is where you start, never where you stop. AWS’s HIPAA-eligible list (3 Sep 2026) includes Bedrock, AgentCore and Kiro (except Kiro Web) but not Amazon Q Developer. Google’s BAA page (17 Sep 2026) covers Agent Platform, Gemini Code Assist and Antigravity in Gemini Enterprise but not Gemini CLI, and it lists products, not models, so Claude’s coverage there needs a written answer. AgentCore’s docs say it “may use and store your content to improve your service experience or performance”. Cursor Cloud Agents are BAA-eligible on Enterprise with Privacy Mode, self-hosted machines aren’t listed, and SpaceX closed its purchase of Cursor’s maker in August 2026, so re-read the terms. Treat Codex cloud as not covered. Front-end work leaks in its own ways: Claude in Chrome shares your browser’s login state and its GIFs capture account details on logged-in pages, Chrome DevTools for agents sends trace URLs to Google’s CrUX service unless you turn that off, screenshots and Figma files can hold real data, and prototyping tools (v0, Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Figma Make, Claude Design) are data processors too; Claude Design’s BAA coverage is not verified. A vendor’s SOC 2 report is not a BAA.

keyIdeas.title: Segregation of duties as settings, not trust
keyIdeas.body: SOC 2 CC8.1 needs independence between whoever initiated a change and whoever approved it, with an audit trail. The engineer who prompted the agent is the initiator; CC8.1 doesn’t require that a human wrote the code. Make the rule mechanical so it leaves evidence: a GitHub ruleset that requires approval of the most recent reviewable push (someone other than the last pusher), deployment environments with “Prevent self-review” and secrets locked until a reviewer approves, and the Copilot cloud agent’s built-in rule that the person who asked for its PR can’t approve it. Since 9 Jun 2026 GitHub also runs CodeQL, dependency checks and secret scanning on code from third-party agents such as Claude and Codex before their PR is finalized, on by default. Chapter 26, Keep CI safe when agents run in it, builds these settings in a lab.

keyIdeas.title: Threat-model the agents and the code they write
keyIdeas.body: Review every agent workflow against the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026): goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-trust exploitation and rogue agents. Give each agent its own identity with a narrow scope and a way to revoke it, never a shared key; NIST’s AI Agent Standards Initiative (17 Feb 2026) and the NCCoE concept paper on agent identity and authorization are the references. Then the code: correct is not secure (BaxBench above), and in SWE-chat’s study of 6,000 real sessions (Apr 2026) agent-written code added more security vulnerabilities. So review agent code against the OWASP Top 10:2025 and the API Security Top 10, where broken object-level authorization comes first (chapter 14, Keep agent-written back ends safe). labs.title: A dated vendor and data-flow matrix
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): list every AI tool and surface you or your team touch: the CLI, IDE plugins, cloud agents, review bots, browser tools, each MCP server, prototyping tools and any cloud endpoint such as Bedrock. For each one, open the vendor’s own page and record who processes the data, the retention or ZDR setting, the BAA or HIPAA status, whether PHI could reach it (logs, screenshots, a logged-in browser, a pasted thread) and the lane, with the page’s URL and the date you read it. Write “being checked” wherever the page is silent, and turn each one into a question for the vendor. At Rhino: add Byte (Rhino’s AI review bot), the Vanta-to-Jira security pipeline and every MCP server; write Lane A and Lane B as managed settings in the two orgs (availableModels, deniedModels, availableModelsMatch set to exact, maxEffortLevel, connectors off and bypass mode disabled in the ZDR org) with the list of Lane B repos and paths; the security team and the Anthropic account team sign off each cell.

labs.title: Evidence an auditor can check
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): in a repo whose PRs you can read (your scratch repo from chapter 26 or a public project), run `gh pr list --state merged --limit 50 --json number,author,mergedBy,reviews,commits`, and have your agent write a script that flags every PR approved only by its author, by its last pusher or by a bot, and every commit with an agent `Co-Authored-By` trailer that merged without a human approval. Then write a one-page control map: CC8.1 (change management), CC6.1 (logical access) and CC7.2 (monitoring), each with the setting that enforces it, the evidence file and who collects it. At Rhino: the evidence goes to Vanta, Rhino’s compliance tool, and every bot identity is listed with its scopes.
labs.output: A self-approval report and a one-page control map

labs.title: Threat-model one agent workflow
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): pick one agent workflow you run or plan, such as a CI review bot, a ticket-triage agent or a night-shift run. Walk it through the ten OWASP agentic risks: for each, one line on how it could happen here, one mitigation and the test that would prove the mitigation works. Add an identity section: whose token the agent uses, its scopes, where it is stored and how you revoke it. Then run one test for real: plant a harmless canary instruction in the workflow’s input (for example, a ticket line asking agents to end their reply with a code word) and record what the agent did. At Rhino: walk the remote-agent pod design, and red-team the guardian hook from chapter 20, Let agents work alone, safely.
labs.output: A one-page threat model with a mitigation and a test per risk, and the canary result

modules.why: Anthropic’s BAA covers Claude Code only in the CLI and in Desktop local mode, and only with zero data retention (ZDR); cloud sessions, routines, Claude Tag, Remote Control and self-hosted environments are off under ZDR. That line decides which tools each kind of work may use, and in 2026 it kept moving. Claude reached every Bedrock customer with AWS as the data processor (Apr 2026), Anthropic launched Claude Platform on AWS without HIPAA readiness (May 2026), Google renamed Vertex AI to Agent Platform (Apr 2026), and Anthropic announced plans for ZDR on its Fable models (Sep 2026). The code agents write needs checks of its own: on the BaxBench back-end benchmark, the top model was 86.2% correct but only 56.1% correct and secure (leaderboard, Sep 2026). This chapter is the lead’s version of chapter 4, Safety basics for every developer: the full matrix, the evidence and the questions still being checked. For you as a developer, it explains which tool you may open for a given ticket, and why your own approval never counts on your agent’s PR.

modules.title: Operating model and charter

keyIdeas.title: Start from evidence, not a maturity slogan
keyIdeas.body: Dan Shapiro’s L0 to L5 scale is a useful shared vocabulary for how much an agent does alone. His claim that most organisations stall at L3 is his opinion, not a measurement, so don’t plan on it. Use checks with evidence behind them. DORA’s seven AI capabilities are a clear and communicated AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, strong version control, working in small batches, a user-centric focus and a quality internal platform. At repo level, the RAMP study of 441 repos (observational, Aug 2026) found agents added 28 to 38% more commits at every maturity level, but agent-first repos with no committed AI configuration saw about twice the rise in complexity (+53% against +27%) and 1.7 times the rise in warnings; 73.8% of AI config files were committed once and never touched again. Amazon’s faster teams shared five habits: they wrote down what lived in their heads for the agents and pruned it as models improved, expected to get slower first, fed agents work instead of babysitting them, fixed the intent in a document before arguing with generated code, and shifted testing left with local mocks (Clare Liguori, AWS, Aug 2026). Its headline case, six senior engineers rebuilding the Bedrock inference engine in 76 days against an estimate of 30 engineers for 12 to 18 months, is one team that she herself calls not reproducible.

keyIdeas.title: Autonomy, gate and evidence per work type
keyIdeas.body: One level for everything is the most common charter mistake. A draft for Rhino: L4 for dependency bumps and flaky tests, L3 for features, L2 for the on-prem client and gRPC, which are hard to verify and run at customer sites. Each work type also names its gate on the seven-stage loop (chapter 3, How we build software with AI agents), the evidence that gate needs and who reviews it. Published models are good to borrow from: AWS’s AI-DLC (inception, construction, operations) and Red Hat’s plan, build, verify and ship with humans approving the spec and the final PR. Raise a level only when the numbers say the gate holds (keep rate, revert rate, review findings), and re-check the levels with each new model.

keyIdeas.title: Buy the harness, build a thin platform, and plan for churn
keyIdeas.body: The companies that scaled agents bought or adopted a harness and built only their own layer: triggers, sandboxes, credentials, context and measurement. Stripe forked Goose and built devboxes and a 400-tool Toolshed; its Minions produce more than 1,000 merged PRs a week, all reviewed by humans (Stripe, Feb 2026). HubSpot runs one Kubernetes Job per session, the closest match to Rhino’s remote-agents project. Dropbox’s Nova snapshots per commit, and Uber generates tools from 10,000+ interface definitions and drove its shift with a cross-functional tiger team. Tools change under you: Amazon Q Developer’s IDE plugins reach end of support on 30 April 2027, with Kiro as the replacement; Gemini CLI moved free and AI Pro and Ultra users to Antigravity CLI on 18 June 2026; and SpaceX closed its purchase of Cursor’s maker in August 2026, so its terms need a fresh look. The charter therefore names one owner for a monthly check: every new model or tool runs on the same five to ten sealed tasks from chapter 21, Test your agents like code, before it is let in or pinned.

keyIdeas.title: Team shape and roles
keyIdeas.body: A small platform team in a hub-and-spoke model, with one champion per squad. Roles are merging: Anthropic’s 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report says the engineer’s value moves to system architecture, agent coordination, quality evaluation and breaking problems down; PMs build prototypes and evals (Cat Wu, Anthropic, Apr 2026) and designers ship code (Jenny Wen, Anthropic, Mar 2026). Anthropic’s own staff use Claude in about 60% of their work but can fully delegate only 0 to 20% of it (132 people surveyed, Dec 2025, one company’s data). The rules don’t bend for any role: whoever starts an agent run owns its PR and someone else approves it, a PM or a designer included (rules 3 and 5). Chapter 31 shows how to shape one team around who checks the work.

keyIdeas.title: Plan for people, not only tools
keyIdeas.body: The charter makes four people decisions. Hiring: pick an interview stance on purpose, whether AI-assisted interviews (Canva, Jun 2025), one AI-enabled round in a classic loop (Meta, since Oct 2025) or no AI in live interviews unless stated (Anthropic); chapter 31 has a round to copy. Juniors: employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below trend, mostly through fewer hires (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, payroll data, revised Aug 2026), and 62% of leaders expect fewer junior hires (LeadDev AI Impact Report 2026, a survey), while Shopify went the other way and grew its intern capacity from 75 to 1,000 (First Round, Jul 2025). This course’s view, an opinion: keep a junior intake, because the people who will review agents in three years have to learn now. Fair review load: in the CMU and Stanford “2x mandate” study (802 developers, Jul 2026), each reviewer’s load roughly doubled, commented reviews stayed flat and silent approvals roughly doubled, so measure review load per person, spread it with a rota, and count review and harness work in performance reviews. Sceptics: about 30% of developers trust AI output “a little” or “not at all” (DORA, 2025), so give sceptics a seat in the first cohort and a standing slot to report what went wrong. Tokens never measure people (rule 6); Meta took token counters out of its performance reviews in September 2026 (The Decoder, citing The Information).

labs.title: Baseline one team, honestly
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): pick one team and repo you know well, your own or an open-source project you follow. Score DORA’s seven AI capabilities from 0 to 2, with one line of evidence each: a written AI policy, a committed CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, typical PR size, a paved path for new services. labs.title: Autonomy, gate and evidence per work type
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): list the eight to ten kinds of work your team does, such as dependency bumps, flaky tests, a React component, a Django endpoint, a migration, an infrastructure change and anything that runs at customer sites. For each, write an autonomy level, the gate it must pass, the evidence that gate needs and who reviews it. Test the table on one ticket you shipped: place each step on the seven stages from chapter 3 and circle each gate that left no evidence. If you have time, run the same ticket through AWS’s aidlc-workflows and note what it adds. Back one part with data: in any repo with a few months of reviews, run `gh pr list --state merged --limit 200 --json number,author,reviews` and have your agent count reviews per reviewer. Report the spread, such as “the top two reviewers did 60% of all reviews”, not a ranking, and write one rota rule that would even it out. modules.why: The tool is rarely the variable; the way of working is. Amazon followed 50 ordinary teams for most of a year, and about 90% of them used the same coding assistant. Half improved their deployment velocity by less than 3x. The other half, which had changed how they worked, reached a median of 4.5x and sometimes more than 10x (AWS about its own teams, Jun and Aug 2026, vendor data). DORA calls AI “an amplifier”: in its 2025 research (a survey of about 5,000 people), higher AI adoption went with higher throughput and higher instability. So the operating model decides whether agents speed a company up or only fill its review queue. For you as a developer, the charter decides which work you may hand to an agent, who reviews it, how you are interviewed and how your work is measured. Chapter 31, The AI team lead’s job, runs one team this way; this chapter sets the rules for the whole company, and chapter 36, Teach the whole company, rolls them out.

modules.title: Teaching the whole company

keyIdeas.title: Champions first, sceptics included
keyIdeas.body: Start with a two-week champions cohort of six to eight people that includes sceptics, a PM and a designer. Anthropic’s champion kit is a channel, a weekly show-and-tell, shared skills, a team onboarding guide and 15-minute pairing sessions. Block paired a champions program with an engineer AI maturity model and work to make repos ready for agents (Angie Jones, Apr 2026 talk, one company’s account). Sceptics belong in the first group because about 30% of developers trust AI output “a little” or “not at all” (DORA, 2025), and their objections are your best test cases. Aditya Khandelwal of Amazon’s AGI Lab gets the basics right and ships one high-value skill before he turns to winning over the sceptics (Aug 2026).

keyIdeas.title: Cohorts that ship, with role tracks
keyIdeas.body: Engineering cohorts of 10 to 12 people over five weeks, with a daily 20-minute champion stand-up and no sprint talk. Zocdoc’s five sessions were 101, deterministic guardrails, making it yours, the full orchestra and the moonshot. Role tracks keep everyone on the same loop: PMs prototype and write evals, designers take a prototype to a PR with stories (chapter 16, From quick prototype to real product), and QA owns the checks every screen must pass (chapter 12, Let agents check every screen); an engineer who is not the requester approves each of their PRs. Bloomberg built a paved path, one standard way to build and share agent tools, and backed it with training and communities (Lei Zhang, Dec 2025). Meta’s Reality Labs moved tool use from 50% to over 90% through community and platform integration (Ian Thomas, Jun 2026, one organization’s account).

keyIdeas.title: A clear stance beats a usage mandate
keyIdeas.body: This is the course’s view, an opinion backed by the case files below. DORA lists a “clear and communicated AI stance” among its seven AI capabilities, because “ambiguity creates risk”. Mandates buy speed and pay for it later: Coinbase told engineers to onboard by the end of the week or attend a Saturday meeting, and fired some who had no good reason (Aug 2025); Shopify made AI use “a fundamental expectation” and ran a token leaderboard that later became a usage dashboard with circuit breakers; Meta graded AI-driven impact, got tokenmaxxing, and removed token counters from reviews. The other road works too: a Zapier hackathon moved adoption from 10% to 50% (CEO interview, Apr 2026), and Ramp’s own background agent wrote about 30% of merged PRs within a couple of months with “no mandate”, by working in public channels, and over half by February 2026 (Ramp’s blog, and a Modal video). When Amazon faced a Financial Times report tying an AWS interruption to its Kiro agent, it blamed “misconfigured access controls” and added “mandatory peer review for production access” (Amazon, Feb 2026): the gate was the fix, not the tool.

keyIdeas.title: Expect the dip, and plan the refresh
keyIdeas.body: DORA’s ROI report (Apr 2026) is built around the “productivity dip” of a new rollout, and AWS tells its teams the first two weeks feel slower (Jun 2026). Rollouts elsewhere also saw uneven cohorts and content going stale within weeks. So plan a monthly refresh from day one: an owner for each part of the path, stale videos retired, new ones added, and each one marked as checked against its transcript or only its chapter list.

keyIdeas.title: Protect juniors, and the people doing the reviews
keyIdeas.body: Juniors use the Learning output style and do the weekly comprehension check (chapter 10, Your workday with an AI agent). In Anthropic’s randomized study of 52 mostly junior developers (Jan 2026), those using AI scored 50% on a quiz against 67% for those coding by hand, and those who asked for explanations kept their scores at 65% or more. Kent Beck argues that juniors who learn with a “genie” become profitable sooner, if they still learn. Hiring is shrinking at the entry level: employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below trend (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, revised Aug 2026), so this course’s view is to keep a junior intake and put juniors in cohorts from the start. A rollout also loads the reviewers: in the CMU and Stanford “2x mandate” study, each reviewer’s load roughly doubled (Jul 2026). Train reviewers along with writers, and ask about fatigue in 1:1s; Block’s talk ends on “the human cost of success”.

keyIdeas.title: Certifications, for those who want them
keyIdeas.body: Anthropic’s exams run through Pearson VUE: 60 questions, with a pass mark of 720. Check Partner Network eligibility before booking. The free Anthropic Academy courses cover most of the ground, and a badge from shipped work shows more than a certificate.

labs.title: Plan cohort one
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): design a two-week champions cohort for a team you know, or for an imagined company of 40 engineers. Pick six to eight champion profiles, including at least one sceptic, a PM, a designer and a junior. Schedule the sessions on this course’s chapters by number, for example chapters 1 to 4 in the first week and chapters 5 to 8 in the second, with a daily 20-minute stand-up and a weekly show-and-tell. For each person, write the one real task they will ship by the end, and who will review it. At Rhino: real names and dates, Lane A tasks on synthetic data only, and a reviewer who is not the requester for every PR.
labs.output: A dated cohort plan with one shipped task per person

labs.title: A badge rubric that counts shipping
labs.body: Solo (about 45 min): write one badge per part of the path, each earned only by shipped work with evidence. For example, the “Work with one agent, well” badge needs a real ticket shipped with an evidence block, a skill with an eval (chapter 8, Teach the agent with skills, and chapter 21, Test your agents like code) and one kept night-shift run; write the others from each part’s Ship it tasks. Then earn the first badge yourself on any repo, and ask a peer to score your evidence against the rubric. At Rhino: publish the rubric where every cohort can see it, and never award a badge for videos watched.
labs.output: A published rubric and one scored example

labs.title: Refresh the content, and hear a sceptic
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): pick five videos or readings from this course. For each, check that it is still online, that the settings and commands it shows still exist, and whether there is a newer source; mark each as checked against its transcript or only its chapter list, with the date. Write the monthly refresh checklist with an owner for each part of the path. Then spend 30 minutes with a colleague who doubts agents: collect their top three objections, answer each with evidence from this course, and put any you can’t answer on the refresh list. At Rhino: the refresh owner posts the log in the champions channel each month.
labs.output: A refresh log for five items and an objections log with answers

checks.q: What did Zocdoc measure?
checks.a: What people built, not hours of training.

checks.q: Mandate or voluntary?
checks.a: Neither alone, in this course’s view. A clear, communicated stance with a good paved path and visible wins from peers: DORA lists a clear AI stance among its seven AI capabilities, and Microsoft’s data shows use spreading from person to person.

checks.q: What does the first badge, “Work with one agent, well”, require?
checks.a: A real ticket shipped with an evidence block, a skill with an eval, and one kept night-shift run.

checks.q: Why put a sceptic in the champions cohort?
checks.a: About 30% of developers trust AI output little or not at all, so a sceptic’s objections show the weak spots early, and a convinced sceptic persuades others better than a fan.

watchOut: Training that ends when the cohort ends.
Badges for watching videos instead of shipping.
A usage target, in tokens or sessions, as the goal of the rollout.
Cohorts that train more writers but no new reviewers.

modules.watchTime: 27 min core, 1 h 18 min with electives
modules.goal: Roll the practice out so it lasts: champions first with sceptics among them, small cohorts that ship real work, role tracks for PM, design and QA, a clear stance instead of a usage mandate, room for juniors and for the people doing the reviews, a monthly refresh, and badges earned by shipping.
modules.why: Adoption spreads through people, not memos. In Microsoft’s early-2026 rollout of Claude Code and Copilot CLI to tens of thousands of engineers, first use spread through social networks, whether people kept using the tools followed how much they coded rather than who they were, and adopters merged about 24% more PRs, a lift that lasted (a telemetry study over four months, Jul 2026; merged PRs are a proxy, not value). Zocdoc trained 300 engineers in three cohorts over six weeks and measured what people built, not hours of training. The mandates of 2025 and 2026 taught the same lesson the hard way: Coinbase’s one-week deadline, Shopify’s token leaderboard that became a usage dashboard, and Meta’s token counters, removed from performance reviews in September 2026. For you as a developer, this chapter is what to expect when your cohort starts, what you will ship to earn a badge, and how to raise a doubt without being seen as against the change.
