modules.headlineSrc: 300 · engineers in three cohorts over six weeks

modules.title: One feature, idea to production

keyIdeas.title: Two tracks, one loop
keyIdeas.body: The solo track runs on any small full-stack app you can run locally, a public sample app or your own project, with synthetic data only; anyone can do it, in about four hours spread over three labs. You play every role, so you review your own stack the next morning and note where, at work, someone else must approve (rule 3). The team track runs at Rhino on a real Lane A ticket: factory-seeded data, a teammate who is not the requester approves every PR, the pipeline deploys, and the builder runs in the remote-agent pod when it is available or in local worktrees until then.

keyIdeas.title: Plan: spec, contract, slices
keyIdeas.body: Size the spec to the risk (chapter 5, Tell the agent what you want), and write acceptance checks that become tests. Settle the data model and the contract before any slice code, because they hurt most to change (chapter 15, Build a whole feature with agents). A slice can run in parallel only if it touches different files and waits on nothing unfinished. At Rhino, a program-design doc comes first for any change to the gRPC contract, the SDK’s public API or PHI-handling code.

keyIdeas.title: Build and merge: parallel slices, one stack, one preview
keyIdeas.body: Two builders in their own worktrees, the UI against a mock of the contract and the API for real, with checks they can’t edit and one contract test that runs against both. The work ships as a stack of small PRs (contract, migration and API, UI, then the flag), each with its own evidence, and a preview environment lets the reviewer try it before it merges. Agents open PRs; pipelines deploy (rule 4).

keyIdeas.title: Infrastructure goes through the same gate
keyIdeas.body: One infrastructure change, a Terraform or OpenTofu module or a Helm value, travels the loop like code: a saved plan, its JSON, a policy check, a short summary a person can read, and an apply that only the pipeline runs (chapter 27, Let agents write infrastructure code). “It validates” means little: in an August 2026 benchmark, the best model’s Terraform passed the Checkov scanner only 23.1% of the time. Customer-side infrastructure is never applied by an agent.

keyIdeas.title: Release, verify, learn
keyIdeas.body: The feature merges with its flag off, the pipeline deploys it, and a deploy check proves it on the preview or on QA before the flag turns on for anyone (chapter 30, Agents after release). Then write a postmortem even if nothing broke: what repeated, what surprised you, where work waited. The project isn’t finished until one harness change (a lint rule, a test, a hook or a skill line) ships because of it (rule 7).

keyIdeas.title: Measure every stage
keyIdeas.body: Log time, agent dollars and your own minutes per stage, and where work waited. Report dollars and minutes per merged feature (chapter 33, Measure results and cost), not per seat, and compare your loop map before and after.

labs.title: Plan one feature: spec, contract and slices
labs.body: Solo (about 60 min): pick a small full-stack app you can run locally, such as a public sample with a React or Next.js front end, a Django, FastAPI or Node back end and Postgres, or your own project, with synthetic data only. Choose a real feature that crosses layers, such as “export a filtered list as CSV” or “add a notes field to a record”. Write a one-page spec: What, Why and How, three to five acceptance checks that will become tests, and the line “PHI data flow: none”. Ask a fresh agent session with no write tools to research the code and propose the data model and the contract (an OpenAPI path or a typed client interface), then review and fix the contract yourself. Split the work into slices, mark the two that can run in parallel because they touch different files, and name the one infrastructure change the feature needs, such as a new setting, a storage bucket, a Helm value or a Terraform variable. At Rhino (team track): a real Lane A ticket, acceptance checks the requester confirms, a program-design doc if it touches the gRPC contract, the SDK’s public API or PHI-handling code, and the code owner’s sign-off on the plan.
labs.output: A spec with acceptance checks, a reviewed contract file and a slice plan with two parallel slices marked

labs.title: Two slices in parallel, one stack, one preview
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): give each parallel slice its own git worktree and agent session, with the contract file and one test per slice that the builder may not edit. The UI builder works against a mock of the contract, the API builder writes the real handler and migration, and one contract test runs against both. Ship the result as a stack of three or four small PRs (contract, migration and API, UI, then a flag that defaults to off), with GitHub’s stacked PRs or branches that each target the one below, and give every PR its own evidence: test output, a screenshot or clip, the contract test. Open a preview environment for the top of the stack: a free preview deploy for the front end, or a CI job that starts the app with docker compose and runs the acceptance checks against it. Log time, agent dollars and your own minutes per stage. You are the only person in the solo track, so review the stack yourself the next morning, and note that at work someone else must approve it. At Rhino: a teammate who is not the requester approves each layer; the builders run in the remote-agent pod if it is available, or in local worktrees on factory-seeded data; and the upper layers get no frontend CI or preview links until they target main, so attach local test output.
labs.output: A stack of small PRs with evidence, a preview link or recording, and a stage log

labs.title: Infrastructure through the gate, a deploy check and your postmortem
labs.body: Solo (about 90 min): write the feature’s infrastructure change as code, either a Terraform or OpenTofu module (a local kind cluster with the Kubernetes provider needs no cloud account, as in chapter 27) or a Helm value. Put it through the plan gate: `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, `terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json`, then `checkov` or `conftest test plan.json` with at least one policy of your own, and a five-line summary from a fresh agent session with no write tools. Apply it only from a pipeline job, never from your laptop. Then verify the deploy with a smoke test that checks the flag is off, turns it on for one test user and runs one acceptance check against the running app. Finally write a one-page postmortem, even if nothing broke (what repeated, what surprised you, where work waited), and ship one harness change because of it in its own PR: a lint rule, a test, a hook or a skill line. At Rhino: the change goes through the release path behind an environment with “Prevent self-review”, the pipeline deploys to QA and posts the deploy check to the release thread, and customer-side infrastructure, such as the on-prem agent’s chart, is never applied by an agent.
labs.output: A saved plan with its policy results and summary, a deploy check result, a postmortem and one merged harness PR

checks.q: When is the final project finished?
checks.a: When one harness change has shipped because of something in your postmortem, and your loop map is redrawn with real times.

checks.q: What evidence should the infrastructure change carry?
checks.a: The saved plan and its JSON, the policy results, a short summary a person can read, and proof that only the pipeline applied it.

checks.q: In the solo track you are the only person. Who approves, and what changes at Rhino?
checks.a: You review your own stack the next morning and note it as a gap. At Rhino the requester never approves: a teammate who is not you approves every PR, and the pipeline deploys.

checks.q: Why build two slices against a contract instead of one big PR?
checks.a: The contract lets the UI and API builders work in parallel without touching the same files, a contract test proves the two fit, and small stacked PRs can really be reviewed.

watchOut: A toy feature. Pick one that crosses at least the UI, the API and the data.
Skipping the learn stage.
An infrastructure change applied from your laptop “just this once”.
Real data in a preview environment.
modules.projects: Remote agents, R&D brain, Tests & fakes, Skills & practices
modules.watchTime: 25 min core, 40 min with electives
modules.goal: Take one feature from idea to production through all seven stages, on your own first, with evidence at every gate: a right-sized spec, a reviewed contract, two slices built in parallel, a stack of small PRs, a preview environment, an infrastructure change with plan and policy evidence, deploy verification, and one harness fix that comes from your own postmortem. Then run the same loop at Rhino on a real Lane A ticket, with a teammate approving, and show what it takes to repeat.
modules.why: A specialist is someone who has run the whole loop on real work and can show the evidence, not someone who has watched the talks. The pieces are all in earlier chapters; the final project is where they meet and where your weak link shows. Most of the risk sits after the code is written: in NBER’s study of 500,000+ developers, autonomous agents raised commits by 240% but releases by only 30% (2026). Stripe’s agents produce more than 1,000 merged PRs a week, every one reviewed by a person, from devboxes with no internet or production access (Stripe, Feb 2026). Your feature is small, but it has the same shape, and at the end you redraw the loop map from chapter 3, How we build software with AI agents, with real times.

shipIt.title: Final demo
shipIt.body: Ten minutes: the evidence pack stage by stage, your loop map from chapter 3 redrawn with real times and owners next to the first one, dollars and minutes per stage, the harness fix, and one change you propose to the team’s charter (chapter 35, Plan how the company uses agents) or scorecard (chapter 33). In the team track, give it to engineering leadership.

modules.headlineSrc: 7 · stages, with evidence at every gate

debates.q: Should you plan before the agent codes?

sides.claim: Stopped using plan mode
Design doc and outline before any code

debates.call: Plan in proportion to how many sessions the work spans. A visible one-line fix needs none; cross-session work needs a design doc.

debates.q: Read the plan, or read the code?

sides.claim: HumanLayer read the plans and skipped the code for 4 to 5 months, until its codebase was unusable
Open a plan-only PR and review every line

debates.call: Review the short design doc, skip the long plan, and always read the code before merge. HumanLayer tried the reverse, and rebuilt its product from scratch.

sides.claim: AI is weak at frontend work
A DOM verification contract the agent checks

debates.call: Give the agent a contract to check, not pixels to judge. Start with one screen that already has Storybook stories.

debates.q: Should the coding agent obey review bots?

sides.claim: Let the agent defer or reject bot feedback
Two bots with different jobs; the human waits for the deep one

debates.call: Bots filter and argue. A human who isn’t the requester decides, with depth set by risk tier.

sides.claim: Killed the multi-agent pipeline and consolidated to one agent
Missions: orchestrator, workers and validators

debates.call: Parallelize reading and verifying. Keep one writer unless the paths are disjoint and a mechanical check exists.

seeAlso.label: Uber’s uReview: parallel readers, one output

sides.claim: Letting the bot merge into main
Every agent PR gets human review

debates.call: Today, a human who isn’t the requester approves and merges every agent PR, which keeps SOC 2 independence. Letting an agent approve low-tier PRs is a proposal: run the tiers in shadow mode first (chapter 32, Run the team’s review and merge flow).

sides.claim: Exposes 1,000+ MCP servers to coding agents as a CLI
A gateway as the enterprise control point

debates.call: MCP for auth, governance and surfaces without a shell. A CLI where the agent has a shell. A skill for the workflow on top.

debates.q: Mandate adoption, or let it spread?

sides.claim: Tobi’s memo: AI use is a baseline expectation
No mandate: nobody was forced to use Inspect, its background agent, and it spread by working in public

debates.call: State a clear stance, give people time, good tools and public wins, and measure what they ship. No quotas and no leaderboards: when one company mandated twice the merged PRs per engineer, the share of PRs with any human review fell from 89% to 68% (CMU and Stanford, 2026).

debates.q: Is the spec the source, or scaffolding?

sides.claim: The spec is the real source. Keeping the code and deleting the prompt is like shredding the source and versioning the binary
Spec-as-source repeats model-driven development. Today, the way we write down in detail what we want is the code

debates.call: Scaffolding, kept with the PR. The code is the source of truth. The What / Why / How ticket and the acceptance checks the requester confirmed travel with the PR, each check proved by a test, and spec depth grows with risk.

debates.q: Can you ship code you haven’t read?

sides.claim: I ship code I don’t read.
Tech debt can’t be checked without reading the code, so keep unread agent code in the leaf nodes and understand the trunk

debates.call: Not at Rhino. You own every line you merge, so read it all. Leaf and trunk decide where you slow down: login, data access, API contracts and shared components are always trunk.

seeAlso.label: Dex Horthy: “there will always be alpha in reviewing something”

debates.q: Should an ops agent fix the cluster itself?

sides.claim: Agents with runbooks remediate incidents in Argo CD in minutes instead of hours
Claude is superhuman at gathering signals but confuses correlation with causation: in a KV-cache outage it kept asking for more servers

debates.call: Agents observe and diagnose with read-only access. The fix, often a revert, becomes a PR, and the pipeline deploys it. No agent holds deploy credentials, including the incident agent that found the fix.

debates.q: Spend more tokens, or measure the return?

sides.claim: Tokenmaxxing: spend tokens freely, and one builder can do the work of a whole team
The vibe has shifted from token-maxing to measuring return on investment

debates.call: Spend what the work needs, and judge it by what ships and how it holds up. Tokens are a cost line, never a performance metric. Meta graded engineers on AI-driven impact in 2026, got tokenmaxxing, and took token counts out of reviews in September.

debates.q: Many vendors’ agents, or one harness you own?

sides.claim: Agent HQ welcomes all coding agents: Claude, Codex and others side by side in GitHub
Own the harness and build one platform, not point solutions, for leverage over cost, model choice and developer experience

debates.call: One default harness, Claude Code, with a thin platform of our own around it. Another vendor’s agent must first beat it on an eval of our own tasks, and it stays in Lane A. Every agent follows the same rules: it opens PRs, and its requester never approves them.

glossary.def: A software lifecycle in which agents do much of the planning, building and checking, and humans own intent, approval and judgment.

loop.rule: A ticket in What / Why / How. A skill drafts acceptance checks at run time and the requester confirms them. They are never a Jira field.
loop.gate: The requester can say what done looks like in one sentence.

loop.who: An agent drafts, a human approves
loop.rule: Research runs without seeing the ticket, then a short design doc and a structure outline. Planning depth grows with risk and with how long the agent runs alone.
loop.gate: The code owner signs off on the design for anything above the lowest risk tier.

loop.rule: One writer per change, in its own worktree or pod, on synthetic or factory-seeded data.
loop.gate: Tests, types and lint pass before a PR opens.

loop.rule: Deterministic checks first, then reviewers with clean context. Every PR carries an evidence pack.
loop.gate: The evidence shows the change working, not a claim that it works.

loop.who: A human who is not the requester
loop.rule: The risk tier sets review depth. A human who isn’t the requester approves every PR; an agent approval lane for low-tier PRs is only a proposal.
loop.gate: SOC 2 CC8.1: the initiator and the approver are different identities.

loop.rule: Feature flags and canaries. Agents open PRs; pipelines deploy.
loop.gate: Deploy verification passes on QA before production.

loop.rule: Agents gather signals and humans orient. Every repeated failure becomes a lint rule, a test, a hook or a lookup.
loop.gate: The postmortem names the harness change that prevents a repeat.

Every module gains readings, labs and a knowledge check. Videos keep their verification status.
howBuilt: “Verified” videos were read in full from their transcripts and every segment was checked. “Chapter-based” videos were checked against YouTube’s metadata (title, channel, length) and their segments follow the creator’s chapter marks, because YouTube blocked further transcript downloads. Re-verify chapter-based picks before a cohort starts.
Vendor figures are marked as such. Numbers from vendors, surveys and single-company reports are claims, not benchmarks, and the course says so where it uses them.
